Bermuda buttercup
Oxalis pes-caprae
bermuda-buttercup		shipped
careRequired		4May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Octcomplete
3 owed to a person
  • Habitat, filled 16/10/2026 (wood sorrel and clover audit; resolves the OWED habitat line of the 13/10/2026 page sweep): Plants of South Eastern New South Wales (Lucid), 'Oxalis pes-caprae', Where found, author Betty Wood, CC BY 4.0, https://apps.lucidcentral.org/plants_se_nsw/text/entities/oxalis_pes-caprae.htm, retrieved 16/10/2026 — first sentence verbatim; its Australian distribution ('Widespread. Not in Kosciuszko NP.') omitted. This is an Australian habitat statement, not a New Zealand one; no openly licensed New Zealand habitat text was found (Flora of New Zealand's Weed tab redirects to the Taxon profile, which has none). Tags from Tools/classify_habitats.py: forest (woodland), grassland (grassy areas), urban (gardens), disturbed (arable land, roadsides); 'along waterways' is not read as wetland by the classifier. The previous native-range sentence (Pacific Bulb Society) is range, not habitat, and was removed. Not used: Useful Temperate Plants' 'Roadsides and grassy places in S. Africa' (native range).
  • Edible parts, preparation and warning, 16/10/2026 (wood sorrel and clover audit; resolves the OWED warnings line of the 13/10/2026 page sweep): Useful Temperate Plants (Ken Fern), 'Oxalis pes-caprae', https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Oxalis+pes-caprae, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, retrieved 16/10/2026 — Edible Uses 'Leaves - raw or cooked' (cited there to Hedrick, Sturtevant's Edible Plants of the World; Crowe, Native Edible Plants of New Zealand; Kermath et al.), 'A pleasant acid flavour, the make a pleasant addition to mixed salads' and 'Use in moderation', 'Flowers - raw', 'A pleasant acid flavour, they make an attractive addition to the salad bowl' (the tasting notes are Ken Fern's own), 'Root - cooked' and 'The small bulb is sometimes eaten'; General Information 'The flowers, leaves and bulbs are all edible, being gathered from the wild and consumed locally.' Known Hazards (cited to Bown, Encyclopaedia of Herbs and their Uses) is word for word the text on Useful Tropical Plants 'Oxalis corniculata' and Useful Temperate Plants 'Oxalis magellanica', so the warning is the same sentence as on creeping-wood-sorrel, shamrock-wood-sorrel and snowdrop-woodsorrel: oxalic acid, all right in small quantities but not in large amounts since it can bind the body's calcium, less after cooking, especial caution for rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity. It replaces the Wikipedia warning ('The leaves or roots are used in some parts of the world as a food, although the high levels of calcium oxalate in the plant may bear some risks. Such risks can be reduced if the plant parts are boiled first.'), from a Hazards section tagged as possibly original research and cited to a general vegetable-oxalate study; the two agree. Weeds Australia's 'mildly toxic to humans especially if eaten in large quantities' (cited above) agrees with it too. Wikipedia's runner sentence and the waterblommetjiebredie sentence are kept after the Useful Temperate Plants text. Not used: its cultivation, propagation and weed notes.
  • Shipped-entries sweep 03/11/2026: leftover 'OWED' drafting text reworded; harvestEthics is required only on native entries.

  • Edible parts, preparation and warning: Wikipedia, 'Oxalis corniculata', Uses section (revision 1368886676, 11/08/2026; CC BY-SA 4.0), cited there to Lee Allen Peterson, Edible Wild Plants (Houghton Mifflin, 1977), p. 104 — leaves edible with a tangy lemon taste; drink of leaves infused in hot water about 10 minutes, sweetened and chilled; 'Any woodsorrel is safe in low dosages, but if eaten in large quantities over a length of time can inhibit calcium absorption'. Useful Tropical Plants (Ken Fern), 'Oxalis corniculata', https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Oxalis+corniculata, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, retrieved 15/10/2026 — leaves raw or cooked, flowers raw; added to salads, cooked as a potherb with milder greens or used to sour other foods; 'very small and fiddly to harvest'; Known Hazards (cited to Bown, Encyclopaedia of Herbs and their Uses): not to be eaten in large amounts since oxalic acid can bind the body's calcium, less after cooking, especial caution for rheumatism, arthritis, gout, kidney stones or hyperacidity. This replaces the OWED warnings line written when the recipes were added; those recipe pages' warnings agree with it. That they look alike: Wild Food UK, 'Pink-Sorrel' (Oxalis articulata page; all rights reserved, facts only), https://www.wildfooduk.com/wild-plants/pink-sorrel/, retrieved 16/10/2026 — names Pale Pink-sorrel (O. incarnata) among the pink-flowered Oxalis it calls 'all too similar' to pink-sorrel. Petal lengths for O. incarnata outside New Zealand: Flora of Tasmania Online, Oxalidaceae (12–20 mm), https://flora.tmag.tas.gov.au/vascular-families/oxalidaceae/, and Plants of South Eastern New South Wales (10–22 mm, CC BY 4.0, cited above), retrieved 16/10/2026; the Tasmanian key also separates O. incarnata ('Stems well developed and leafy') from species with 'Stems absent or very short, never leafy'. Every test: Flora of New Zealand Online (Webb et al. 1988; CC BY 3.0 NZ), retrieved 16/10/2026: 'Oxalis incarnata', https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Oxalis-incarnata.html; 'Oxalis articulata', https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Oxalis-articulata.html. 'Almost hairless' is Flora's 'almost glabrous'. Ranges overlap: both are Exotic in New Zealand (Flora) and shamrock wood sorrel's habitat text (Plants of South Eastern NSW) names gardens, roadsides and other disturbed areas; Flora of Tasmania (cited above) gives O. articulata 'along roadsides, in waste places and some cultivated areas', and pale-pink wood sorrel's habitat text names roadsides and disturbed sites (the owner's own text since 16/10/2026; it was Plants of South Eastern NSW's when the card was written). Risk edible on cards opening pale-pink wood sorrel: its edibility is recorded only in all-rights-reserved, species-specific sources (Knox, Wild Picnic; Heartland Folk — see the OWED and web-search lines on that entry); Calflora's 'Do not eat' is a genus-wide flag. Owner to confirm. The owner has since written that page's edible parts in their own words ('Leaves, flowers and stems.'), which the risk matches; its preparation and warnings are still owed. Risk edible on the card opening shamrock wood sorrel: when the card was written its own page had no edible parts and the basis was Wild Food UK's O. articulata page (cited above), 'The leaves, stem and flowers are edible' — all rights reserved, species-specific. Since 16/10/2026 its page lists edible parts from Useful Tropical Plants 'Oxalis articulata' (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, species-specific), which supports the risk.

Beach spinach

beach-spinach		shipped

1 owed to a person
  • OWED, a person's sentence — warnings: Diego Bonetto, 'Native spinach' (all rights reserved; https://www.diegobonetto.com/blog/native-spinach), covering both T. tetragonioides and T. implexicoma, says the leaves contain oxalic acid, are not to be eaten raw in large quantities, and are blanched one to two minutes with the water discarded; people with a history of kidney stones are to eat them in moderation. No openly licensed source says this of T. trigyna, so the warning is not on the page. SEARCH, 10/10/2026: the open text on oxalates is all about T. tetragonioides — Wikipedia, 'Tetragonia tetragonioides' (CC BY-SA 4.0) says its medium to low oxalate levels are removed by blanching one minute and rinsing in cold water. Wikipedia's 'Tetragonia' genus article and 'Tetragonia implexicoma' say nothing on oxalates. The all-rights-reserved sources also describe T. tetragonioides, and disagree on the blanch: Warndu 10–15 seconds (https://warndu.com/blogs/first-nations-food-guide/get-your-warrigal-greens), ABC Organic Gardener about one minute, ANPSA three to four minutes with the water discarded, calling the oxalic acid high, and ASNSW about three minutes (https://anpsa.org.au/plant_profiles/tetragonia-tetragonioides/). Quoting a sentence about one species on another's page would be the inference this guide leaves to a person, so nothing was carried across. The owner searched as well on 10/10/2026 and found no warning for this species.

Checked against Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, legislation.govt.nz, https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1975/0116/latest/whole.html, retrieved 01/11/2026: Schedule 1 (Class A) lists "Psilocine" and "Psilocybine" and, in clause 5, "Substances containing any proportion of a substance mentioned in clause 1", so a mushroom containing them is itself a Class A drug; s 7(1)(a) makes it an offence to "procure or have in his possession" a controlled drug, and s 7(2)(a) sets "imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months or to a fine not exceeding $1,000 or to both" for Class A; s 6(2)(a) sets "imprisonment for life" for dealing, which includes "produce or manufacture" (s 6(1)(b)) and "supply" (s 6(1)(c)).

Alexanders Smyrnium olusatrum 6 recipes

Alexanders soup

Serves 6

Ingredients
  • 4 large heads of alexanders, stems peeled
  • 1 large parsnip
  • 1 bunch of wild garlic or wild leeks
  • 6 strands of dulse
  • 2 onions
  • 1 tbsp coconut oil
  • 2 litres good stock
  • 1 tbsp birch bolete or porcini powder
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Lightly scrape the alexanders stems and the parsnip with a potato peeler to take off the outer fibres, and trim any roots off the wild garlic.
  2. Chop the onions and fry them gently in the coconut oil until translucent.
  3. Add the chopped parsnip and fry 3 minutes, then add the stock and the rest of the ingredients.
  4. Bring to the boil and simmer 10 minutes.
  5. Take off the heat, let it cool a little and blend.
  6. Season with salt, pepper and the bolete powder, and reheat to serve, garnished with a sprig of alexanders leaf.

Candied alexanders stems

Makes roughly 120 g

Ingredients
  • 200 g alexanders stems
  • 5 mm–1.5 cm thick
  • 100 g golden or brown granulated sugar
Method
  1. Wash, dry and finely chop the stems.
  2. Cook in a heavy-based pan over medium-high heat for about 8 minutes, until the liquid they give off has gone.
  3. Stir in the sugar and cook a further 10 minutes, until it crystallises around the pieces.
  4. Cool in the pan, then store in a dry jar — they keep about 6 months.

Alexander seeded bread

Ingredients
  • 1 heaped tbsp alexander seeds
  • 500 g white or wholemeal flour (or half of each)
  • a pinch of sea salt
  • 1 tsp quick yeast
  • 1 tsp sugar or honey
  • 400 ml warm water
  • 15 ml olive oil (optional)
Method
  1. Grind or chop the seeds roughly — you want texture, not powder; dry-roasting them at 140 °C for 10–20 minutes first makes them easier to grind, so long as they do not burn.
  2. Mix them through the flour and salt.
  3. Dissolve the yeast and honey in the warm water, stir into the dry mix and combine well.
  4. Knead about 10 minutes, until the dough springs back when pressed.
  5. Leave covered somewhere warm until doubled, knock it back, drop it into an oiled tin and prove again until doubled.
  6. Bake at 200 °C for 40–45 minutes, until the loaf sounds hollow tapped underneath.
  7. Rest 10 minutes in the tin, then cool on a rack before slicing.

View source recipe

Alexander and orange shortbread

Makes about 25

Ingredients
  • 100 g salted butter
  • 40 g demerara sugar
  • a heaped tsp of orange zest
  • 1 tsp roughly ground alexander seeds
  • 125 g plain flour
  • 1/4 tsp baking powder
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180 °C (160 °C fan) and grease a large tray.
  2. Cream the butter and sugar, then beat in the zest and seeds.
  3. Mix the flour and baking powder separately and work them in, stopping as soon as it comes together — overworking makes the shortbread tough.
  4. Flatten the dough to roughly 20 x 15 cm and cut about 25 rectangles.
  5. Lift them onto the tray with a palette knife, at least 1 cm apart, and prick each with a fork.
  6. Bake 8–10 minutes, until light brown.
  7. Cool 5 minutes before moving them to a rack.

They keep a week in an airtight tin.

Alexander seed and chocolate truffles

Built from leftover alexander seed cake.

Ingredients
  • 150 g of the cake (undrizzled)
  • 125 g mascarpone or another soft cream cheese
  • 120 g dark cooking chocolate
  • 1/2–1 tsp roughly ground alexander seeds if you want more of them
Method
  1. Crumble the cake into small pieces rather than crumbs and work in the cheese and seeds.
  2. Roll into balls about 2.5 cm across on greaseproof paper and chill for an hour.
  3. Melt the chocolate in a bowl set over a little simmering water, taking it off the heat when about half has melted and letting the rest come on its own.
  4. Dip each ball with a teaspoon until fully coated, return it to the paper, and leave to set hard.

They keep several days.

Apple mint Mentha suaveolens 2 recipes

Apple mint jelly

Ingredients
  • A kilo of green cooking apples
  • a small bunch of apple mint
  • 250 ml cider vinegar
  • 500 g sugar for every 500 ml of juice
  • 60 ml finely chopped apple mint leaves
Method
  1. Simmer a kilo of green cooking apples, quartered but not peeled or cored, with a small bunch of apple mint under water until tender, about 40 minutes.
  2. Strain overnight through a jelly bag, stir the 250 ml cider vinegar into the juice and measure it, then add 500 g sugar for every 500 ml.
  3. Dissolve the sugar gently, boil hard to setting point, about 10 minutes, and stir the 60 ml finely chopped leaves through off the heat before potting into warm sterilised jars.

Arrow bamboo Pseudosasa japonica 1 recipe

Preparing fresh shoots

Method
  1. Cut the shoots when they stand about 8–10 cm above the ground, taking them 5 cm or more below the soil.
  2. Handle the husk with care: it is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs.
  3. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base.
  4. They have a rather bitter flavour: cover the core with water and boil for 20 minutes, change the water and simmer until tender, then boil again in fresh water for 5 minutes, repeating until the flavour is milder.

Wild greens with garlic and chilli

Serves 2–4

Written for any wild greens, dandelion among them.

Ingredients
  • About 225 g cooked wild greens
  • a medium clove of garlic (about 5 g)
  • 2 tbsp olive oil, plus more to serve
  • a pinch of chilli flakes
  • salt, or a finely chopped anchovy fillet or a dash of fish sauce
  • lemon wedges
Method
  1. Blanch the greens in boiling salted water until they taste good to you — for wild greens this can take 10–15 minutes — and chop long ones coarsely; you want about 225 g cooked.
  2. Slice a medium clove of garlic (about 5 g) as thinly as you can and cook it in 2 tbsp olive oil in a 20 cm pan over medium-low heat for 4–5 minutes, until lightly browned and fragrant but not burnt.
  3. Add a pinch of chilli flakes, then the greens; season, stir to coat and heat through; with bitter greens, a finely chopped anchovy fillet or a dash of fish sauce can stand in for the salt.
  4. Serve with lemon wedges and more olive oil.

Sautéed greens with pine nuts

Written for dandelion greens.

Ingredients
  • Garlic
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 4 tbsp pine nuts
  • about 1.25 litres (loosely packed) greens
  • 1 tbsp balsamic vinegar
  • about 45 g grated Parmesan
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Gently cook garlic in 2 tbsp olive oil over medium-low heat for 3–4 minutes without letting it burn, then lift it out onto a paper towel.
  2. Toast 4 tbsp pine nuts in the same oil over low heat for 3–4 minutes until browned and lift them out too.
  3. Add about 1.25 litres (loosely packed) of greens cut into 5 cm pieces and cook on low for 2–3 minutes until wilted.

Roast pumpkin and sautéed greens salad

Written for dandelion leaves.

Ingredients
salad
  • 1.75 kg butternut pumpkin
  • olive oil
  • salt and pepper
  • about 60 ml pumpkin seeds
  • garlic salt
  • 200 g washed leaves
dressing
  • 60 ml honey
  • 2 tbsp balsamic vinegar
  • 1 tbsp olive oil
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 250 °C.
  2. Cut 1.75 kg butternut pumpkin into 2 cm-thick pieces, toss with olive oil, salt and pepper, and roast in one layer on two lined trays for about 20 minutes, turning once, until golden and tender; let it cool.
  3. Toast about 60 ml pumpkin seeds, tossed in olive oil and garlic salt, in a moderate oven for about 5 minutes.
  4. Tear 200 g washed leaves into bite-sized pieces and sauté in a hot oiled pan until cooked.

Banana passionfruit Passiflora tarminiana 4 recipes

Banana passionfruit jelly

Makes about six 250 ml jars

Ingredients
  • 20–30 banana passionfruit
  • around 1–1.5 litres water
  • the juice of 2 lemons (6–8 tbsp)
  • up to 1.1 kg sugar
Method
  1. Halve the fruit and scrape the pulp and seeds into a pot, then drop the empty skins in with them — in the hope they release pectin into the juice.
  2. Add just enough water to cover, around 1–1.5 litres, bring to the boil and simmer 30–45 minutes, stirring now and then.
  3. Strain, pressing the pulp to get all the juice out, and throw away the skins and spent seeds.
  4. Return the juice to the pot with the lemon juice and sugar, and boil until it reaches setting point — allow another half hour, longer if it started watery.
  5. Pour into clean jars and water-bath 15 minutes to seal.

The author notes you might not want to add the skins if the fruit is not organic. The author says the sugar can come down from 1.1 kg if that is too sweet, but some is needed for the pectin to set.

Curuba milk drink (jugo de curuba en leche)

Ingredients
  • 12 ripe fruit
  • 240 ml water
  • about 300 g sugar
  • 2 litres milk
  • 60 ml cream
  • ice
Method
  1. Halve the fruit and scoop the pulp into a blender with the water, and blend to a cream.
  2. Add the milk, the sugar and a little crushed ice and blend at medium speed, then add the cream and blend one minute more.
  3. Strain out the seeds if you like, and serve cold.

Curuba sorbete with chocolate

Ingredients
  • 8 fruit
  • 240 ml water
  • 4 tablespoons sugar
  • 480 ml milk
  • a 200 g pot of cream
  • a little ice, if you like
  • a bar of chocolate
Method
  1. Blend the pulp with 240 ml water and strain out the seeds.
  2. Blend the juice again with the sugar, the milk and 6 tablespoons of the cream, with a little ice if you like.
  3. Melt the chocolate, coat the inside of each glass and chill to set it.
  4. Whip the rest of the cream until firm, pour the sorbete into the glasses and top with the cream.

Tumbo jam (mermelada de tumbo)

Ingredients
  • 10 fruit
  • 600 ml water
  • about 400 g sugar
  • 2 cloves
  • the juice of 1 lemon
Method
  1. Scoop out the pulp, blend it for only about 3 seconds with 120 ml of the water, and strain to keep the liquid.
  2. In a large pot put the remaining 480 ml water, the sugar, the cloves and the lemon juice, add the strained liquid and cook over medium-low heat for about 40 minutes, until it thickens.
  3. Take out the cloves before it comes off the heat, and let it cool.

Good on bread.

Barberry Berberis glaucocarpa 1 recipe

Barberry and peach bliss balls

Written for barberry (Berberis glaucocarpa) by the New Zealand forager who picked it.

Ingredients
  • ½ cup (125 ml) barberries
  • ¾ cup (185 ml) dates
  • ¾ cup (185 ml) almonds
  • ¼ cup (60 ml) sunflower seeds
  • ¼ cup (60 ml) dried peaches
  • a pinch of salt
  • a pinch of cinnamon
  • 1 tablespoon carob powder
  • ¼ cup (60 ml) desiccated coconut, plus more to coat
Method
  1. Soak ½ cup (125 ml) barberries if they have shrivelled, and soak ¾ cup (185 ml) dates.
  2. In a food processor, grind ¾ cup (185 ml) almonds and ¼ cup (60 ml) sunflower seeds to crumbs.
  3. Add the barberries, dates, ¼ cup (60 ml) dried peaches, a pinch of salt, a pinch of cinnamon, 1 tablespoon carob powder and ¼ cup (60 ml) desiccated coconut, and process until the mixture holds together.
  4. Roll into balls and coat them in more coconut.

The source leaves out the unit for the almonds, barberries and coconut; cups are assumed here, matching its other lines. Millilitres use the 250 ml metric cup.

Bay leaf and lemon shortbread

Ingredients
shortbread
  • 3 small dried bay leaves
  • 200 g sugar
  • 454 g soft butter
  • 1 tsp lemon zest
  • ⅛ tsp salt
  • 480 g flour
icing
  • 5 small bay leaves
  • 67 g sugar
  • 120 g icing sugar
  • 1 tbsp meringue powder
  • 3 tbsp lemon juice
Method
  1. Grind 3 small dried bay leaves with 1–2 tbsp of 200 g sugar to a powder, sifting out any stubborn bits.

Horta (boiled wild greens with olive oil and lemon)

For 4

Ingredients
  • About 450 g freshly picked young greens
  • 3 tbsp kosher salt, for the cooking water
  • olive oil
  • lemon wedges
  • about ½ tsp finishing salt
Method
  1. Soak about 450 g of freshly picked young greens in cold water for 10 minutes.
  2. Bring about 3.8 L of water and 3 tbsp kosher salt to the boil in a large lidded pot, add the greens, cover and bring back to the boil.
  3. Uncover and cook for 60 seconds, stirring until all are wilted, then taste one — some greens take longer — and drain in a colander once tender.

Bermuda buttercup Oxalis pes-caprae 2 recipes

Leafy green tart with Bermuda buttercup

Ingredients
filling
  • about 680 g leafy greens (spinach, Swiss chard leaves, nettles, lamb's quarters, amaranth or quickweed)
  • 3 egg yolks
  • 1 egg
  • 250 ml (1 cup) crème fraîche or sour cream
  • 125 ml (½ cup) whipping cream
  • 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt, plus more if needed
  • plenty of black pepper
  • 45 ml (3 tbsp) chopped Bermuda buttercup stems
pastry
  • 560 ml (2¼ cups) plain flour
  • 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt
  • 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil
  • 125 ml (½ cup) tepid water
Method
  1. Make the filling first; the pastry needs no resting.
  2. Bring 2.5 cm of water to the boil in a large pot, pack in about 680 g of leafy greens (spinach, Swiss chard leaves, nettles, lamb's quarters, amaranth or quickweed), cover and cook on high for 2 minutes, stir, then cook 2 minutes more until just tender but still bright green.
  3. If you use nettles, cover them in boiling water instead and cook about 5 minutes.
  4. Drain, refresh in cold water, squeeze as dry as you can, roll in a clean tea towel to press out the rest, and chop roughly.
  5. Beat 3 egg yolks and 1 egg with 250 ml (1 cup) crème fraîche or sour cream, 125 ml (½ cup) whipping cream, 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt and plenty of black pepper, then stir in the greens and 45 ml (3 tbsp) chopped Bermuda buttercup stems, adding more salt if needed.
  6. For the pastry, stir 560 ml (2¼ cups) plain flour, 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) salt, 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil and 125 ml (½ cup) tepid water together and form a ball.
  7. Heat the oven to 200 °C.
  8. Roll the pastry into a disc about 30 cm across on an oiled or lined baking tray, turn up and crimp the edge into a lip, spread in the filling and bake 40–45 minutes, until the pastry is crisp and the centre is set.

Black bamboo Phyllostachys nigra 2 recipes

Preparing fresh shoots

Method
  1. Cut the shoots at about 8 cm above the ground, 5 cm below the soil.
  2. Handle the husk with care: it is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs.
  3. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base.
  4. The shoots are wide — about 5 cm across — so slice them before boiling if you want the leaching to reach the middle.
  5. They are somewhat acrid raw: cover with water, boil, and change the water once after 8–10 minutes, then simmer until tender.

They keep a distinct taste and smell of their own.

Black cherry Prunus serotina 1 recipe

Fermented wild black cherry cordial

Ingredients
  • 5 cups fully ripe cherries
  • 15 cups cold water
  • 5 cups raw cane sugar
  • 2 tsp citric acid (or 8 tbsp lemon juice)
Method
  1. Use fully ripe cherries, so dark purple they look black; red ones are under-ripe.
  2. If they need cleaning, float 5 cups of cherries in a large pot of cold water, pour off whatever rises, and drain.
  3. In a large glass jar (about 7.5 L) crush the raw cherries by hand to break every skin — hands are gentler on the stones than a masher.
  4. Add 15 cups cold water, 5 cups raw cane sugar and 2 tsp citric acid (or 8 tbsp lemon juice) and stir until the sugar dissolves; any left will dissolve over the next day.
  5. Cover with cheesecloth or a linen towel tied on with string, so it can breathe but fruit flies cannot get in, and keep it in a cool spot out of direct sun, such as a kitchen counter.
  6. Stir vigorously with a clean spoon about once every 12 hours (at least once a day) and taste a teaspoon after each stir.
  7. After 2–3 days it should be bubbly; fewer days give a sweeter, less fizzy drink, more days a drier, fizzier one — the recipe's authors bottle theirs after 5–7 days.
  8. Strain out the stones, skins and pulp, finishing through a fine-mesh strainer, pour into swing-top bottles or jars (not plastic or metal) and refrigerate at once.
  9. Never store the bottles at room temperature: the fermentation keeps building pressure and they can burst.

It keeps in the fridge for months, and is lightly alcoholic, probably about 1–2.5%.

Black locust flower fritters, Italian style

  1. Clean the flowers and strip them from the central stalk.

Beer-batter black locust fritters (vegan)

Makes 10–12 fritters, for 2

Ingredients
  • 60 g (½ cup) plain flour
  • ½ tsp baking powder (optional; more makes the fritters bitter)
  • 120 ml (½ cup) light-coloured or non-alcoholic beer
  • 10–12 freshly picked black locust flower clusters
  • 1 tbsp brown sugar
  • ½ lemon
  • vegetable oil for frying
Method
  1. Shake and look over the flowers to remove dirt and insects.
  2. Whisk the flour, the baking powder if using, and the beer into a smooth batter, slightly thick but still runny.
  3. Holding each cluster by its stalk, dip it in the batter and let the excess run off.
  4. Heat enough oil to cover the base of a large frying pan; it is ready when a drip of batter fizzes and starts to brown.
  5. Fry over medium-high heat until golden underneath, turn and brown the other side, adding oil between batches.
  6. Eat soon after cooking, sprinkled with the brown sugar and a squeeze of lemon.
  7. Pull the stalks out as you eat; they are not eaten.

Black passionfruit Passiflora edulis 2 recipes

Passionfruit curd

Ingredients
  • The pulp of about 12 passionfruit (250 ml)
  • 125 g unsalted butter
  • 165 g caster sugar
  • 5 eggs
  • 2 extra yolks
Method
  1. Whisk the pulp to loosen it and push it through a sieve, then stir half the seeds back into the juice.
  2. Put the juice, butter and sugar in a heatproof bowl over a pan of simmering water, keeping the bowl clear of the water, and stir until the butter melts.
  3. Beat the eggs and yolks lightly, whisk them in gently, and keep stirring for 20–25 minutes until it thickens: it is ready when a finger drawn across the curd on the back of a spoon leaves a line that holds.
  4. Pour into warm sterilised jars, seal, cool, and keep in the fridge for up to 8 weeks.

Blackberry jam

Makes about 8 jars

Written for blackberries; the page names no species.

Ingredients
  • 1.8 kg blackberries
  • 1.5 kg jam sugar (sugar with added pectin)
  • the juice and pips of 1 lemon
  • a fingertip-sized knob of butter (optional)
Method
  1. The night before, layer the berries and sugar in a very large bowl, cover and leave at room temperature so the sugar starts to dissolve; stir once in the morning.
  2. Put a small saucer in the freezer.
  3. Tip everything into a preserving pan or a large, wide pan and stir in the lemon juice; tie the lemon pips in muslin or a tea strainer and add them, because they give up pectin and help the set.
  4. Warm gently until all the sugar has dissolved, then bring to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes.
  5. Take off the heat and put a little on the cold saucer: once it is cool, push it with a finger, and if it wrinkles it has set.
  6. If not, boil 2–3 minutes more and test again, until it wrinkles.
  7. Skim, stir in the butter if using, and leave 15 minutes so the fruit settles before ladling into sterilised jars (wash them in hot soapy water and dry them in an oven at 170 °C, 150 °C fan, for at least 10 minutes).

Keeps at least 6 months somewhere cool and dark; refrigerate once open.

  1. Wash the leaves well, watching for insects.

Method
  1. Spread the gathered seeds on a baking tray and dry them in a low oven until slightly toasted, without burning them (about 625 ml, 2½ cups, of dried seed makes 250 ml, 1 cup, of flour); soaking them overnight first takes out some bitterness.

  4. Add up to 125 ml (½ cup) water a little at a time until it holds together without sticking, knead, cover and rest 10 minutes.
  5. Roll half the dough out about 2 mm thick on a greased, floured tray, cut into crackers or leave whole, and bake for 15 minutes; repeat with the rest.
  6. Cool completely.

Ingredients
puddings

  1. Boil 400 g pearl barley until tender, drain and cool.

Dock soup with rice, egg and lemon

Serves 4

Written for dock generally — the author thinks his leaves were most likely curled dock but is not certain; the New Zealand version below names broad-leaved and curled dock; use young leaves.

  • 170 g young dock leaves, washed

Method

Brush cherry Syzygium australe 2 recipes

Brush cherry jelly

Makes about five 250 g jars

Ingredients
  • 2 kg brush cherry fruit
  • 1 litre (4 cups) water
  • 1 kg sugar
Method
  1. Pick off any stalks, wash the fruit and drain it in a colander.
  2. Put it in a saucepan with the water, bring to the boil over a moderate heat, then cover and simmer for 20 minutes until soft.
  3. Let cool.
  4. When it is cool enough to handle, strain it through a jelly bag, or a sieve lined with two layers of flannelette, squeezing out as much juice as you can.
  5. Bring the juice to the boil over a high heat in a preserving pan or large, wide saucepan, stir in the sugar and bring back to a rapid boil, stirring and skimming off any scum.
  6. Boil until it sets, about 20–30 minutes.
  7. To test, put a teaspoonful on a saucer chilled in the freezer and let it cool for a couple of minutes: if the surface wrinkles clearly when pushed, it is ready.
  8. Pour into hot, sterilised jars and seal.

View source recipe

Brush cherry cordial

Makes about two 750 ml bottles

Ingredients
  • 1 kg brush cherry fruit
  • 750 ml (3 cups) water
  • juice of 2 lemons
  • 750 ml (3 cups) sugar
  • 3 teaspoons citric acid
Method
  1. Pick off any stalks and wash the fruit.
  2. Put it in a large saucepan with the water and bring to the boil, then cover and simmer for 20 minutes until cooked.
  3. Let cool.
  4. Line a sieve with a jelly bag or flannelette and set it over a large clean saucepan; tip in the cooked fruit and its juice and pour in the lemon juice.
  5. Gather the bag around the fruit and squeeze and twist it until all the juice is forced out, then discard the remains.
  6. Bring the liquid to a rapid boil, stir in the sugar and citric acid, and when they have completely dissolved, pour through a funnel into hot, clean bottles and seal.
  7. To drink, put 1–2 tablespoons in a glass and dilute with tap or soda water.
  8. Refrigerate after opening.

Classic stinging nettle soup

Serves 6

Written for common stinging nettle (Urtica dioica and similar nettles) in North America, not for this species.

  • About 225 g nettles

Method
  1. Blanch about 225 g nettles in salted boiling water until just wilted, about 30 seconds, cool them in cold water, squeeze dry and finely chop a handful to finish the soup.

  3. Add about 1 litre chicken stock and 2 cups diced potato and simmer until tender, about 15 minutes.
  4. Add the blanched nettles and blend, then stir in the chopped nettles and 120 ml cream and season with salt and white pepper.
  5. Serve with crème fraîche and chopped dill or mint.

Cherry-plum Prunus cerasifera 3 recipes

Cherry plum jam

Makes about 7 jars

Ingredients
  • 1.8 kg cherry plums
  • 1.8 kg brown cane sugar
  • about 285 ml water
Method
  1. Put everything in a large, flat-bottomed pan, stir, and bring to the boil.
  2. Boil until the skins start to come off and the fruit comes away from the stones.
  3. Pour the mixture into a large piece of muslin and squeeze the pulp through it back into the pan.
  4. Keep boiling until it reaches setting point, which can take as long as 30 minutes.
  5. To test, chill a couple of saucers in the fridge before you start; drip a little jam onto one, let it cool for a moment, then push it sideways with a finger — it is ready when it wrinkles and feels tacky.
  6. Pour into sterilised jars and screw on the lids.

View source recipe

Cherry plum wine

Ingredients
  • 2.8 kg cherry plums
  • 1.4 kg sugar
  • about 4 litres water
  • 1 sachet wine yeast (any red wine yeast will do)
  • 1 tsp yeast nutrient
  • 1 tsp pectolase
Method
  1. Boil 1 litre of the water, pour it over the fruit and crush the fruit with the end of a rolling pin until no lumps are left.
  2. Leave it a few hours, then add the rest of the water and the pectolase — plums are rich in the pectin that sets jam and also clouds wine.
  3. Leave a couple of days, then strain through a fine sieve.
  4. Bring the juice quickly to the boil in a saucepan and turn off the heat straight away; the author once skipped this and lost the whole batch to acetobacter.
  5. Pour the hot juice over the sugar and stir until it dissolves, cool to room temperature, then add the yeast and yeast nutrient.
  6. Top up to 4.5 litres if necessary, funnel into a demijohn and fit an airlock.
  7. Rack into a clean demijohn after four to six weeks, and again a few weeks later if you want.
  8. Bottle when clear — or, if it will not clear completely, bottle it anyway.

Written for plums in general rather than cherry plums.

Ingredients
  • 250 g granulated sugar

  • ½ tsp crushed coriander
  • 1 tsp ground cardamom
  • 750 g plums, stoned and halved
  • 1 small cinnamon stick
  • 1 red chilli cut into quarters
  • 1 star anise
Method
  1. In a large saucepan, bring the sugar, vinegar, coriander and cardamom to a gentle simmer and cook for 5 minutes to infuse.
  2. Add the plums and cook for about 2 minutes, until just softened but still holding their shape.
  3. Put the cinnamon, chilli and star anise in a sterilised 1-litre jar (or two or three smaller ones), scoop in the plums and pack them tightly, leaving about 1.25 cm at the top, then pour the vinegar over until they are completely covered.
  4. Seal while still warm, leave to cool at room temperature, then refrigerate for 2 weeks before serving.

They keep about a couple of weeks in the fridge; for longer storage they can be processed in a water bath. Good on toast with farmhouse cheese, on savoury porridge, in salads, or with pork chops, chicken or turkey.

Method
  1. Peel the chokos, take out the seed, cut them into quarters and then into spears about as thick as your thumb.

  4. Bring the vinegar, sugar and spices to the boil and simmer for 5–10 minutes.
  5. Drain the liquid off the chokos without rinsing them.
  6. Take the jars out with tongs and stand them on a wooden board or tea towel; put any dill or bay leaves straight into the jars.
  7. Pack the spears evenly into the jars, ladle the hot vinegar over them, and screw the boiled lids on tightly.
  8. Store in a cool, dark place and wait at least three weeks before eating.

They keep for about two years.

Chinese stir-fried choko

Serves 2

Ingredients
  • 12–18 g (2–3 tbsp) dried shrimp
  • 600 g choko
  • 22 ml (1½ tbsp) canola, vegetable or almond oil
  • 35 g shallots or onion, sliced
  • 2 cloves garlic, smashed
  • a few slices of ginger
  • 300 ml water or broth
  • 2.5 ml (½ tsp) sea salt (1.25 ml, ¼ tsp, if using broth)
  • 1.25 ml (¼ tsp) chicken bouillon powder (optional)
  • sliced spring onions and toasted sesame seeds to serve
Method
  1. Rinse the dried shrimp and soak them in cold water for 30 minutes (or hot water for 15–20 minutes), then drain.
  2. Peel the chokos, cutting the skin off any deep ridges with a paring knife.
  3. Slice off the top, stand each one cut side down and halve it, trim any skin left on the bottom ridges, and dig out the seed.
  4. Cut each half lengthwise into two, slice 6–12 mm thick, and rinse and drain the slices.
  5. Heat the oil in a wok over medium-high heat and cook the shallots, garlic, ginger and shrimp for 1–2 minutes.
  6. Add the choko, water or broth, salt and bouillon powder and stir.
  7. Cover and cook for 7–8 minutes, until the choko is fork-tender but still a little firm.
  8. Taste the broth and add salt if needed.
  9. Serve topped with spring onions and sesame seeds.
  10. For a vegan version, cook a few diced shiitake mushrooms with the choko and use vegetable broth.

Method
  1. Peel the chokos and halve them lengthwise.

  4. Heat the oil in a 30 cm non-stick or cast-iron frying pan over medium heat until it shimmers.

Clustered dock Rumex conglomeratus 1 recipe

Dock soup with rice, egg and lemon

Serves 4

Written for dock generally — the author thinks his leaves were most likely curled dock but is not certain; the New Zealand version below names broad-leaved and curled dock; clustered dock is very bitter, more so as it ages, so use only young leaves.

Ingredients
  • 170 g young dock leaves, washed
  • salt
  • 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish
  • 50 g (¼ cup) basmati or other long-grain rice
  • 1 small onion, chopped
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped garlic
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped fresh oregano
  • a pinch of ground cumin
  • 1 litre chicken or vegetable stock
  • 1 large egg, beaten
  • black pepper
  • plenty of fresh lemon juice
Method
  1. Drop the dock leaves into boiling salted water for a few seconds until just wilted, cool them in cold water and squeeze them dry (about 180 ml).
  2. Toast the rice on a tray in a 175 °C oven until just golden, then simmer it, covered, with a pinch of salt and 125 ml water until tender.
  3. Chop the dock both ways so no long strands are left.
  4. In a 3-litre pot, soften the onion and garlic in the oil over medium heat for about 10 minutes, until just browning at the edges.
  5. Add the stock, dock, oregano and cumin, bring to a simmer and season, then add the rice and simmer gently for about 10 minutes.
  6. Pour the beaten egg in a spiral over the surface without stirring and let it heat through.
  7. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil, black pepper and enough lemon juice that the soup tastes lemony.
  8. For a simpler version without egg (Wild Botanica, New Zealand): soften the onion and garlic, wilt the chopped leaves (central veins removed) in the pot, add the stock, cumin, oregano and salt, simmer for 10 minutes, then stir through 60 ml (¼ cup) cooked rice and finish with lemon juice.

Written for mallow in general; the page names no species.

  • 450 g mallow leaves

  • 1 medium onion, diced

Method
  1. Pull the leaves off the stems and soak them in water with a small pinch of salt, then rinse well under running water to remove any dirt or grit and drain completely.
  2. Fry the onion in the oil until soft and translucent, then lift it out.
  3. In the same pan, cook the leaves with a splash of water over medium heat, stirring now and then, until they wilt and shrink.
  4. Once they are tender, stir the onion back in, tip onto a plate and finish with lemon juice, to taste, and a drizzle of olive oil.

The source notes that young leaves are best; older ones are tougher and have less flavour. Good with vermicelli rice or fresh pita bread.

Method
  1. Rinse the leaves gently, pat them dry and, if fresh, chop roughly.

Ingredients

  • 1–2 tbsp chopped ginger or citrus zest
  • 250 ml sugar
  • juice of ½ lemon
  • 1 litre filtered water
  • optional: a grape or a few raisins, to start the wild yeast
Method
  1. Combine everything in a clean 2-litre glass jar and stir to dissolve the sugar.
  2. Cover with a thin cloth or coffee filter held on with a rubber band.
  3. Leave at room temperature, out of direct sun, for 2–4 days, stirring once a day, until it bubbles and is lightly fizzy.

Ingredients

Method
  1. Heat the oven to 170°C fanbake; line the base of a 22 cm springform tin and grease the sides.

  9. Walnut flour can be made by blitzing walnut pieces.

Dock seed crackers

Makes about 30

Written for the seeds of broad-leaved and curled dock.

Ingredients
  • 250 ml (1 cup) dock flour (from about 625 ml, 2½ cups, of dried seed)
  • 250 ml (1 cup) oat flour
  • ½ tsp salt
  • 1 tsp onion powder
  • 1 tbsp yeast flakes
  • up to 125 ml (½ cup) water
Method
  1. Spread the gathered seeds on a baking tray and dry them in a low oven until slightly toasted, without burning them (about 625 ml, 2½ cups, of dried seed makes 250 ml, 1 cup, of flour); soaking them overnight first takes out some bitterness.
  2. Heat the oven to 180 °C.
  3. Grind the seeds in a coffee grinder or food processor, and mix 250 ml (1 cup) of the dock flour with 250 ml (1 cup) oat flour, ½ tsp salt, 1 tsp onion powder and 1 tbsp yeast flakes.
  4. Add up to 125 ml (½ cup) water a little at a time until it holds together without sticking, knead, cover and rest 10 minutes.
  5. Roll half the dough out about 2 mm thick on a greased, floured tray, cut into crackers or leave whole, and bake for 15 minutes; repeat with the rest.
  6. Cool completely.

They keep a week in an airtight container.

Potato gnocchi with porcini sauce and wilted dock

Serves 4

Written for curly (curled) dock; dandelion or other greens work too.

Ingredients
gnocchi
  • 900 g golden potatoes, halved
  • 60 ml (¼ cup) lightly beaten egg
  • 185 ml (¾ cup) plain flour, plus up to 60 ml (¼ cup) more
sauce
  • 375 ml (1½ cups) low-salt chicken stock
  • 20 g rinsed dried porcini
  • 1 tbsp olive oil, plus another 1 tbsp
  • 1 minced small shallot
  • 1 sliced garlic clove
  • 80 ml (⅓ cup) dry white wine
  • 2 tbsp chopped parsley
To serve
  • a few handfuls of washed, trimmed dock leaves
  • olive oil
  • salt and pepper
  • parmesan shavings
Method
  1. Gnocchi: boil 900 g golden potatoes, halved, in salted water until tender, 25–30 minutes, and keep the water.
  2. Lift them out one at a time, peel while hot and fluff with a fork without overmashing.
  3. Cool 5 minutes, then drizzle over 60 ml (¼ cup) lightly beaten egg, scatter over 185 ml (¾ cup) plain flour and fold together; knead very gently, adding up to 60 ml (¼ cup) more flour if it is gummy.
  4. Cut into 8, roll each into a thumb-thick log and cut every 2 cm; press each piece lightly with a fork and dust with flour.
  5. Sauce: heat 375 ml (1½ cups) low-salt chicken stock with 20 g rinsed dried porcini to a simmer, cover off the heat for 5 minutes, then lift out and dice the mushrooms, keeping the liquid.
  6. Fry them in 1 tbsp olive oil over a medium heat with 1 minced small shallot and 1 sliced garlic clove until lightly browned, 2–4 minutes.
  7. Add the liquid, 80 ml (⅓ cup) dry white wine and another 1 tbsp olive oil, scraping up the browned bits, and boil hard, whisking now and then, about 5 minutes.
  8. Stir in 2 tbsp chopped parsley, season and keep warm.
  9. To serve: bring the potato water back to the boil and cook the gnocchi in small batches, lifting them out about 10 seconds after they rise.
  10. Lay them straight onto a platter of a few handfuls of washed, trimmed dock leaves, which wilt in the heat.
  11. Top with the sauce, a drizzle of olive oil, salt, pepper and parmesan shavings.

Dock, dandelion and nettle puddings

Makes about 35 small puddings or one large one

Written for broad-leaved dock; the author says any dock picked in spring, before flowering, will do, and so will other strong-tasting spring greens such as nettle, plantain or watercress.

Ingredients
  • 400 g pearl barley
  • 4 eggs, hard-boiled
  • 2 large leeks
  • a little oil
  • about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves
  • 3 raw eggs, plus 1–2 more if needed
To finish
  • flour
  • 1 beaten egg
  • 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs
  • 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle (optional)

Method
  1. Boil 400 g pearl barley until tender, drain and cool.
  2. Hard-boil 4 eggs and chop finely.
  3. Finely chop 2 large leeks and soften them in a little oil.
  4. Blanch about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves in boiling water for 20 seconds, then plunge into iced water (skip this and the puddings are more bitter and less green); squeeze out every drop of water and chop finely.
  5. Mix the chopped eggs, leeks, barley and greens with 3 raw eggs, and season very well.
  6. Wrap the mixture tightly in a tray covered with cling film, set in a larger tray of hot water, or seal it in a pudding bowl with baking paper, foil and string and stand it in a pan of water reaching at least halfway up.
  7. Steam for 45–60 minutes, in a 160 °C oven or on the hob, until it holds together; if it won't roll into balls, mix in 1–2 more raw eggs and steam longer.
  8. Turn out and serve as one pudding, or roll into small balls while warm and chill them (they freeze individually at this stage).
  9. Roll the chilled balls in flour, then in 1 beaten egg, then in 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs (mixed, if you like, with 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle), and deep-fry for 1–2 minutes until browned; or simply flour and fry them.

Dock soup with rice, egg and lemon

Serves 4

Written for dock generally — the author thinks his leaves were most likely curled dock but is not certain; the New Zealand version below names curled and broad-leaved dock; use young leaves.

Ingredients
  • 170 g young dock leaves, washed
  • salt
  • 30 ml (2 tbsp) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish
  • 50 g (¼ cup) basmati or other long-grain rice
  • 1 small onion, chopped
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped garlic
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped fresh oregano
  • a pinch of ground cumin
  • 1 litre chicken or vegetable stock
  • 1 large egg, beaten
  • black pepper
  • plenty of fresh lemon juice
Method
  1. Drop the dock leaves into boiling salted water for a few seconds until just wilted, cool them in cold water and squeeze them dry (about 180 ml).
  2. Toast the rice on a tray in a 175 °C oven until just golden, then simmer it, covered, with a pinch of salt and 125 ml water until tender.
  3. Chop the dock both ways so no long strands are left.
  4. In a 3-litre pot, soften the onion and garlic in the oil over medium heat for about 10 minutes, until just browning at the edges.
  5. Add the stock, dock, oregano and cumin, bring to a simmer and season, then add the rice and simmer gently for about 10 minutes.
  6. Pour the beaten egg in a spiral over the surface without stirring and let it heat through.
  7. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil, black pepper and enough lemon juice that the soup tastes lemony.
  8. For a simpler version without egg (Wild Botanica, New Zealand): soften the onion and garlic, wilt the chopped leaves (central veins removed) in the pot, add the stock, cumin, oregano and salt, simmer for 10 minutes, then stir through 60 ml (¼ cup) cooked rice and finish with lemon juice.

Method
  1. Boil 400 g pearl barley until tender, drain and cool.

Prickly pear juice

Written for prickly pears (Opuntia) in general; the guide names no species.

Method
  1. Handle the fruit with tongs throughout.
  2. Singe the spines off the whole fresh fruit over the high flame of a gas stove or grill, turning it so the flame reaches as much of the skin as possible, then scrub the fruit with a vegetable brush under running water to remove the singed skin.
  3. Halve the fruit, put it in a large pan with enough water to cover and boil for about 20 minutes, until tender.
  4. Line a colander with two layers of closely woven muslin, cheesecloth or coffee filters, set it over a bowl, and crush the fruit in it with a potato masher or large spoon to collect the juice.
  5. Juice from unripe fruit holds more pectin, so collect it separately.
  6. The juice keeps 3 days in the fridge or up to 12 months frozen in a labelled, sealed container.

Prickly pear jelly (low sugar)

Makes about five 250 ml jars

Written for prickly pears (Opuntia) in general; the guide names no species.

Ingredients
  • 1 litre prickly pear juice (fresh or frozen)
  • 1 packet (3 tablespoons) low-sugar powdered pectin
  • 2 tablespoons bottled lemon juice
  • about 600 g (3 cups) sugar
Method
  1. Read and follow the pectin instructions.
  2. Put the juice and pectin in a 5-litre pot and bring to a rolling boil, stirring all the time.
  3. Add the lemon juice and sugar, bring back to a hard boil and boil 3–4 minutes.
  4. Test for a set: the most dependable test is to cook it to 4.5 °C above the temperature at which water boils where you are; or let it run off the side of a metal spoon, where at setting point the drops join into a sheet that breaks cleanly from the edge; or chill a little on a cold plate in the freezer for a few minutes to see whether it gels.
  5. Take it off the heat, let it stand about a minute, and skim off the foam.
  6. Ladle into hot, clean jars one at a time, leaving 6 mm headspace, and put on the lids and bands.
  7. Process 10 minutes in a boiling-water bath (the guide's time for 300–1,800 m above sea level; 15 minutes from 1,800 to 3,000 m).
  8. Lift the jars out onto a clean, dry cloth and leave them to cool overnight (12–15 hours), then take off the bands, dry the lids and put on clean, dry bands.
  9. Store in a cool, dry place for up to 12 months.

Elderflower cordial

Makes just over 1 litre

Ingredients
  • 20 elderflower heads (more if they are small or you want a stronger taste)
  • 1 litre boiling water
  • 75 g citric acid
  • 1 kg sugar
  • 4 lemons
Method
  1. Pick heads whose flowers are white, not yellow or brown, and fully open, ideally mid-morning on a sunny day, and use them as soon as you can; left too long they start to smell sour.
  2. Pick out insects, large leaves and brown bits, but don't rinse the flowers, or the cordial loses flavour.
  3. Put the flowers in a large pot and pour the boiling water over them.
  4. Add the citric acid and sugar and stir until they dissolve.
  5. Grate in the lemon zest, cut the lemons into quarters, add them and stir.
  6. Cover the pot and leave to infuse for at least 24 hours.
  7. Strain through muslin or a fine strainer into another pot, squeezing the pulp hard to get all the flavour out.
  8. Sanitise bottles or jars by washing them in soapy water, rinsing, then filling them with boiling water for 5 minutes and emptying them.
  9. Funnel in the cordial, filling to overflowing so little air is left, and keep it in a cool, dark place; refrigerate once opened.
  10. It is strong: dilute it with still or sparkling water, or mix it into drinks or cakes.

Written for elderflowers in Britain; the page names no species.

  • sunflower oil, for deep-frying
  • icing sugar, to dust

batter
  • 80 g plain flour
  • 20 g cornflour
  • 1 tablespoon caster sugar
  • 225 ml chilled sparkling water
  • 1 egg white
Method
  1. Put the flour, cornflour and sugar in a large bowl, add the sparkling water and mix very briefly and lightly, just until combined.
  2. Leave it to stand for an hour.
  3. Meanwhile, shake any insects out of the flower heads without washing them, and trim each stalk to about 5 cm below the head to use as a handle.
  4. When you are ready to fry, whisk the egg white to soft peaks and fold it gently into the batter with a metal spoon.
  5. Heat the oil to 190 °C in a deep-fryer; or use a wide, deep pan no more than a third full, over high heat, until a drop of batter rises at once in a ring of bubbles.
  6. Hold a flower head upside down by its stalk, dip it into the batter and let the excess drip off.
  7. Lower it gently into the oil, where it will spread and float, and use the stalk to push it under a little so all the batter cooks.
  8. Fry one at a time until light golden and crisp, then lift out by the stalk and rest on kitchen paper for a moment.
  9. Dust with icing sugar and serve with lemon wedges to squeeze over.
  10. Eat the flowers off the stalk, not the stalk itself (see Warnings).

Method
  1. Snip each berry cluster off the tree with scissors.
  2. At home, hold a cluster by its stalk and push the berries off with the prongs of a dinner fork.
  3. Put the fruit, the bag of spices and the water in a preserving pan, bring to the boil, then lower the heat and cook gently until the fruit is soft.
  4. Crush the fruit with the back of a wooden spoon to release the juice and keep cooking until it is a soft pulp, then take out the spices.
  5. Tip the pulp into a jelly bag or muslin tied with string and hang it over a large bowl somewhere cool overnight.
  6. Don't squeeze the bag, or the jelly will be cloudy.
  7. Next day, measure the juice and allow 450 g sugar for every 600 ml.
  8. Put the juice and sugar in a clean preserving pan over low heat and stir until the sugar dissolves, then raise the heat and boil until setting point: 105 °C on a sugar thermometer, or a teaspoon dropped on a chilled saucer wrinkles when pushed once it has cooled.
  9. Skim if needed, pour into sterilised jars and seal.
  10. To sterilise the jars, run them through the hottest dishwasher cycle, or wash them by hand and dry them in the oven at 120 °C for 20 minutes.

Elderflower champagne

Ingredients
  • 10–16 large elderflower heads (or 1 tablespoon dried elderflowers for each fresh head)
  • 650 g sugar
  • 4.5 litres of cold water
  • 1 lemon
  • 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar
Method
  1. Pick 10–16 large elderflower heads in full bloom, on a sunny morning if you can.
  2. Shake out the insects but don't wash them.
  3. To be careful, snip the flowers off the thick stalks.
  4. Dissolve 650 g sugar in 4.5 litres of cold water — warm a little of the water to dissolve the sugar, cool it, then mix it into the rest.
  5. In a large bucket or bowl, combine the sweetened water with the flowers, the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon, and 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar.
  6. Cover and leave for 4 days, somewhere cool; if mould forms, scrape off the mat of flowers on top and carry on.
  7. Fine-strain into clean screw-top plastic fizzy-drink bottles, leaving a few centimetres of air at the top.
  8. Never use corked bottles, and avoid glass flip-tops: you can't feel the pressure through them, and they are far more dangerous if they burst.
  9. Leave at room temperature for 6–14 days.
  10. From day 6, squeeze the bottles every day, and as soon as the bases start to round out, ease the caps to let off some (not all) of the pressure; a forgotten bottle can explode.
  11. Once it tastes right, move it to the fridge to slow the fermentation, and keep checking the pressure.

The author uses whole heads, green stalks and all, as is traditional. The source says one tablespoon of dried elderflowers replaces one good-sized fresh head. The author drinks it between 2 and 4 weeks; it is lightly alcoholic after a week and starts turning vinegary at 5–6 weeks. The source notes that the yeast comes from the flowers, so in a cool room it can take a while to get going. The author sometimes uses an infused vinegar, such as pineapple weed vinegar, for a twist.

View source recipe

Elderflower champagne vinegar

Method
  1. If a batch of elderflower champagne goes flat and vinegary, mix it with some live vinegar (with its mother).
  2. Leave it in an open container covered with cheesecloth, somewhere dark, for 2–3 months, until it reaches about 3–4% acidity.
  3. Use it for pickling.

View source recipe

Elderberry vinegar

Ingredients
  • Ripe elderberries
  • apple cider vinegar (or white wine vinegar), 500 ml for every 350 g of berries
  • sugar, 350 g for every 260 ml of liquid
Method
  1. Strip the ripe berries off every stalk — freezing the heads first makes this easier — and weigh them.
  2. For every 350 g of berries add 500 ml apple cider vinegar (or white wine vinegar) in a jar or tub.
  3. Cover and leave for 5 days, stirring now and then.
  4. Strain, pressing the berries, and throw them away.
  5. Add 350 g sugar for every 260 ml of liquid, simmer for 10 minutes, and bottle.

The recipe's final simmer is essential: raw elderberries are not safe to eat. The recipe works with less sugar too, if you want it less sweet.

Barberry jelly

From a German herbal page about the common barberry (Berberis vulgaris).

Ingredients
  • 1 kg washed berries
  • 500 ml water

Method
  1. Bring 1 kg washed berries to the boil with 500 ml water and simmer for about 20 minutes.
  2. Pour through a sieve and catch the juice.
  3. Mix the juice with 500 g jam-setting sugar of the 2:1 kind (Gelierzucker 2:1, sugar with added pectin for twice its weight of fruit), bring back to the boil, boil hard for about 4 minutes and pour into sterilised jars.

View source recipe

Barberry jam

Written for European barberry (Berberis vulgaris) by a forager who picks it wild from hedgerows in Vermont.

Ingredients
  • 450 g stemmed barberries (about 3 cups)
  • 250 ml water
  • sugar, the same volume as the pulp (about 375 ml)
Method
  1. Put 450 g stemmed barberries (about 3 cups) in a saucepan with 250 ml water and simmer gently for about 5 minutes, mashing, until the berries fall apart and release their juice.
  2. Press through a fine sieve to remove the seeds, stalk bits and black flower remains; sieve again through a finer sieve or muslin for a smoother jam; expect about 375 ml of pulp.
  3. Return it to a clean pan with the same volume of sugar (about 375 ml for 375 ml of pulp), bring to a rolling boil over high heat and boil, stirring all the time, for 2 to 3 minutes, until it starts to gel; test on a plate chilled in the freezer; it sets soft and spoonable.
  4. Ladle into two hot, sterilised 250 ml jars, leaving 6 mm headspace.
  5. Keep in the fridge or freezer, or process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes (15 minutes above about 1,800 m) and leave undisturbed for 12 to 24 hours before checking the seals.

Keeps 12 to 18 months in sealed jars; once opened, refrigerate and use within 2 to 3 weeks.

European plum Prunus ×domestica 6 recipes

Plum Jam

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 1 kg plums, halved and stoned
  • juice of 1 large lemon or 1 orange
  • 700 g granulated sugar
Method
  1. Simmer the plums gently with the juice and 150 ml water for about 5 minutes, until they begin to soften; softening them before the sugar goes in keeps the skins from toughening.
  2. Add the sugar a third at a time, stirring until it dissolves, then take the pan off the heat, cover and leave for a couple of hours or overnight while the plums sink into the syrup.
  3. Bring back to the boil, stirring off any sugar stuck to the base, and boil rapidly for about 10 minutes to setting point: the pale froth has almost gone, the surface is glossy, the boil slows, and a drop on a cold plate sets to a light gel.
  4. Rest 5 minutes so the fruit settles, then fill four sterilised 300 ml jars to the brim and seal at once.
  5. Store cool and dark; best eaten within a year.
  6. Variations: 2–3 star anise or a couple of cinnamon sticks in the poaching fruit (remove at the end), 1–2 tsp brandy in each jar, or 75–100 g walnut pieces towards the end of the boil.

Blackberry, Plum & Apple Crumble with Toasted Hazelnut Custard

Ingredients
Ingredients (serves 4)

  • 1 vanilla pod, split
  • 1 star anise
  • 1 small cinnamon stick

  • 6 plums, stoned and quartered

Crumble

Method
  1. Heat the butter with the vanilla, star anise and cinnamon for 2 minutes, add the apple and sugar and cook 5 minutes, then add the plums and blackberries and simmer gently for 15 minutes, until soft but holding their texture; keep warm.
  2. Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan).

  4. For the custard, simmer the crushed hazelnuts in both milks, then cook gently for 30 minutes; strain out the nuts and return the milk to the pan.
  5. Mix the yolks with the cornflour and sugar, pour into the hot milk and stir over a medium heat until thick, 5–8 minutes; let it boil a few minutes to lose the floury taste, then strain and keep warm.
  6. Put the filling in a dish, scatter over the crumble, warm through in the oven and serve with the custard.

Spiced Pavlova with Plums

Ingredients
Ingredients (serves 8)
  • pavlova: 5 egg whites
  • 1 tsp ground cinnamon
  • 250 g caster sugar
  • 1 tsp white wine vinegar
Cherries
  • 100 g dried cherries

Spiced plums
  • 200 ml red wine

  1. Heat the oven to 150°C (130°C fan) and line a tray with baking paper marked with a 23 cm circle.

Dried Plums & Plum Fruit Leather

Method
  1. Dried plums: use freestone plums.

Fairy ring mushroom risotto

Serves 4–6 as a side or 2–3 as a main

Written for dried fairy ring mushrooms, or the same amount fresh.

Ingredients
  • 250 ml (1 cup) dried fairy ring caps
  • 375 ml (1½ cups) Arborio rice

  • 45 g (3 tbsp) butter
  • 45 ml (3 tbsp) extra virgin olive oil
  • 160 ml (⅔ cup) grated Parmesan
  • 60 ml (¼ cup) balsamic vinegar
Method
  1. Soak the mushrooms in hot water until soft, drain them and use the liquid as part of the stock.
  2. Fry the mushrooms slowly in half the butter and oil for 10 minutes and set aside.

  4. In a heavy pan, soften the shallot in the rest of the butter and oil until lightly coloured.
  5. Add the rice and stir for about a minute until coated.
  6. Add 125 ml (½ cup) of simmering stock and stir over medium heat until the rice has taken it up; keep adding stock this way, stirring, until the rice is creamy but still al dente, about 30 minutes.
  7. If the stock runs out, use hot water.
  8. About 10 minutes before the end, add the mushrooms; about 5 minutes before the end, stir in the Parmesan and balsamic vinegar.

Fat hen raita

Written for bathua, the north Indian name for fat hen; the author names it Chenopodium album.

Ingredients
  • 250 g fat hen leaves
  • 1 green chilli (more if you want it hotter)

The author says the plant does not work raw and is tamed by boiling.

Field mushroom tartlets

Makes six 10 cm tartlets or one 25 cm tart

Written for field mushrooms in the UK; the recipe links to the site's Agaricus campestris guide.

Ingredients
pastry
  • 175 g plain flour
  • 85 g fridge-cold unsalted butter, plus extra for the tins
  • a pinch of salt
  • 1 egg yolk
  • 1 tablespoon iced water
filling
  • 250 g field mushrooms
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
  • salt and black pepper
  • 250 ml double cream
  • 1 egg
  • 3 egg yolks
  • 1½ tablespoons freshly grated parmesan
  • 1 tablespoon finely chopped chives
Method
  1. Rub or pulse the flour, butter and salt to fine crumbs, add the egg yolk and half the water and mix to a soft dough, adding more iced water if needed.
  2. Flatten the dough into a ball (for tartlets, cut it into 6 wedges, roll each into a ball and flatten it slightly), bag it and chill for at least 30 minutes.
  3. Brush the mushrooms clean and slice them thickly.
  4. Heat enough oil to cover the base of a large frying pan over a medium heat, add a single layer of mushrooms and let them fry undisturbed for about 2 minutes, until lightly browned, then turn and cook the other side.
  5. Drain them on kitchen paper, season, and fry the rest the same way.
  6. Heat the oven to 200 °C and butter the tins.
  7. Roll the pastry about 3 mm thick, line the tins, trim and prick the bases, and bake on a baking sheet for 15 minutes, until lightly golden.
  8. Turn the oven down to 180 °C.
  9. Beat the cream with the whole egg, the yolks, plenty of seasoning and 1 tablespoon of the parmesan, then stir in the chives.
  10. Share the mushrooms between the cases, pour the cream mixture over without overfilling them and scatter over the rest of the parmesan.
  11. Bake for 10–15 minutes, longer for one large tart, until risen, golden and set.
  12. Serve warm or cold.

Fishpole bamboo Phyllostachys aurea 1 recipe

Preparing fresh shoots

Method
  1. Cut the shoots at about 8 cm above the ground, 5 cm below the soil; the canes are slender, about 15 mm, thicker in their native China.
  2. Handle the husk with care: it is many overlapping brown layers covered in fine, sharp hairs.
  3. Run a knife up the side of the shoot to slit it, then unwrap and throw away the layers until you reach the pale core; cut off the pointed tip and the fibrous base.
  4. They are said to be the sweetest of the genus, with very little bitterness, but cook them: cover with water and boil for 20 minutes, change the water and simmer until tender.
  5. If they are still bitter, boil again in fresh water for 5 minutes, and repeat until the flavour is milder.

Flowering currant Ribes sanguineum 5 recipes

Flowering currant syrup and cordial

Ingredients
  • Flowering currant flowers and young leaves
  • equal parts sugar and water
  • lemon juice, citric acid or flowering currant vinegar, for a cordial
Method
  1. Use the flowers and young leaves; with flowers alone the results turn pink.
  2. For a syrup, infuse them into a syrup of equal parts sugar and water by heating gently, without boiling.
  3. Cool, and keep in sterilised jars in the fridge for a couple of weeks.
  4. Pour it over puddings or add it to gin.
  5. For a cordial, sharpen the syrup to taste with lemon juice, citric acid or the flowering currant vinegar below; this also helps it keep.
  6. Dilute to drink.

Flowering currant vinegar and shrub

Ingredients
  • Flowering currant flowers and young leaves
  • cold white wine or apple cider vinegar
  • flowering currant syrup or cordial, or honey, for a shrub or oxymel
Method
  1. Use the flowers and young leaves; with flowers alone the results turn pink.
  2. Infuse them straight into cold white wine or apple cider vinegar for a week, then strain.
  3. Use it in salad dressings or as a pickling liquor — the author pickles magnolia petals and Japanese knotweed in it.
  4. Mix the vinegar with flowering currant syrup or cordial for a shrub, or with honey for an oxymel, to add fruity sourness to gin drinks.

Flowering currant champagne

The author's elderflower champagne with flowering currant flowers in place of the elderflowers. He gives no amount; for a subtler flower he says to use more plant material than the 10–16 elderflower heads.

Ingredients
  • Flowering currant flowers and young leaves
  • 650 g sugar
  • 4.5 litres of cold water
  • 1 lemon
  • 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar
Method
  1. Dissolve 650 g sugar in 4.5 litres of cold water — warm a little of the water to dissolve the sugar, cool it, then mix it into the rest.
  2. In a large bucket or bowl, combine the sweetened water with the flowers or leaves, the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon, and 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar.
  3. Cover and leave for 4 days, somewhere cool; if mould forms, scrape off the mat of flowers on top and carry on.
  4. Fine-strain into clean screw-top plastic fizzy-drink bottles, leaving a few centimetres of air at the top.
  5. Never use corked bottles, and avoid glass flip-tops: you can't feel the pressure through them, and they are far more dangerous if they burst.
  6. Leave at room temperature for 6–14 days.
  7. From day 6, squeeze the bottles every day, and as soon as the bases start to round out, ease the caps to let off some (not all) of the pressure; a forgotten bottle can explode.
  8. Once it tastes right, move it to the fridge to slow the fermentation, and keep checking the pressure.

The author drinks it between 2 and 4 weeks; it is lightly alcoholic after a week and starts turning vinegary at 5–6 weeks. The source notes that the yeast comes from the flowers, so in a cool room it can take a while to get going.

Japonica jelly

Written for japonica (Chaenomeles, the red-flowered shrub with yellow-green apple-like fruit).

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • japonica fruit (the author gathered about a kilo of windfalls)
  • water
  • sugar — jam (setting) sugar or ordinary sugar — at a kilo for every litre of juice
Method
  1. Keep the fruit for a few days in a bowl in a warm room.
  2. Quarter it, put it in a large pot, just cover with water and boil until soft and mushy.
  3. Strain the juice off the pulp; the author skips the jelly bag and accepts a cloudy jelly.
  4. Measure the juice and boil it with the sugar: with jam sugar, boil vigorously for one minute; with ordinary sugar, keep boiling until a teaspoonful on a cold saucer wrinkles into a set after a few seconds.

The source gives no jarring instructions.

View source recipe

Japonica and tarragon jelly

Written for Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica).

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 750 g Japanese quince
  • water to cover
  • 3 large stalks of tarragon plus 3 more sprigs for chopping
  • caster sugar at 400 g for every 600 ml of juice
  • 3 jam jars and wax discs
Method
  1. Sterilise the jars and lids.
  2. Quarter the fruit and take out the seeds; wrap about half the seeds in muslin (for pectin) and put the bag in a pan with the fruit.
  3. Cover with water, bring to the boil and simmer until tender, 40 minutes to an hour and a half depending on how bletted the fruit was.
  4. Strain through muslin, keeping the liquid (the pulp can go into jam).
  5. Measure the liquid and weigh out the sugar.
  6. Heat the liquid, sugar, tarragon stalks and the seed bag gently, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then bring to a rolling boil without stirring until it reaches 104.5 °C, or passes the fridge test.
  7. Take off the heat, lift out the seed bag and tarragon stalks, stir in the finely chopped tarragon and leave to cool for 10–15 minutes so the herb spreads evenly.
  8. Pour into the sterilised jars to within a couple of mm of the top, lay the wax discs on wax side down and screw the lids on tightly while hot.

View source recipe

Flowering quince jam

Makes about three 250 ml jars

Written for flowering quince (Chaenomeles speciosa), fruit about the size of a small lemon; adapted by the author from a Simply Recipes quince jam.

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 10–12 flowering quinces (about 950 ml, 4 packed cups, once minced)
  • 830 ml (3½ cups) water
  • 30 ml (2 tablespoons) lemon juice
  • the zest of one lemon
  • 700 g (3½ cups) sugar
Method
  1. Wash the fruit and cut it in half; remove the core, seeds and any blemished bits, rinse, and do not peel.
  2. Mince the fruit finely with a large knife or a food processor.
  3. Put two small plates in the freezer for testing the set.
  4. Bring the water to the boil in a large heavy pan, add the minced fruit, lemon juice and zest, lower the heat and simmer until the fruit is soft, about 10 minutes.
  5. Add the sugar, bring back to the boil and stir until it has all dissolved.
  6. Lower the heat to medium-high and cook uncovered, stirring now and then, until the jam turns pink and thickens, about 30–50 minutes.
  7. To test, dab a little hot jam on a cold plate, wait a few seconds and run a finger through it: if the streak stays, it is ready; if not, cook a few minutes more and test again.
  8. Mash with a potato masher for a less chunky jam.
  9. Ladle into sterilised jars, wipe the rims clean, and screw on lids sterilised in boiling water.
  10. Turn the jars upside down under a tea towel; when cool, turn them upright and press the lids.
  11. A lid that springs back has not sealed: keep that jar in the fridge.

View source recipe

Flowering quince jam with cloves and rosewater

Makes 1 litre

Written for Japanese flowering quince (Chaenomeles japonica); the author's own recipe, loosely based on a Greek quince jam.

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 800 g whole fruit (about 600 g once cored and chopped)
  • 400 g sugar
  • 1 lemon (zest and juice)
  • 4–6 whole cloves
  • 1 tablespoon rosewater (optional)
Method
  1. Put the jars in an oven at 75 °C until needed.
  2. Put half the lemon juice in a large bowl and half-fill it with cold water.
  3. Wash, quarter, core and slice the fruit thinly, dropping each handful into the lemon water as you go so it does not brown.
  4. Drain and weigh the fruit; if it is not 600 g, use sugar at 2 parts to 3 parts fruit.
  5. Put the fruit in a stainless steel pan with just enough water to nearly cover it and bring to the boil; cook 5–10 minutes until soft.
  6. Add the sugar, cloves, zest and half the remaining lemon juice, lower to medium heat and cook, stirring now and then with a wooden spoon, until the fruit breaks down and the liquid reduces to the thickness you want.
  7. Add the last of the lemon juice and the rosewater and boil 15 minutes more.
  8. Take off the heat and leave to stand 15–30 minutes, then ladle into the hot jars and seal.
  9. Lower the sealed jars into a tall pot of hot (not yet boiling) water, bring to the boil and process for 5–10 minutes, then cool on a wooden board.
  10. After 12–24 hours, check the seals: any jar that has not sealed goes in the fridge and is eaten within a week.
  11. This makes a soft jam; for a firmer set, use less water at the start or cook the fruit until about half the water has evaporated before adding the sugar.

French mallow Malva nicaeensis 1 recipe

Stuffed mallow leaves

Serves 8

Written for mallow in general; the page names no species. The author was told by Turkish cooks that large mallow leaves are used as wrappers for dolma, and went looking for the biggest-leaved mallows they could find.

Ingredients
  • Large mallow leaves
  • about 240 ml short- or medium-grain rice (not long-grain, which sets hard when cold)
  • about 240 ml water
  • ½ onion, finely chopped
  • about 225 g fresh mushrooms, finely chopped
  • about 80 ml pesto
  • 3 tbsp (45 ml) olive oil
  • salt
Method
  1. Prepare the leaves as you would grape leaves: boil them in salted water for a minute or two, cool them in iced water, and let them drip dry.
  2. Heat a large frying pan over high heat, add the mushrooms and shake the pan often until they give up their water.
  3. When most of it has gone, add the onion, oil and a little salt and fry until the onion starts to colour.
  4. Add the rice, toast it for a minute, then add about 240 ml water and a little salt, turn the heat to medium and cook until the water is absorbed.
  5. Take off the heat, let the rice cool, and stir in the pesto (with a little more oil if the pesto is dry).
  6. Lay a leaf smooth side down, base towards you, and put about a tablespoon of filling in a short log across the bottom, leaving at least 1 cm clear at each side.
  7. Fold the bottom up once, fold in the sides and roll up; leaves vary in size, so adjust the filling to suit.
  8. Pack the rolls seam side down and snug together in a steamer insert or on the bottom of a large pot, up to three layers deep; mallow rolls do not need weighing down.
  9. Add water to just below the rolls, cover, bring to the boil and steam gently for 40 minutes to an hour, until the rice is no longer crunchy.
  10. Serve warm or at room temperature; they keep a week in the fridge.

French rose Rosa gallica 4 recipes

Rose petal jam

Written for apothecary roses (Rosa gallica) and 'Charles de Mills'.

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 4 cups (1 litre) rose petals, cleaned and pressed down into the cup
  • 4 cups (1 litre) sugar
  • 2 cups (500 ml) cold water
  • juice of 2 lemons
  • 1 envelope liquid pectin
  • 2 tablespoons (30 ml) rose water, optional
Method
  1. Put the petals in a large bowl, mix in the sugar by hand, cover tightly and leave in a cool spot for 4 hours so the petals sweat.
  2. Tip into a large saucepan, add the water and stir until the sugar dissolves, then add the lemon juice.
  3. Heat over medium heat until it boils (about 10 minutes), stirring so it does not scorch, and boil for 1 minute.
  4. Add the liquid pectin, return to a rapid boil for 2 minutes and test the set; take off the heat when it gels and stir in the rose water if using.
  5. Skim off foam, ladle into clean half-pint (about 250 ml) jars leaving about 6 mm (1/4 inch) headspace, seal, and process in a water-bath canner for 10 minutes plus the altitude adjustment.
  6. For jelly, strain through cheesecloth before adding the pectin.

The source gives the yield as 5 half-pint jars in the text but says 7 jars in the method.

View source recipe

Sugared rose petals

Method
  1. Written with apothecary rose petals.
  2. Ingredients: 1 pasteurised egg white beaten with a little water (or simple syrup, or prepared meringue powder); granulated sugar; fragrant, unsprayed rose petals, rinsed and patted dry; a small watercolour brush.
  3. Cut off and discard the white base of each petal, which is bitter.
  4. Paint both sides of each petal with the egg wash, sprinkle both sides with sugar, and leave on baking or wax paper to dry overnight.
  5. Petals done with syrup hold their shape less well than with egg wash.
  6. Use as decorations on cakes, puddings, sweets, biscuits and pastries; store in the freezer if not using straight away.

Rose sugar

Method
  1. Written with apothecary rose petals.
  2. Ingredients: fragrant, unsprayed rose petals, rinsed and patted dry; sugar; a clean jar with a seal.
  3. Cut off and discard the white base of each petal.
  4. Sprinkle sugar over the bottom of the jar, then a layer of petals, and keep layering sugar and petals until the jar is full.
  5. Store in a cool, dark cupboard for several weeks; remove the petals before use if you like.

Simmered rose water

Written for unsprayed garden roses generally (damask roses suggested), not for this species.

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 1/2 cup (125 ml) fresh rose petals
  • 1–1 1/2 cups (250–375 ml) water
Method

Garden orache Atriplex hortensis 3 recipes

Romanian orache soup (ciorbă de lobodă)

Serves 4

Written for red garden orache.

Ingredients
  • 3 bunches of garden orache, red or green
  • 1 carrot
  • 1 onion
  • 100 g rice
  • 10 black peppercorns
  • 1–2 eggs
  • 250–500 ml (1–2 cups) borș (the Romanian fermented wheat-bran liquid), or lemon juice, vinegar or sauerkraut juice to taste instead
  • salt
  • a small bunch of fresh lovage
  • 3 litres water
  • sour cream, to serve
Method
  1. Finely chop the onion, grate the carrot and cut the orache leaves into thin strips.
  2. Put the water and peppercorns in a large pot with the onion, carrot and orache, bring to the boil and simmer for 20 minutes.
  3. Add the rice and simmer for 10 minutes more, until it is tender.
  4. Heat the borș in a small pan until it just boils, then stir it into the soup a little at a time, tasting, until it is as sour as you like.
  5. Whisk the egg and pour it slowly into the boiling soup, stirring all the time, so it sets in ribbons.
  6. Season well with salt, turn off the heat and stir in the chopped lovage.
  7. Serve hot, with sour cream on the side.
