Raw chickpea hummus with wild greens

Written for chickweed, nasturtium and onion weed.

Ingredients
  • 500 ml (2 cups) sprouted chickpeas
  • 185 ml (¾ cup) tahini (the author grinds whole sesame seeds instead)
  • 2–4 garlic cloves, minced
  • the juice of 2 large lemons and 1 orange
  • 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil
  • 5 ml (1 tsp) sea salt
  • 5 ml (1 tsp) cumin
  • a big handful of chickweed
  • some nasturtium leaves
  • a small bunch of onion weed leaves
  • a sprig of parsley or another herb
Method
  1. Soak 500 ml (2 cups) chickpeas overnight, drain and rinse them well, and sprout them for 48 hours, rinsing twice a day, until the tails are as long as the peas; or cook them, as the author also allows.
  2. Process the chickpeas with the citrus juice until still slightly chunky, then add everything else and process to the consistency you want.

Wild weed pesto

The author's weeds were chickweed, nasturtium, dandelion, pūhā, ox-eye daisy and plantain, with parsley and garden herbs (the page does not say which plantain). She also adds a handful of New Zealand spinach; it is At Risk and its page says to blanch it first, so it is left out here.

Tabbouleh

Serves 6

Ingredients
  • 1.5 litres (6 cups, loosely packed) flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped by hand
  • 125 ml (½ cup) fine bulgur wheat
  • 250 ml (1 cup) fresh mint leaves, finely chopped
  • 450 g ripe tomatoes, seeded and finely diced
  • 2 cucumbers, seeded and finely diced
  • 1 small red onion, minced
  • the juice of 4 lemons
  • 125 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil
  • sea salt, black pepper and allspice
Method
  1. Soak the bulgur in the juice of two lemons, without water, for 20 minutes.
  2. Wash the parsley whole, dry it completely, then chop it fine with a very sharp knife; a food processor bruises it into a sludge.
  3. Salt the tomato and let it drain for 10 minutes.
  4. Mix everything with the rest of the lemon juice, the oil, salt, pepper and a pinch of allspice, and rest it for 15 minutes so the bulgur finishes softening.
  5. Serve with cos lettuce leaves as scoops.

Parsley-crusted salmon

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 500 ml (2 cups) flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped and completely dry
  • 1.1 kg skin-on salmon fillet, portioned
  • 250 ml (1 cup) panko breadcrumbs
  • 6 garlic cloves, grated
  • 2 lemons, zest and juice
  • 80 ml (⅓ cup) extra virgin olive oil
  • 30 ml (2 tbsp) Dijon mustard
  • salt and black pepper
Method
  1. Mix the parsley, panko, garlic, lemon zest, oil, salt and pepper until the mixture clumps when squeezed; wet parsley would steam the crust soft.
  2. Pat the salmon dry, season it and brush the top thinly with the mustard.
  3. Press the parsley mixture on in a thick, even layer.
  4. Roast at 220 °C for 12–14 minutes, until the crust is set and just golden at the edges.
  5. Rest it for 3 minutes and finish with lemon juice.

Roast potatoes with garlic and parsley

Serves 6

Ingredients
  • 375 ml (1½ cups) chopped flat-leaf parsley, plus leaves to finish
  • 1.4 kg baby potatoes, halved
  • 8 garlic cloves, finely minced
  • 125 ml (½ cup) olive oil or duck fat
  • 85 g butter
  • 125 ml (½ cup) grated parmesan (optional)
  • flaky salt and black pepper
Method
  1. Parboil the potatoes in well-salted water for 8 minutes, drain them and shake them hard in the colander to rough up the edges.
  2. Toss them in hot oil on a preheated oven tray and roast at 220 °C for 35 minutes, turning once, until deep gold.
  3. Warm the butter with the garlic without letting it sizzle.
  4. Tip the potatoes into a bowl, pour the garlic butter over and toss them with the chopped parsley while everything is still very hot; parsley added before roasting turns to bitter black flecks.
  5. Finish with salt, pepper, the cheese if using and a last handful of parsley leaves.

Chicken piccata with parsley

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 250 ml (1 cup) finely chopped flat-leaf parsley, plus leaves to finish
  • 900 g chicken breasts, butterflied and pounded thin
  • 170 g cold unsalted butter, cubed
  • 3 lemons, juiced, plus slices
  • 80 ml (⅓ cup) capers, rinsed
  • 250 ml (1 cup) dry white wine
  • 250 ml (1 cup) flour for dredging
  • olive oil
  • salt and black pepper
Method
  1. Pound the chicken to an even 6 mm, season it and dredge it lightly in seasoned flour.
  2. Sear it in olive oil with a little butter over medium-high heat, 3 minutes a side, until golden, and keep it warm.
  3. Deglaze the pan with the wine, scraping, and reduce it by half; add the lemon juice and capers.
  4. Off the heat, whisk in the cold butter a cube at a time until the sauce is glossy and thick.
  5. Stir in the parsley, chopped at the last moment with a very sharp knife, return the chicken briefly to coat it, and serve with lemon slices and whole parsley leaves.

Giant knotweed Reynoutria sachalinensis 10 recipes

Fermented knotweed pickles

Written for Japanese knotweed; giant knotweed's shoots are eaten the same way.

Ingredients
  • 280 g young knotweed shoots
  • thick ones under 30 cm tall
  • peeled
  • the tips discarded
  • 550 ml water
  • 24 g salt (a 3% brine)
  • 4–5 sprigs fresh dill
  • 1–2 garlic cloves
  • 5 ml (1 tsp) black peppercorns
  • 1–2 small hot chillies
  • a couple of strips of lemon zest
  • 5 ml (1 tsp) dried Sichuan peppercorns
Method
  1. Cut the shoots into 8–10 cm lengths, toss them with the seasonings and pack them into a 1-litre jar.
  2. Dissolve the salt in the water and pour it over.
  3. Put the lid on and leave the jar at room temperature, opening it now and then to let the gas out.
  4. The pickles start to sour in a few days; after that keep them in the fridge or the cupboard.
  5. Brining keeps the stems crisp and stops them turning slimy.
  6. Unpeeled thin shoots ferment too, but are not as good.
  7. Slice them to eat with fish, in fish cakes, or with ramen.
  8. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).

Knotweed sorbet

Makes about 750 ml

Written for Japanese knotweed; giant knotweed's shoots are eaten the same way.

Ingredients
  • 450 g tender young knotweed shoots, leaves removed, peeled if you can
  • 150 g (¾ cup) sugar
  • 250 ml (1 cup) water
  • 2 green apples, peeled and cored (about 210 g)
  • 30 ml (2 tbsp) glucose or corn syrup
  • 30 ml (2 tbsp) cornflour (optional, slows crystals forming)
  • a pinch of salt
  • lime juice to taste
Method
  1. Roughly chop the knotweed and apples, or pulse them in a food processor.
  2. Put them in a large pan with the sugar, water, syrup, cornflour and salt and cook over medium-high heat until the apple is soft, about 10 minutes, then keep cooking until the mixture is thick.
  3. Blend until very smooth; sieve it if your shoots were older.
  4. Cool to room temperature, add lime juice to taste — don't skip it — and churn in an ice-cream maker for 30–45 minutes, until it is as thick as sour cream.
  5. Freeze in a lidded container for at least 2–3 hours.
  6. Add more or less apple to taste.
  7. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).

Knotweed and apple leather

Written for Japanese knotweed; giant knotweed's shoots are eaten the same way.

Ingredients
  • 1.4 kg young knotweed shoots
  • 1.4 kg cooking apples such as Granny Smith
  • 30 ml (2 tbsp) torn mint leaves (optional)
Method
  1. Peel the apples and knotweed, chop both into 2–3 cm pieces and cook in a deep pan over medium heat, stirring now and then, until soft and the knotweed has given up its juice, about 20 minutes; reduce it a little longer if it looks watery.
  2. Blend with the mint until as smooth as you can get it.
  3. Spread about 3 mm thick on non-stick or silicone sheets and dry slowly in a dehydrator or an oven on its lowest setting until completely dry but still pliable.
  4. Store airtight.
  5. Pears can stand in for the apples; with knotweed alone, sweeten it or the leather will be brittle.
  6. Snack for 6–8.
  7. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).

Knotweed and mint mousse

Serves 4

Written for Japanese knotweed; giant knotweed's shoots are eaten the same way.

Ingredients
  • 225 g young knotweed shoots, peeled if you can
  • 100 g (½ cup) sugar, or 80 ml (⅓ cup) maple syrup
  • 3 leaves gelatine (or 15 ml / 1 tbsp powdered)
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) chopped mint
  • 500 ml (2 cups) cream, chilled
  • 30 g (4 tbsp) icing sugar
  • a tiny pinch of salt
Method
  1. Cut the shoots into 2–3 cm pieces, cook with the sugar in a small pan until wilted, and blend to a purée.
  2. Chill a bowl and beaters.
  3. Warm the purée gently without boiling and stir in the mint.
  4. Soak the gelatine in very cold water for 10 minutes until limp, squeeze it out and whisk it into the warm purée, then chill the pan for 10 minutes.
  5. Whip the cream with the icing sugar and salt to stiff peaks.
  6. Whisk the purée to loosen it, fold in a third of the cream, then gently fold in the rest.
  7. Press cling film onto the surface and refrigerate until set, preferably overnight.
  8. Pipe or spoon it out to serve, with toasted cake or biscotti.
  9. Warm spices — cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, nutmeg — can replace the mint.
  10. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).

Grilled knotweed with roe mayonnaise

Written for Japanese knotweed; giant knotweed's shoots are eaten the same way.

Ingredients
  • 10 knotweed tops
  • 200 g raw flatfish or cod roe
  • 400 ml neutral oil such as grapeseed
  • 10 ml (2 tsp) mustard
  • salt, pepper and lemon juice
Method
  1. For the mayonnaise, whisk the roe in a bowl until its structure breaks down.
  2. Add a little oil and whisk hard until the two bind completely, then keep adding oil a little at a time — too much at once and it curdles — until it is firm enough to stay put when the bowl is tipped.
  3. Season with salt, pepper, lemon juice and the mustard and keep it cool.
  4. Rinse the knotweed, cut it into pieces about 20 cm long and grill for a couple of minutes.
  5. Serve with the mayonnaise on the side.
  6. No grill: use a dry frying pan on full heat — you lose the smoky flavour, but it works.
  7. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).

Pink knotweed jelly

Written for Japanese knotweed; giant knotweed's shoots are eaten the same way.

Ingredients
juice
  • 1 litre (4 cups) water
  • 2 litres (8 cups) chopped knotweed stalks
  • leaves removed — stalks about 20–30 cm tall have more flesh and less string than taller ones
jelly
  • 800 ml (3¼ cups) knotweed juice
  • 60 ml (¼ cup) lemon juice
  • one 50 g packet powdered pectin
  • 800 g (4 cups) sugar
Method
  1. Bring the water and chopped stalks to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes.
  2. Cool, then hang the stewed knotweed in a jelly bag or muslin and let it drip for an hour or two, until you have 800 ml of juice.
  3. Put the juice, lemon juice and pectin in a large pan and bring to a rolling boil.
  4. Add all the sugar at once, bring back to a rolling boil and boil for 1 minute, stirring constantly.
  5. Take off the heat, ladle into hot sterilised jars, seal, and process in a boiling-water bath for 10 minutes.
  6. Makes about six 250 ml jars of surprisingly pink jelly; serve it over yoghurt or on bread.
  7. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).

Knotweed curd

Makes 3–4 medium jars

Written for Japanese knotweed; giant knotweed's shoots are eaten the same way.

Ingredients
  • 500 g young knotweed stems, chopped
  • 100 ml water
  • 4 large free-range eggs
  • 200 g butter
  • 150 g caster sugar
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) cornflour
Method
  1. Cook the knotweed with the water for 15 minutes, until it is soft and falling apart.
  2. Pass it through muslin or a fine sieve, pressing only lightly — press too hard and the juice turns green instead of pink — and leave to cool for 30 minutes.
  3. Put the eggs, butter, sugar, cornflour and 250 ml of the juice in a pan over a very low heat and stir until the butter melts, then keep stirring on low for about 10 minutes, until as thick as custard.
  4. Sieve into a clean bowl to catch any scrambled egg, pour into sterilised jars and keep in the fridge; use within 10 days.
  5. On scones or toast, or baked in sweet pastry.
  6. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).

Knotweed syrup

Makes about 500 ml

Written for Japanese knotweed; giant knotweed's shoots are eaten the same way.

Ingredients
  • 300 g chopped knotweed stems — older stems too fibrous to eat are fine here
  • 300 ml water
  • 300 g sugar
Method
  1. Boil the stems and water in a covered pan for 10 minutes, until the stems turn to pulp.
  2. Pour through a fine sieve over a bowl, pressing lightly with a spoon to get out as much juice as you can.
  3. Return the liquid to a clean pan with the sugar and heat for 10 minutes until it has dissolved, then bottle.
  4. It tastes like rhubarb syrup: use it as a cordial, in tea, wherever a recipe calls for rhubarb syrup, or with lemon juice and a pinch of salt as knotweed lemonade.
  5. Cook or burn every peel and trimming, or bag it for the transfer station — never compost it (see Warnings).

Ultimate wild mushroom risotto

Serves 4

Written for mixed wild mushrooms — the author's are puffball (giant or common), dried porcini (cep) and chanterelles.

Ingredients
  • 2 litres good chicken or vegetable stock
  • 30 g dried porcini
  • 150 g chanterelles
  • 1 large onion, finely diced
  • 3 garlic cloves
  • 3 bay leaves
  • 1 courgette, finely diced
  • 1 small leek, finely diced
  • 100 g butter
  • a few sprigs of thyme
  • 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice
  • 300 ml dry white wine
  • 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes
  • 300 g parmesan, finely grated
  • 75 ml double cream
  • a handful of parsley and tarragon, finely chopped
  • the juice of 1 lemon
  • a few drops of truffle oil
  • a sprinkle of hairy bittercress (optional)
Method
  1. Heat 2 litres of good chicken or vegetable stock in a separate pan and add 30 g dried porcini to soak and enrich it.
  2. Sweat 150 g chanterelles in a frying pan until they give up their juice, and strain the juice into the stock.
  3. In a heavy pan, sweat 1 finely diced large onion, 3 garlic cloves, 3 bay leaves, and 1 courgette and 1 small leek (both finely diced) in 50 g of 100 g butter until soft and translucent.
  4. Add a few sprigs of thyme and 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice and stir over a medium heat for a couple of minutes.
  5. Add 300 ml dry white wine and keep stirring as it absorbs.
  6. Add 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes, and the soaked porcini with a little hot stock.
  7. Keep stirring briskly, adding the stock a ladleful at a time; when about half is in, add the chanterelles.
  8. Season, and stop when the rice keeps a hint of bite (no chalkiness) and the risotto is like a very thick soup — you may not need all the stock.
  9. Off the heat, stir in half of 300 g finely grated parmesan, the remaining 50 g butter, 75 ml double cream and a handful of finely chopped parsley and tarragon.
  10. Cover and rest for a few minutes.
  11. Stir in the juice of 1 lemon, check the seasoning and add a little more stock if needed.
  12. Serve in shallow bowls with a few drops of truffle oil, the rest of the cheese on the side, and, if you like, a sprinkle of hairy bittercress for a sharp note.

Puffball parmigiana

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 2 tbsp oil
  • 4 slices of giant puffball, peeled
  • each about 2 cm thick
  • 10 cm square
  • 35 g sweet rice flour or plain flour
  • ½ tsp salt
  • 1 tsp pepper, divided
  • 2 eggs
  • 25 g finely grated parmesan
  • 40 g instant polenta or fine cornmeal
  • ½ tsp garlic powder
  • 250 ml or more tomato pasta sauce
  • about 150 g grated mozzarella
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180 °C.
  2. Mix the flour with the salt and half the pepper in one shallow bowl, beat the eggs in a second, and mix the parmesan, polenta, garlic powder and the rest of the pepper in a third.
  3. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat.
  4. Coat each slice in flour, then egg, then the parmesan mixture, covering every surface, and fry for 2–3 minutes a side until deep golden.
  5. Lay them in a baking dish with a little space between them, spoon a generous 60 ml of tomato sauce down the middle of each and pile about 60 ml of mozzarella on top.
  6. Bake for 30 minutes, until the cheese is bubbling and golden in spots.
  7. To freeze, lay the crumbed, uncooked slices apart on baking paper, freeze them solid, then bag them for up to 3 months; fry them from frozen, then add the sauce and cheese and bake.

Sweet and sour puffball

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 2 tbsp oil
  • 1 tbsp minced ginger
  • 3 garlic cloves, minced
  • 1 jalapeño with its seeds, minced (or 1–2 Thai chillies, or ¼–½ tsp dried chilli flakes)
  • 1 onion, diced
  • 1 red capsicum, in 2 cm pieces
  • 450 g giant puffball, peeled, in 2 cm cubes
  • 375 ml chicken stock, divided
  • 60 ml soy sauce
  • 3 tbsp dark brown sugar
  • 2 tbsp white vinegar
  • 2 tbsp cornflour
  • 4–5 spring onions, sliced on a steep diagonal
  • 125 ml roasted salted peanuts or cashews, roughly chopped
  • cooked rice to serve
Method
  1. Heat the oil over medium heat in a large heavy pan, add the garlic, ginger and chilli, and stir for 1 minute.
  2. Add the onion and capsicum and cook for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the onion is translucent, then add the puffball.
  3. Mix 250 ml of the stock with the soy sauce, sugar and vinegar, pour it over, bring to the boil and cook for 5 minutes, stirring now and then.
  4. Stir the cornflour into the remaining stock, stir it into the bubbling pan with the spring onions and cook until thickened, about 30 seconds.
  5. Sprinkle with the nuts and serve over rice.

Puffball pizza

Ingredients

Method
  1. Brush both sides of each slice with olive oil, then cook the slices until browned and a little dried out, so they are firm enough to hold the toppings: grill them on a barbecue over medium heat for about 10 minutes a side, roast them on a rack over a baking tray at 220 °C for 30 minutes, turning once, or fry them in a little extra oil until golden and drain on paper towels.

  4. Leave for 5 minutes before serving.

Cheesy puffball pasta bake

Serves 6

Ingredients
  • 2–3 tbsp butter or oil
  • 450 g giant puffball, peeled, in 2.5 cm cubes
  • ½ tsp salt
  • 450 g short pasta (macaroni, fusilli or shells)
  • 750 ml tomato- or cream-based pasta sauce
  • 100 g grated aged cheddar
  • 300–400 g grated mozzarella
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180 °C and grease a 23 x 33 cm baking dish.
  2. Cook the pasta in boiling salted water until about 2 minutes short of done, still firm in the centre; keep 125 ml of the cooking water and drain.
  3. Meanwhile heat the butter or oil in a large frying pan, add the puffball and salt (the pan will be very full, but the puffball shrinks) and cook, stirring now and then, until it has given up its moisture, the liquid has evaporated and the cubes are golden in spots, about 10 minutes.
  4. Toss the puffball with the pasta, sauce, reserved water and cheddar, tip into the dish and cover with a thick layer of mozzarella.
  5. Bake for about 30 minutes, until the cheese is bubbling and golden in spots.

Written for puffball; the page does not name the species.

  • 1 small puffball, peeled and cubed (about 500 ml)
  • 1 medium shallot, finely chopped
  • 4 eggs, well beaten

Gorse Ulex europaeus 6 recipes

Gorse flower wine

Written for gorse in Ireland; the page names no species.

Ingredients
  • 2 litres gorse flowers
  • 1 kg sugar
  • 2 lemons, preferably unwaxed
  • 2 oranges
  • 4.5 litres filtered water
  • champagne yeast or a general-purpose white wine yeast
Method
  1. Pick fresh, fully open flowers, ideally on a calm, sunny day.
  2. Start the yeast as the sachet directs.
  3. Simmer the flowers in the water for 15 minutes, then stir in the sugar until it dissolves.
  4. Let it cool a little, pour it into a bucket and add the thinly pared rind and the juice of the lemons and oranges.
  5. When it has cooled to lukewarm (about 35–37 °C), add the yeast, mix well and cover with a cloth.
  6. Stir it every day for 3–4 days, then strain off the solids through a fine sieve into a demijohn, fit an airlock and leave it to ferment for at least five months.
  7. Rack it into a clean demijohn, topping it up to the full amount with boiled and cooled water, and leave it another month.
  8. Filter it, or leave it until completely clear, then bottle it in sterilised bottles; if it is too dry at bottling, add more sugar.
  9. It can take up to nine months to mature.

The authors find champagne yeast (they use 5 g of Lalvin EC-1118) clears the wine much faster than general-purpose yeast.

Gorse flower tea

Serves 2

Written for gorse in Ireland; the page names no species.

Ingredients
  • 2 tablespoons (30 ml) fresh gorse flowers
  • hot water
Method
  1. Wear thick gloves to pick.
  2. Take the flowers off the prickly stalks and leave them somewhere cool outdoors for a few hours so the insects living in them can leave.
  3. Give the flowers a little squeeze to bruise them and put them in a small teapot.
  4. Pour on hot water and leave to infuse for 7–10 minutes, then strain and serve, hot or as iced tea.

Gorse flower cordial

Ingredients
  • 500 ml (2 cups) gorse flowers
  • 1 litre water
  • 375 ml (1½ cups) sugar
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) grated lemon, lime and/or orange zest
  • the juice of 1 lemon, lime or orange
Method
  1. Pick the flowers on a sunny day — the author finds them a little bitter otherwise — plucking small clusters gently; gloves help with the spines.
  2. Bring the sugar, water and zest to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes.
  3. Take it off the heat, stir in the juice and the flowers, and leave until cool, or overnight.
  4. Strain through muslin into a sterilised bottle, cap it and keep it in the fridge.
  5. To keep it longer than a month, bring it back to a simmer and pour it into a warm sterilised bottle; it seals as it cools.
  6. To drink, stir 45–60 ml (3–4 tbsp) into 500 ml of hot, cold or fizzy water.

Ground-ivy, butternut squash and bacon quiche

Serves 6

Ingredients

  • ½ tbsp olive oil
  • salt and pepper
  • 100 g diced bacon
  • 3 eggs
  • 300 ml double cream
  • a handful of ground-ivy
  • a blind-baked pastry case

Method
  1. Toss 200 g butternut squash, in 1 cm dice, with ½ tbsp olive oil, salt and pepper, add 100 g diced bacon, and roast on a tray at 180 °C for 20–25 minutes, turning halfway, until the squash is soft and the bacon crisp; let it cool.

  5. Bake at 180 °C for about 25 minutes, until golden and just set, and let it cool to warm before serving.

Ground-ivy ale

Ingredients
  • 2.3 kg malted barley
  • 15 litres water in all
  • 85 g dried ground-ivy
  • 900 g brown sugar
  • yeast
  • ½ tsp sugar for each bottle
Method
  1. Mash 2.3 kg malted barley in water at 65 °C for 90 minutes, then sparge, slowly adding boiling water until 15 litres in all has gone in.
  2. Add 85 g dried ground-ivy and boil for an hour.
  3. Strain, stir in 900 g brown sugar until it dissolves, cool to 21 °C, pour into the fermenter and add the yeast.
  4. Ferment for about a week, until it has finished, then siphon into bottles each primed with ½ tsp sugar, cap and store.

Hawthorn Crataegus monogyna 10 recipes

Hawthorn berry syrup

Written for hawthorn berries in general; the page names no species.

Ingredients
  • 1 kg haws
  • 200 ml lemon juice
  • 500 g sugar
  • water, to cover
Method
  1. Take the stalks off the haws and rinse them.
  2. Put them in a pan, cover with water and boil for about 10 minutes, then lower the heat and simmer for about an hour, until the berries change colour and are tender.
  3. Strain through a fine sieve or muslin, mashing to press out as much liquid as you can, leaving the stones and skins behind.
  4. Return the liquid to the pan with the sugar and lemon juice, bring it back to the boil and simmer until the sugar has dissolved and it forms a clear syrup.
  5. Take it off the heat and pour it into a bottle.

It keeps about 3 months in the fridge.

Hawthorn and apple fruit leather

Written for Crataegus monogyna, C. laevigata or C. pinnatifida in Tasmania.

Ingredients
  • 1 kg ripe haws, washed
  • 1 kg apples, peeled and chopped
  • a couple of strips of lemon rind
  • 125 ml water
  • honey or maple syrup, to taste
  • fresh ginger, grated or juiced (optional)
Method
  1. Cut five pieces of baking paper to fit your dehydrator or oven trays.
  2. Put the haws, apples, lemon rind and water in a large pot over a low to medium heat.
  3. Stir often so all the fruit cooks and none of it sticks.
  4. When the fruit is mushy and the liquid almost all absorbed, take it off the heat.
  5. Pass the fruit through a sieve fine enough to hold back the stones, and throw the stones away whole.
  6. Sweeten the pulp to taste with honey or maple syrup, adding ginger if you are using it.
  7. Spread the pulp on the baking paper about 4 mm thick, thick enough that it isn't see-through.
  8. Dry it in a dehydrator at about 55 °C, or in the oven on its lowest setting, about 50 °C, for several hours until the leather is dry.
  9. Keep the sheets whole, or cut them into strips and roll them, and store in an airtight container.

Hawthorn jelly

Makes 1 jar; scale up for more

Written for Crataegus monogyna.

Ingredients
  • 680 g (1½ lb) ripe haws
  • 850 ml (1½ pints) water
  • sugar, 450 g for every 570 ml (1 pint) of juice

Method
  1. Strip the haws off their stalks by rolling the clusters between your hands, then wash and drain them.

  3. Strain overnight through muslin or a jelly bag; leave it to drip rather than squeezing if you want a clear jelly.

  • 200 g caster sugar

Method
  1. Pick the blossom in the morning, then rinse it, removing any insects and dirt.

Hwerneh (hedge mustard in yoghurt)

Ingredients
  • Fresh hedge mustard
  • salt
  • 1 litre (4 cups) Greek yoghurt
  • olive oil and warm pita bread, to serve
Method
  1. Wash the hedge mustard four or five times to get rid of the dirt on the leaves.
  2. Take off the thick stalks, keeping the leaves and tender stalks, and cut them into thin strips.
  3. Sprinkle generously with salt and massage it into the leaves.
  4. Leave them in a strainer over a bowl for 6–8 hours, in the fridge if the weather is hot, until they wilt.
  5. Squeeze out as much liquid as you can, a handful at a time; the squeezed greens can be frozen in a freezer bag at this point.
  6. Stir 250 ml (1 cup) of the squeezed hedge mustard into the yoghurt in a jar or bowl until evenly mixed.
  7. Keep it in the fridge for at least 24 hours, better 2–4 days, so the hedge mustard flavours the yoghurt and it ferments slightly.
  8. Serve with a drizzle of olive oil and warm pita bread.

  • 4 garlic cloves
  • 8–10 black peppercorns
  • 3 bay leaves
  • 3–4 whole cloves
Method
  1. Sort and clean the mushrooms, cut off the tough lower stems and wash them in several changes of cold water.
  2. Put them in a large pot, cover with cold water and bring to the boil, skimming off the foam.
  3. Simmer for 15–20 minutes, then drain and rinse them in a colander.
  4. For the marinade, bring the litre of water to the boil, add the salt, sugar, peppercorns, bay leaves and cloves and simmer for 3–5 minutes.
  5. Add the parboiled mushrooms and cook over medium heat for another 15 minutes.
  6. Slice the garlic thinly, add it with the vinegar and simmer 2–3 minutes more, then turn off the heat.
  7. Ladle the hot mushrooms and marinade into sterilised jars, keeping the mushrooms covered by the liquid, seal with sterilised lids, cool to room temperature and refrigerate.
  8. They are ready in about 24 hours and better after a few days.
  9. To serve, drain them and toss with a little olive or sunflower oil and chopped spring onion or red onion.

Sautéed honey mushrooms with onion

Serves 2

Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general.

Ingredients
  • 500 g honey mushrooms
  • 1 large onion (about 120 g)
  • 3 tbsp vegetable oil
  • 20 g butter

  • fresh parsley
Method
  1. Clean the mushrooms, put them in a pot of salted water, bring to the boil and simmer for 15 minutes.
  2. Drain well and pat them as dry as you can with paper towels.
  3. Cut the onion into half-rings and mince the garlic.
  4. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat, add the mushrooms and fry for 10–12 minutes, stirring now and then, until their moisture has gone and they start to brown.

  6. In the last 2 minutes add the butter, garlic, salt and pepper and toss to coat.
  7. Sprinkle with chopped parsley.

Honey mushrooms in sour cream

Written for honey mushrooms (Armillaria) in general.

Ingredients
  • 600 g honey mushrooms
  • 250 g sour cream, at least 20% fat, at room temperature
  • 2 medium onions
  • 40 g butter

  • a small bunch of fresh dill
Method
  1. Clean the mushrooms, boil them in salted water for 15–20 minutes and drain well; chop large ones and leave small ones whole.
  2. Finely dice the onions.
  3. Melt the butter in a deep frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions until translucent, 5–7 minutes.

Hop syrup

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 200 g (1 cup) sugar, or honey
  • 250 ml (1 cup) water
  • enough hop cones, picked green and closed, to sit under the syrup
Method
  1. Make as much syrup as you need to cover the hops.
  2. Warm the sugar and water until the sugar dissolves, without letting it boil, which changes the syrup's texture.
  3. Add the hops and leave them to infuse for at least 30 minutes; the source takes it off the heat after about 15 minutes and lets it finish infusing cold.
  4. Strain and keep in the fridge.

  6. Use it in soft drinks or tea, or with rum and a ginger syrup made the same way for a bitter cocktail.

Hopped cheesecake with citrus glaze

Serves 14; start the hop extract a week ahead

Method
  1. Hop extract (from the same author's 'Homemade Hop Extracts', https://celebrationgeneration.com/homemade-hop-extracts/): put 250 ml (1 cup) fresh hops, gently rinsed, or 180 ml (¾ cup) dried hop 'leaves' (cone petals) in a clean jar, pour over 500 ml (2 cups) good vodka, close tightly and shake.
  2. Keep it in a cool dark place, shaking a couple of times a day, for about a week, then taste: it should be a strong flavouring like vanilla extract, not something to drink.
  3. Strain through a fine sieve and then a coffee filter and bottle.
  4. Crust: 375 ml (1½ cups) graham cracker crumbs; 50 g (¼ cup) sugar; 5 tablespoons melted butter.
  5. Filling: 900 g (2 lb) cream cheese at room temperature; 300 g (1½ cups) sugar; 250 ml (1 cup) sour cream; 250 ml (1 cup) cream; 6 large eggs; juice of 1 lemon; 1 tablespoon hop extract.
  6. Topping: 250 ml (1 cup) citrus marmalade; juice and zest of 1 lemon; 1 teaspoon hop extract; a pinch of salt.
  7. Mix the crumbs, sugar and butter until moistened, press firmly over the base and partway up the sides of a 23 cm (9 inch) springform tin, and chill for at least 1 hour.
  8. Heat the oven to 220 °C.
  9. Beat the cream cheese and sugar just until smooth, add the sour cream, cream, eggs, lemon juice and extract and beat on low just until smooth.
  10. Pour into the crust and chill 10 minutes.
  11. Bake 15 minutes, then turn the oven down to 160 °C and bake 50 minutes more.
  12. Turn the oven off and leave the cake inside to cool for 2 hours without opening the door, then chill for at least 3 hours.
  13. For the topping, whisk everything together in a small pan over medium heat just until smooth and liquid, pour over the cold cake and chill at least 10 minutes before slicing.

Sweet horopito sauce

Written for fresh horopito leaves in New Zealand.

Ingredients
  • 190 ml water
  • 60 ml vinegar
  • 125 ml sugar
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • a good handful of fresh horopito leaves
  • 3–6 garlic cloves, to taste
  • ¼ red capsicum
  • ⅓ medium carrot
  • 1 tablespoon cornflour
  • 10–15 cm piece of fresh ginger
Method
  1. Bring the water, vinegar, sugar and salt to a simmer in a saucepan.
  2. Add the horopito leaves, tearing them a little so they give up their heat and flavour, and simmer for 5–10 minutes.

  6. Mix the cornflour with a little more water, stir it into the hot liquid and simmer for about a minute, until it turns translucent.
  7. Take the pan off the heat.
  8. Grate the ginger, squeeze the juice out of the gratings by hand into the pan and stir it in.
  9. Pour the hot sauce into hot sterilised jars and seal.

It keeps sealed in a cool, dark place for up to 6 months; refrigerate it to be sure. The author uses it as you would sweet chilli sauce.

granita

Japanese cherry Prunus serrulata 6 recipes

Preserved cherry blossoms (sakura no shiozuke) and sakura vinegar

Makes about 1 cup of flowers and 240 ml of vinegar

Ingredients
  • About 50 g cherry blossoms (around 5 very loosely packed cups)
  • 2 tsp flaky or fine sea salt, plus 5 g (1 tsp) more if needed
  • 240 ml rice vinegar
  • 2 tsp umezu (Japanese plum vinegar), if you have it
Method
  1. Pick from an unsprayed tree, choosing flowers that are just starting to open.
  2. Soak them gently in clean water, stirring lightly with your hands, then lay them out to dry or give them a quick, gentle spin in a salad spinner.
  3. Layer the flowers in a small jar, sprinkling each layer with salt, and refrigerate for 3 days.
  4. Cover with the vinegar and refrigerate for another 3 days.
  5. To keep them as a pickle, simply leave the flowers in the vinegar in the fridge; they keep 6 months or more but fade.
  6. To dry them, drain off and keep the vinegar, then spread the flowers on a tray lined with a soft cloth in a warm, dry place out of direct sun, checking once a day — about three days on average — or dry them in a dehydrator at about 35 °C for 6–8 hours.
  7. Keep the heat low, or they turn brown.
  8. Toss flowers left a little moist with a further 5 g (1 tsp) sea salt.
  9. Use the pink sakura vinegar, which is salty, like a seasoned vinegar, for example in sushi rice.

They keep, dried, at room temperature, out of direct sun, for about a year; the vinegar keeps in the fridge for 6 months or more.

Method
  1. Put the blossoms in a dish, pour over enough water just off the boil to cover them, cover the dish and leave to infuse for 24 hours.

Honeysuckle syrup

Ingredients
  • 250 ml fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers (or 125 ml dried)
  • 310 ml water
  • about 200 g sugar
Method
  1. Shake the flowers gently to remove dirt and insects, separate them from the stems and discard any leaves and berries.
  2. Put the flowers in a heatproof glass or ceramic container, pour the boiling water over them, cover and leave at room temperature for 12–24 hours.
  3. Strain through a fine sieve and measure the liquid (about 250 ml).
  4. Heat it with an equal volume of sugar over medium-low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then simmer for one more minute.
  5. Cool and keep in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.

Honeysuckle jelly

Makes about 4 jars of 250 ml

Ingredients
Infusion
  • 625 ml fresh Japanese honeysuckle flowers with the green tips pinched off
  • 750 ml water
Jelly
  • 625 ml of the infusion
  • 2 tbsp lemon juice
  • 500 g sugar
  • one 50 g packet of powdered pectin for low- or no-sugar jams
  • ½ tsp butter (optional, to stop foaming)
Method
  1. Put the flowers in a heatproof container, pour the simmering water over them, stir and cover loosely.
  2. Steep for 12–24 hours, moving it to the fridge after the first 2 hours.
  3. Strain, squeezing the flowers, to get about 625 ml of golden infusion (it freezes for up to 3 months).
  4. Put the infusion in a large pot and stir in the lemon juice.
  5. Take 50 g of the sugar, mix the pectin into it, stir this into the pot and bring to a rolling boil over high heat, stirring constantly.
  6. Add the rest of the sugar all at once, return to a full rolling boil and boil for exactly one minute, still stirring, adding the butter if it foams.
  7. Take off the heat and quickly pour into hot sterilised jars, leaving 5 mm headspace, wipe the rims and seal.
  8. Process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes, or leave unprocessed jars to set for 12–24 hours and keep them in the fridge for about 3 weeks.

Method
  1. To serve: a handful of jellybean ice plant leaves.

Larch needle cordial

Written for European larch. The author makes it by his nettle cordial method, with young larch needles in place of the nettle.

  • Equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar)
  • at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of young larch needles, pressed down

Method
  1. Pick the young needles in spring, while they are bright, almost luminous green and taste sharp, like sorrel.
  2. Make a syrup of equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar), heating gently and stirring until the sugar dissolves.
  3. Add at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of needles, pressed down, or more.
  4. Keep it on the heat until steaming hot, but don't let it boil.
  5. Strain out the needles.
  6. Stir in a little citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar, until it tastes slightly sharp.

It keeps for several weeks in the fridge.

Lemon balm champagne

The author's elderflower champagne with lemon balm leaves in place of the elderflowers, or added to them. He gives no amount for the leaves.

Ingredients
  • 650 g sugar
  • 4.5 litres of cold water
  • lemon balm leaves, or elderflowers and lemon balm leaves
  • the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon
  • 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar
Method
  1. Dissolve 650 g sugar in 4.5 litres of cold water — warm a little of the water to dissolve the sugar, cool it, then mix it into the rest.
  2. In a large bucket or bowl, combine the sweetened water with the flowers or leaves, the juice and quartered skin of 1 lemon, and 3 tbsp white wine or apple cider vinegar.
  3. Cover and leave for 4 days, somewhere cool; if mould forms, scrape off the mat of flowers on top and carry on.
  4. Fine-strain into clean screw-top plastic fizzy-drink bottles, leaving a few centimetres of air at the top.
  5. Never use corked bottles, and avoid glass flip-tops: you can't feel the pressure through them, and they are far more dangerous if they burst.
  6. Leave at room temperature for 6–14 days.
  7. From day 6, check the bottles regularly by squeezing them, and as soon as the bases start to round out, ease the caps to let off some (not all) of the pressure — a forgotten bottle can explode.
  8. Once it tastes right, move it to the fridge to slow the fermentation, and keep checking the pressure.

The author drinks it between 2 and 4 weeks: it is lightly alcoholic after a week and starts turning vinegary at 5–6 weeks. The recipe's yeast comes from the flowers, so in a cool room it can take a while to get going.

Raspberry and lemon balm jam

Makes 5–6 jars of about 250 ml

Ingredients
  • 900 g raspberries
  • 1.1 litres (4½ cups) white sugar
  • 1 bunch lemon balm, flowers removed
  • the juice of 1 lemon (listed in the recipe, though its steps do not say when to add it)
Method
  1. A day ahead (12–14 hours), rub the lemon balm leaves and stalks into the sugar until it is fragrant, cover, and leave it to sit: tender leaves turn black when cooked, so the herb flavours the sugar instead.
  2. Pick out the stalks and any loose leaves.
  3. Sterilise the jars, lids and any equipment, and get a water bath ready.
  4. Heat the raspberries gently in a large non-reactive pan, pressing them against the pan, for about 10 minutes, until very soft and juicy.
  5. Push 250 ml of the fruit through a fine sieve to take out some of the seeds, and return it to the pan.
  6. Add the sugar and stir over low heat until it dissolves, then boil rapidly for 10–15 minutes, until the jam passes the wrinkle test or reaches 104 °C.
  7. Take it off the heat for at least 3 minutes, fill the sterilised jars, and process them in the water bath for 10 minutes.

  1. After a recipe in Janet Ross's Leaves from our Tuscan Kitchen (1899).

  4. Keep the cooked stalks in a sealed container in the fridge.
  5. To serve, cut them into 1 cm pieces and reheat them in their liquid, or brown them in butter.
  6. To serve with roast meat, use red wine for half the stock; it stains them purple.

Lilly pilly jelly

Makes about 2 × 375 ml jars

Method
  1. Wash the fruit well, throwing out any underripe fruit, stems and leaves.
  2. Put it in a pot and add just enough water to cover it, holding the floating fruit down with a plate or lid while you measure.
  3. Bring to the boil and boil for an hour; the fruit will fade to a pale mauve.
  4. Pour the fruit and liquid into a bowl lined with a large cheesecloth, tie the cloth into a bag and hang it over the bowl for several hours or overnight to drip.
  5. Squeeze it only lightly, or the juice turns cloudy.
  6. Measure the juice and, for each cup (250 ml), add 1 cup of sugar and the juice of 1 lemon.
  7. Heat slowly, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then boil, skimming off the foam.
  8. Stay with it: after about 15–20 minutes the bubbles turn thick and syrupy and pop slowly.
  9. Lower the heat so it doesn't scorch, and test by putting a teaspoonful on a plate in the freezer for 5 minutes: if it wrinkles when pushed, it is ready; if not, boil a few minutes more and test again.
  10. No pectin is needed.
  11. Pour into hot, sterilised jars and seal at once with the lids.

Ingredients

Method
  1. Rinse the medlars, mash them into the water in a large pan, bring to a slow boil and simmer 30–40 minutes to free the pulp from the skins and seeds.

Steamed watercress

Serves 4

Written for wild watercress (Nasturtium officinale) by an American chef.

Ingredients
  • 450 g (1 lb) fresh watercress
  • salt
  • soft salted butter or extra virgin olive oil
  • lemon wedges or vinegar, to serve
Method
  1. Wash the watercress, picking out insects and debris, and dry it well, ideally in a salad spinner.
  2. Put a thin film of water in a large pot, fill the pot with the watercress and cover it.
  3. Set it over medium-high heat for a few minutes until the pot is very hot, then lift the lid and stir.
  4. Cover again for a minute or two, stir, and repeat until the watercress has wilted.

Watercress and parmesan tart

Fills a 30 cm tart tin

Ingredients
Pastry
  • 125 g very cold butter
  • 250 g sieved plain flour
  • 50 g finely grated parmesan
  • 1 tsp icing sugar
  • salt
  • plenty of black pepper
  • just enough water
Filling
  • 500 g watercress leaves, with some white flowers kept for garnish
  • 20 g butter
  • the juice of 1 orange
  • 3 large eggs plus 2 extra yolks
  • 300 ml double cream
  • 200 g grated parmesan
  • salt and pepper
  • 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180 °C.
  2. For the pastry, grate 125 g very cold butter into 250 g sieved plain flour, 50 g finely grated parmesan, 1 tsp icing sugar, salt and plenty of black pepper.
  3. Rub together lightly, keeping it cool, then add just enough water to form a rough ball (less water, less shrinking).
  4. Chill for 30 minutes, roll out and line the tin, patching where needed.
  5. Prick the base, chill for 20 minutes, then blind-bake with baking paper and beans for 15 minutes; remove them and bake on until lightly toasted.
  6. For the filling, strip 500 g watercress leaves from the fibrous stalks (some stalk is fine — just a coarser tart), keeping some white flowers for garnish.
  7. Melt 20 g butter in a large heavy pan over a medium heat, add the watercress and the juice of 1 orange, and sweat gently for 10 minutes, stirring often.
  8. Blitz it with its juices, then beat it hard with 3 large eggs and 2 extra yolks, 300 ml double cream, all but a handful of 200 g grated parmesan, and plenty of salt and pepper — the more air, the more it rises.
  9. Pour into the case, sprinkle with the reserved parmesan and 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts, and bake for 20–25 minutes, until bronzed and only slightly wobbly in the middle.
  10. Cool a little and scatter the watercress flowers on top.

  • 4 garlic cloves, sliced
  • 1 avocado, halved and sliced
  • 400 g Greek strained yoghurt
  • 400 g passata
  • rapeseed oil
  • grated cheddar
  • cracked black pepper
Method
  1. Boil the plantain leaves for 3 minutes, drain, squeeze out the water, chop them finely and set aside.
  2. Blanch the aubergine slices in salted water, drain and set aside.
  3. Fry the onion and garlic in a little oil until soft, stir in the plantain for 30 seconds, then add the passata and cook down to a thick sauce; season with black pepper.
  4. Lay half the aubergine in an ovenproof dish and cover it with the avocado slices.
  5. Pour on half the sauce and spread the yoghurt over it.
  6. Add the rest of the aubergine, then the rest of the sauce, and scatter cheese on top.
  7. Bake at 160 °C for about 30 minutes, until done.

Pickled Neptune's necklace

Makes four 250 ml jars (or two 500 ml jars)

Ingredients
  • 1 kg Neptune's necklace
  • 500 ml (2 cups) white wine vinegar
  • 250 ml (1 cup) fine caster sugar
  • 500 ml (2 cups) water
  • 1 slice fresh ginger
  • 5 ml (1 tsp) coriander seeds
  • 5 ml (1 tsp) wild peppercorn berries
  • 5 ml (1 tsp) mustard seeds
Method
  1. Sterilise the jars: wash them well in soapy water, put them in a cold oven and heat it to 110 °C, then leave them for 10 minutes once it gets there, or until completely dry.
  2. Rinse the Neptune's necklace thoroughly in fresh water to remove any sand or tiny stowaways.
  3. Put the ginger and spices in the jars, then pack in the seaweed.
  4. Warm the vinegar, sugar and water in a saucepan over low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then bring to the boil and take off the heat.
  5. Fill the jars with the hot liquid so it covers the seaweed completely and sits 1–2 cm below the rim; let them stand a few minutes and top up if needed.
  6. The seaweed turns brighter green.
  7. To make sure the jars are well sealed, turn them upside down for a few minutes while still warm.
  8. Sealed jars keep up to a year in a cool, dry place away from sunlight; once opened, up to 4 weeks in the fridge.
  9. Use as any other pickle — with cheese, roast vegetables, or a roast sesame dressing.

Baked butternut and nipplewort rice

Written for nipplewort picked in an English garden. The author gives no amounts — use what suits you: butternut squash, peeled and cubed; brown basmati rice; freshly picked nipplewort, chopped; onion and garlic; fresh sage and thyme; vegetable or mushroom stock; olive oil; salt and pepper.

Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180–200 °C and start the rice (for brown basmati, put it in cold salted water, bring it to the boil, then simmer 25–30 minutes; it can go into the oven part-cooked, with more stock, to finish).
  2. Toss the squash with olive oil in a large oven dish and roast it.
  3. When it starts to brown, stir in the chopped onion; when the onion turns translucent, add the garlic and herbs, taking care not to burn them.
  4. When the garlic just colours, add the nipplewort and some stock and cook about 5 minutes more, until the leaves wilt.
  5. Stir in the cooked rice and seasoning, with a little more stock if needed to moisten the rice rather than make soup, and return it to the oven until the rice is hot and has soaked up most of the liquid.
  6. Take out any herb stalks and serve.
  7. Mushrooms roasted with the squash, or chickpeas or other beans, go in well too.

  • red wine vinegar
  • olive oil
Method
  1. Sort the olives by size if you like and discard bruised or damaged fruit.
  2. Rinse and drain.
  3. With a clean, sharp knife make 2 lengthwise cuts about 3 mm deep in each olive.
  4. Put them in a food-grade plastic or glass container, cover with fresh cool water, keep them under with a heavy plate or a sealed bag of water, and close the lid loosely.
  5. Every 24 hours drain and cover with fresh cool water, for 8 to 10 days (up to 20 days for less bitter olives); over-soaking makes them soft and washed-out.
  6. For the finish brine, dissolve 450 g (1½ cups) pickling salt in 3.8 litres (1 US gallon) cool water and add 1 litre (4 cups) red wine vinegar — enough for about 4.5 kg of fresh olives.
  7. Drain the olives, cover with the finish brine, pour 6–10 mm of olive oil over the top, close firmly and keep at about 16–27 °C for about a month to develop the flavour.
  8. Kept airtight in a cool, dark place or the fridge they last about a year.

Mediterranean-style cracked green olives

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • green-ripe olives of any kind
  • pickling salt
  • white wine vinegar
  • optional chopped oregano, lemon slices and garlic cloves
Method
  1. Sort and discard bruised or damaged fruit; rinse and drain.
  2. Strike each olive with the flat of a mallet or a rolling pin just to crack the flesh, without breaking or removing the stone.
  3. Put the cracked olives in a food-grade container, cover with fresh cool water, weigh them under and close the lid loosely.
  4. Drain and replace the water every 24 hours for 6 to 7 days (a few days more for less bitter olives).
  5. For the finish brine, dissolve 450 g (1½ cups) pickling salt in 3.8 litres (1 US gallon) cool water and add 500 ml (2 cups) white wine vinegar — enough for about 4.5 kg of fresh olives.
  6. Drain the olives, cover with the finish brine, add the seasonings if using, close firmly and refrigerate.
  7. They must be kept in the fridge; they are ready after 4 days and keep up to a year in the finish brine.

View source recipe

Greek-style black olives in brine

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • firm, fully coloured (dark red to purplish black) olives picked before the first frost
  • pickling salt
Method
  1. Sort by size so they cure evenly and discard bruised or damaged fruit.
  2. Pack into jars or containers that can be made airtight (a 1-quart, about 1-litre, jar is the smallest recommended).
  3. Make a medium brine of 225 g (¾ cup) pickling salt per 3.8 litres (1 US gallon) cool water, cover the olives, close the lids loosely and keep at about 16–27 °C.
  4. After 7 days replace it with a strong brine of 450 g (1½ cups) salt per 3.8 litres water and close the lids firmly.
  5. Keep the olives in brine for at least 2 months; for less bitter olives replace the strong brine monthly for 2 or 3 months.
  6. If lids bulge from fermentation gas, loosen them carefully to let it out and close again; top up any lost brine with fresh strong brine.
  7. Eat after 2 months if you like them fairly bitter, or after at least 3 months for milder olives.
  8. Kept airtight in a cool, dark place they last at least a year; refrigerate after opening.
  9. To make them less salty, soak overnight in water before eating, then dress with a little olive oil.

View source recipe

Sicilian-style olives in brine

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • fresh green or purple olives
  • unprocessed salt (rock or sea salt)
  • rainwater or other unchlorinated water
  • a little olive oil (optional)
Method
  1. Pick with as little stem as possible and put the olives gently into the bucket so they don't bruise.
  2. There is no need to cut or crack them.
  3. At home put them in a container big enough to hold them all (a chilly bin with a drain plug makes the daily draining easier) and cover with water; it doesn't matter if they float.
  4. Every day drain, give them a rinse and cover with fresh water, for at least 12 days and up to 15 for larger olives; they give off a foamy, slimy liquid as the bitterness leaches out.
  5. On the last day drain and rinse well.
  6. Put the olives in clean food-grade buckets with lids and measure how much water it takes to cover them.
  7. Make a 10% brine: 100 g salt for every litre of that water — take out a few litres, heat them, dissolve all the salt in it, cool completely, then pour back and stir.
  8. Pour a thin layer of olive oil over the top, or weigh the olives under with a plate, so none touch the air.
  9. Close and keep in a cool, dark place for at least 3 months, then taste: leave longer if they are still hard; if too salty, pour off a little brine and top up with water.
  10. Up to 10% vinegar can be added to the brine for flavour.
  11. If any mould appears, throw out the whole batch.

They keep for at least a year in the same brine; spoon into jars as needed, covered with brine, and top up the oil layer.

Salt-water-leached olives in brine

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • green or black (ripe) olives
  • coarse or cooking salt
  • olive oil
  • optional garlic, basil, oregano, thyme or chilli
Method
  1. For green olives, pick once some olives on the tree begin to turn black.
  2. Strip the fruit by hand onto cloth sheets laid under the tree, remove all stems and leaves and rinse in clean water.
  3. Straight away put the olives in a bucket of salt water, 125 ml (½ cup) coarse salt to every 2.5 litres (10 cups) water, with a clean plate on top so that every olive stays under.
  4. Every day (at a stretch every second day) pour the water away and replace it with fresh salt water, for about 20 days for green olives or about 14 days for black.
  5. Bite one to test: they are ready when the bitterness has nearly gone.
  6. Measure the last lot of water you pour off, to know how much brine you need.
  7. Dissolve salt in that much fresh warm water at 250 ml (1 cup) salt to every 2.5 litres (10 cups) water, bring to the boil and leave to cool.
  8. Pack the olives into bottles, pour the brine over until they are completely covered, top with 1 cm of olive oil and seal.
  9. They are ready to eat straight from the brine and keep at least 12 months in a cool cupboard.
  10. For extra flavour, put some in a clean jar with garlic, basil, oregano, thyme or chilli and cover with olive oil.

Baked mushroom gnocchi

Serves 4

Written for oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus) generally, mixed with button mushrooms.

Ingredients
Gnocchi
  • 500 g potatoes
  • 175 g plain (type 00) flour
  • 8 g fine salt
Sauce
  • 300 g oyster mushrooms, cleaned
  • 300 g button mushrooms
  • 100 g prosciutto in one thick slice
  • 1 garlic clove
  • 1 fresh chilli
  • rosemary
  • salt and black pepper
  • olive oil
To finish
  • 150 g aged Valtellina Casera cheese (or another semi-hard cow's cheese), diced
  • 30 g grated Grana Padano
  • butter
Method
  1. Boil the potatoes, starting in cold water, for 30–40 minutes.
  2. Meanwhile tear the oyster mushrooms into rough pieces, slice the button mushrooms about 5 mm thick and dice the prosciutto.
  3. In a large pan fry the garlic and rosemary in a little oil for 1–2 minutes, add the prosciutto and the halved chilli and fry on higher heat for 3–4 minutes.
  4. Add the mushrooms, salt and pepper and cook gently for about 15 minutes; take out the garlic and chilli.
  5. Mash the hot potatoes, work in the flour and salt to a soft but firm dough, roll it into ropes about 2 cm thick and cut them into pieces; roll each over a fork or gnocchi board.
  6. Boil the gnocchi in plenty of water until they float, drain them into the mushroom pan and toss over high heat for a few seconds.
  7. Layer half the gnocchi and half the diced cheese in an oiled baking dish, then the rest of each; dot with butter, scatter the Grana and grind over pepper.
  8. Bake in a 200 °C fan oven for 10 minutes, then grill for 3 minutes to brown.

Greek bread with oregano and olive oil

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 750 g plain flour plus extra for dusting
  • 7 g active dried yeast
  • 1 teaspoon sugar
  • 100 g extra virgin olive oil
  • 1 teaspoon honey
  • 2 teaspoons sea salt
  • 1–1½ cups (250–375 ml) water
  • about 1 tablespoon dried oregano
  • 1 teaspoon coarse sea salt for the top
Method
  1. Stir the yeast into ½ cup (125 ml) warm water with the sugar and 5 tablespoons of the flour; cover and leave somewhere warm for about 30 minutes.

  3. Cover tightly and leave somewhere warm to prove for an hour.
  4. Punch down, shape into a ball on generously floured baking paper, and sprinkle the top with the dried oregano, the coarse salt and a little flour; cover and rest 30 minutes.
  5. Meanwhile heat the oven to 230 °C with a large lidded cast-iron pot inside (the source uses a 5-quart Dutch oven) for 30 minutes.
  6. Lift the dough on its paper into the hot pot and bake covered for 30 minutes, then uncovered for 10–15 minutes until golden and baked through.
  7. Cool slightly before slicing.

Oregon grape Berberis aquifolium 1 recipe

Oregon grape jelly

Written for Oregon grape (Mahonia aquifolium, or its low relative M. nervosa) by a preserving author in Oregon.

Ingredients
  • About 1.6 kg Oregon grape berries
  • water
  • about 450 g (2¼ cups) sugar
Method
  1. Pick about 1.6 kg berries once they are evenly dark; sliding your fingers down a bunch drops them into the basket.
  2. Simmer the berries, covered, with half their volume of water for 15 minutes, mashing them after the first 10.
  3. Let the juice drip through a jelly bag for several hours, then boil it for 10 minutes to reduce it a little.
  4. Combine about 720 ml (3 cups) juice with about 450 g (2¼ cups) sugar in a wide, heavy, non-reactive pan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves.
  5. Raise the heat and boil, skimming now and then, until it begins to jell, which takes only a few minutes: drops falling from a tipped metal spoon thicken and run together.
  6. Skim, pour into three sterilised half-pint (about 240 ml) jars and process in a boiling-water bath for 5 minutes; it should be firm by the next day.

The author advises against doubling the batch. Metric amounts are converted from the source's pounds and cups.

Roast lamb leg with fresh mint topping

Serves 6–8

Written for mint.

Ingredients
Lamb
  • 1 whole lamb leg, bone in
  • 1 bag pickling onions, peeled
  • 500 ml chicken stock and 60 ml flour for the gravy
Marinade
  • 5 cloves garlic, crushed
  • 2 tbsp Dijon mustard
  • 3 anchovy fillets, finely chopped
  • 125 ml finely chopped fresh rosemary
  • 2 tbsp dried marjoram
  • 2 tbsp lemon zest
  • 2 tbsp softened butter
  • 2 tbsp lemon juice
  • 3 tbsp oil

  • 185 ml crème fraîche

  • 1 bunch tarragon, very finely chopped (optional)

Method
  1. Garnish: the green ends of 2 spring onions, cut into thin strips about 8 cm long; a bunch of mint leaves.
  2. Pat the lamb dry, lay it fat side up and make shallow cuts a few centimetres apart.
  3. Mix the marinade, rub it into the cuts, wrap the lamb and chill it for at least 2 hours, better overnight.
  4. Take it out 30 minutes before cooking and heat the oven to 180°C.
  5. Season and roast uncovered, fat side up, for 25–30 minutes per 500 g for medium, basting now and then; add the onions with an hour to go and turn them once.

  7. Meanwhile blend the topping ingredients in a food processor or with a mortar and pestle.
  8. For the garnish, put the spring onion strips and mint leaves in iced water in the fridge for at least an hour so the onion curls, then drain them on paper towels.
  9. For the gravy, pour off the fat and keep the juices in the roasting dish, add the flour mixed with 125 ml water, then the stock, and stir over medium heat for 5–10 minutes until thick, scraping up the browned bits.
  10. Spread the topping over the lamb, garnish, and serve with the onions and gravy.

  • 1 garlic clove, peeled and finely chopped
  • a few sprigs of tarragon, chopped
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) finely chopped curly parsley
  • 22 ml (1½ tbsp) butter
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) cold-pressed rapeseed oil
  • 25 ml double cream
  • 1 slice of good sourdough
  • a knob of butter or bacon fat for the bread, if you like
  • a few watercress leaves
  • a splash of Madeira, if you like
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Warm the oil with 15 ml (1 tbsp) of the butter in a medium frying pan and cook the shallot for a minute or two until soft but not coloured.
  2. Stir in the garlic and give it another minute.
  3. Add the porcini and the rest of the butter and cook for a couple of minutes, tossing the pan if you can.
  4. Stir in the cream, tarragon, parsley, salt and pepper, taste, and add the Madeira if you want it.
  5. Keep cooking until the porcini are cooked through, then check the seasoning.
  6. Toast the sourdough on a chargrill, or fry it in butter or bacon fat.
  7. Spoon the porcini over the toast, scatter with the watercress leaves and serve.

Dried porcini and their stock

Ingredients
  • Fresh porcini
  • a food dehydrator
  • boiling water for soaking
Method
  1. Wipe the caps and stems clean with a damp cloth, without soaking them, as they can turn slimy.
  2. Peel off the brown cap skin if you prefer; if it won't come away easily, pull it off the slices after cutting.
  3. Slice no more than 6 mm thick and spread the slices on dehydrator racks.
  4. Dry at 55–60 °C for two to six hours, depending on how thin the slices are and how many racks you are running.
  5. Stop when they are light and brittle to slightly bendy, with nothing soft left.
  6. Let them cool to room temperature, then seal them in a jar or airtight container and keep them out of the light.
  7. To use, cover a handful with boiling water.
  8. Use both the softened porcini and their soaking broth in risotto, pasta, sauces and other savoury dishes.
  9. You can also drop the dried slices straight into a sauce or stew and let its liquid soften them.

The author finds dried porcini keep for at least one to two years.

Ultimate wild mushroom risotto

Serves 4

Written for mixed wild mushrooms — the author's are dried porcini (cep), puffball and chanterelles.

Ingredients
  • 2 litres of good chicken or vegetable stock
  • 30 g dried porcini
  • 150 g chanterelles
  • 1 finely diced large onion
  • 3 garlic cloves
  • 3 bay leaves
  • 1 courgette, finely diced
  • 1 small leek, finely diced
  • 100 g butter
  • a few sprigs of thyme
  • 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice
  • 300 ml dry white wine
  • 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes
  • salt and pepper
  • 300 g finely grated parmesan
  • 75 ml double cream
  • a handful of finely chopped parsley and tarragon
  • the juice of 1 lemon
  • truffle oil
  • hairy bittercress (optional)
Method
  1. Heat 2 litres of good chicken or vegetable stock in a separate pan and add 30 g dried porcini to soak and enrich it.
  2. Sweat 150 g chanterelles in a frying pan until they give up their juice, and strain the juice into the stock.
  3. In a heavy pan, sweat 1 finely diced large onion, 3 garlic cloves, 3 bay leaves, and 1 courgette and 1 small leek (both finely diced) in 50 g of 100 g butter until soft and translucent.
  4. Add a few sprigs of thyme and 300 g unwashed carnaroli or arborio rice and stir over a medium heat for a couple of minutes.
  5. Add 300 ml dry white wine and keep stirring as it absorbs.
  6. Add 150 g puffball, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes, and the soaked porcini with a little hot stock.
  7. Keep stirring briskly, adding the stock a ladleful at a time; when about half is in, add the chanterelles.
  8. Season, and stop when the rice keeps a hint of bite (no chalkiness) and the risotto is like a very thick soup — you may not need all the stock.
  9. Off the heat, stir in half of 300 g finely grated parmesan, the remaining 50 g butter, 75 ml double cream and a handful of finely chopped parsley and tarragon.
  10. Cover and rest for a few minutes.
  11. Stir in the juice of 1 lemon, check the seasoning and add a little more stock if needed.
  12. Serve in shallow bowls with a few drops of truffle oil, the rest of the cheese on the side, and, if you like, a sprinkle of hairy bittercress for a sharp note.

Wild mushroom pâté

Written for mixed wild mushrooms; the author strongly recommends that some be dried porcini, for their intensity.

Ingredients
  • 1 kg fresh mushrooms, or 250 g dried, or a mix
  • butter or oil
  • 200 g finely grated parmesan or another strong hard cheese
  • up to 500 g cream cheese
  • a large handful of sorrel leaves or a squeeze of lemon juice
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Use 1 kg fresh mushrooms, or 250 g dried (soaked for 30 minutes in boiling water and drained), or a mix.
  2. Chop roughly and cook thoroughly in butter or oil over a medium heat until all the moisture has gone (the juice can be strained off as a mushroom broth).
  3. Cool, then squeeze out any remaining moisture.
  4. Blend in a food processor, then add 200 g finely grated parmesan or another strong hard cheese, up to 500 g cream cheese (less for a more mushroomy pâté), a large handful of sorrel leaves or a squeeze of lemon juice, and salt and pepper, in stages, tasting as you go.
  5. Optional extras: dried porcini powder cooked with the mushrooms, black garlic, finely chopped pickled walnuts stirred through at the end, miso, soy sauce or dried seaweed powder.
  6. Pack into small tubs and label each with the species you used.

Keeps for a week in the fridge, or freeze it.

Prickly pear Opuntia ficus-indica 3 recipes

Prickly pear jam

Ingredients
  • 25–30 prickly pears (about 2 litres of pulp)
  • 200 ml lemon juice
  • 1.5 kg sugar
  • a 3 cm piece of ginger, cut crosshatched
  • 30 g pectin
Method
  1. Wearing good gloves, twist the fruit off the pads with tongs.
  2. Turn each fruit over a gas flame until every surface is scorched and the prickles are burnt off.
  3. Halve the fruit lengthwise, scoop out the seeds with a teaspoon and keep them, flatten the halves and gently scrape the flesh from the skin, then blend it.
  4. Press the seeds through a sieve with a spoon or the back of a plate until what is left is a paste, add the juice to the flesh, and strain the pulp through a sieve to remove all the seeds.
  5. Mix the pectin with the lemon juice, add the sugar and ginger, and stir it into the pulp; the squeezed lemon skins can go in too.
  6. Bring to the boil in a large heavy-based pan, stirring regularly, then boil rapidly for 3 minutes, to 105 °C on a jam thermometer.
  7. To test the set, put a teaspoon of jam on a plate chilled in the freezer or a spoon chilled in iced water: after 2–3 minutes it should be set.
  8. Pour into clean jars heated in a 100 °C oven for a few minutes.
  9. It is best after a few months.

Prickly pear and coriander water kefir

Makes 1.5 litres

Ingredients
  • 50 g water kefir grains
  • 80 g cane sugar
  • 1.2 litres water
  • 1 dried fig
  • 2 tablespoons lemon juice
  • 2 prickly pears
  • 10 sprigs coriander
Method
  1. Dissolve the sugar in the water in a fermentation jar and add the grains, fig and lemon juice.
  2. Leave at room temperature for 24–48 hours, until the fig rises to the surface, then strain, keeping the grains for the next batch.
  3. Wearing gloves, peel the prickly pears, purée them and divide between two bottles with 5 coriander sprigs in each, then top up with the kefir.
  4. Leave at room temperature for about 24 hours, until it is as fizzy as you like, then refrigerate.
  5. The fruit carries a lot of yeast and makes the kefir much fizzier: open the bottles carefully and keep them cool.
  6. A little grated lime zest in the glass is optional.

Sow thistle and chickpea fritters

Makes 6 fritters (2–3 portions)

Written for common sow thistle (Sonchus oleraceus) in Croatia; the recipe names prickly sow thistle as edible too, and any edible greens can stand in.

Ingredients

  • 2 tbsp water or 1 tbsp oil

  • 100 g spelt flour
  • a pinch of baking soda
  • a pinch of salt
  • a pinch of black pepper or other spices
  • 1–2 tbsp oil for frying
Method
  1. Wash and coarsely chop 140 g leaves.
  2. Heat 2 tbsp water or 1 tbsp oil in a pan over low to medium heat, add the leaves and cook until tender, a minute or two.
  3. Drain 250 g cooked chickpeas, keeping 150 ml of their cooking liquid (aquafaba).
  4. Whisk the aquafaba with 100 g spelt flour, a pinch of baking soda and a pinch of salt.
  5. Mash the chickpeas with a fork, mix in the cooked leaves and a pinch of black pepper or other spices, then stir in the batter.
  6. Heat 1–2 tbsp oil in a pan (or use a dry non-stick pan) over low to medium heat, spoon in ladlefuls and cook 2–3 minutes a side, until golden-brown on both sides.

Pōhutukawa fizzy drink

Makes 2.5 litres

Ingredients
  • 1 litre (4 cups) pōhutukawa stamens (stripped from the flowers)
  • 250 ml (1 cup) crushed strawberries
  • the flowers of 1 elderflower head (optional)
  • 375 ml (1½ cups) golden sugar
  • 1 sliced lemon
  • 2.5 litres water
Method
  1. The fizz comes from the wild yeasts on the flowers and strawberries, so use spray-free strawberries and don't wash either; keep as much of the pollen as you can when picking.
  2. Stir the sugar, water and lemon in a large jar until the sugar dissolves, then add the stamens, elderflowers and strawberries and push them under.
  3. Cover with muslin held by a rubber band, and date it.
  4. Stir hard every day for 3–4 days; it is fermenting when the flowers rise and bubbles appear as you stir.
  5. Strain through muslin into flip-top bottles and leave at room temperature for 1–2 days, checking the fizz, then refrigerate once it is as fizzy as you like.
  6. Serve cold; the cold slows the fermentation, so it keeps a long time in the fridge.

  • 60 g sow thistle leaves

Method
  1. Soak 100 g hazelnuts in boiling water for an hour, then drain and rinse well.

  1. Wash and coarsely chop 140 g leaves.

Tamarillo and quince baked cheesecake

Makes one 26 cm cake

Quinces must be cooked; the author warns not to bite into a raw one.

Ingredients
Base
  • 175 g softened butter
  • 115 g unrefined cane sugar
  • 100 g (1 cup) plain flour
  • 50 g rice flour
  • 50 g cornflour

  • 370 g cream cheese at room temperature
  • 350 g ricotta
  • 60 g (¼ cup) liquid honey

  • 2 quinces
  • the juice and zest of 1 lemon
  • 3 tamarillos

Method
  1. Line a 26 cm springform tin and heat the oven to 160 °C.
  2. Cream the butter and sugar, mix in the flours and nuts on slow speed until it just comes together, press it evenly into the tin, prick it and bake 20 minutes.
  3. Beat the cream cheese, ricotta and honey until smooth and scrape into a large bowl.
  4. Whisk the eggs, sugar and vanilla on medium-high for about 10 minutes, until light and fluffy; fold half into the cheese mixture, whisk in the cornflour paste, then fold in the rest gently so you keep the air.

Quince paste

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 700 ml water
  • the juice of 1 lemon

  • 1 kg sugar
Method
  1. Put the cold water and lemon juice in a saucepan.

Quince jelly

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • up to 5 kg quinces
  • water and sugar (the source gives no fixed amounts; sugar is measured against the juice)
Method
  1. Wipe the quinces clean and roughly chop them into medium cubes, unpeeled and uncored.
  2. Put them in a large pot with just enough water to cover, bring to the boil, then simmer gently with the lid on until the flesh turns pink and starts to break down.
  3. Pour the fruit and liquid into a muslin-lined sieve or a jelly bag over a large bowl, tie up the cloth, hang it and leave it to drip overnight.
  4. Next day discard the pulp and measure the juice; you need an equal volume of sugar.
  5. Put a small plate in the freezer.
  6. Bring the juice to the boil in a large pot, stir in the sugar until it dissolves, then boil hard for 10–15 minutes.
  7. Test by dropping a little onto the cold plate: it is ready when it forms a skin.
  8. Take off the heat, skim off any scum and pour into small warm jars to seal.
  9. Fruit picked early in the season sets more firmly; later, riper fruit gives a deeper red jelly.
  10. If jelly has failed before, the author suggests jam setting sugar instead: 1 kg for each litre of juice, boiled for 5 minutes.

Poached quince

Serves 4

Ingredients
Poaching liquid
  • 720 ml cold water
  • 170 g (½ cup) liquid honey
  • 50 g (¼ cup) sugar
  • 4 whole cloves (optional)
  • 1 cinnamon stick
  • two 5 cm strips of lemon peel with as little pith as possible
  • one 6 mm slice of unpeeled fresh ginger
  • 2 teaspoons vanilla extract or paste
  • a pinch of salt
Method
  1. Fruit: 2–3 quinces (about 700–800 g).
  2. Cut a round of baking paper just larger than a 4–5 litre saucepan, to lay on the surface of the liquid.
  3. Put all the poaching ingredients in the pan and bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then take it off the heat.
  4. Without peeling, halve the quinces lengthwise with a large sharp knife, cut out the cores with a sturdy melon baller or cut into quarters and trim the core with a small knife, and slice 6 mm thick.
  5. Put the slices straight into the hot liquid so they are mostly covered, lay the paper round on top and simmer very gently 15–25 minutes, turning once or twice, until tender; check from 10 minutes, as they keep cooking while they cool.
  6. Cool in the liquid, then take out the spices, peel and ginger.
  7. Serve with yoghurt or ice cream, or on pancakes, waffles or porridge.

Keeps up to a week in the fridge in its liquid; the leftover syrup can poach more fruit.

Ingredients

Method
  1. Chop 1.4 kg (3 lb) of the quinces, skin and cores included, and keep the other 900 g (2 lb) aside.

  • olive oil

  • about 50 g dark green leek tops

  1. Heat the oven to 200 °C.

Radish kraut

Makes about 400 g

Ingredients
  • 300 g radishes, washed and finely sliced
  • ½ red pepper, finely chopped
  • 10 ml (2 tsp) sea salt
  • 2.5 ml (½ tsp) demerara sugar
  • 2 crushed garlic cloves
  • 1 red chilli, deseeded and finely chopped
  • still mineral water, if needed
Method
  1. Sterilise a jar first, and plan to check the ferment every day for 4–5 days.
  2. In a bowl, combine 300 g radishes, washed and finely sliced (a mandolin is best), and ½ red pepper, finely chopped, with 10 ml (2 tsp) sea salt and 2.5 ml (½ tsp) demerara sugar, and scrunch them hard with your hands to start the juices running.
  3. Leave for 1 hour, then squeeze again for about 10 minutes.
  4. Add 2 crushed garlic cloves and 1 red chilli, deseeded and finely chopped, and squeeze some more.
  5. Pack it into the jar, pressing down hard (the end of a clean rolling pin works) so there are no air pockets and the brine covers the vegetables, leaving 2–3 cm of space at the top.
  6. If the brine does not cover them, top up with still mineral water — they must be fully under liquid.
  7. Push a scrunched piece of baking paper firmly down on top to keep them under, cover with clean muslin held on with a rubber band, and leave on a cool, dark shelf for 4–7 days, to taste; it ferments faster when warm, slower when cold.
  8. Each day, lift off the muslin and paper to check it and let the gas escape, then cover it again.
  9. When it tastes right, take out the paper and muslin, put the lid on and refrigerate to stop the ferment; it keeps for months.
  10. Use it in salads, hot dogs and burgers.

The author's wild greens were creeping mallow, dandelion, plantain, chickweed and red clover flowers (the page does not say which plantain).

Ingredients
  • 12 creeping mallow leaves
  • 6 dandelion leaves
  • 4 plantain leaves
  • 1 leaf of spinach, sugar beet or beetroot
  • 1 large sprig of sweet basil
  • a handful of chickweed
  • 3 red clover flowers
  • 2.5 ml (½ tsp) turmeric
  • 6 cardamom, freshly ground with 15 ml (1 tbsp) pumpkin seeds
  • a pinch of sea salt
  • 2 peaches
  • 1 banana
  • 30 ml (2 tbsp) Chilean guavas
  • ½ avocado
  • 10 ml (2 tsp) lemon juice
  • 750 ml (3 cups) water
Method
  1. Put the greens in the blender with the water, fruit, spices, salt and avocado and blend for about 60 seconds, until smooth.
  2. Taste it, and add a teaspoon of honey if it needs sweetening.

Red deadnettle rice pilaf

Serves 5–7

Written for Lamium purpureum in the United States.

Ingredients
  • About 2 cups red deadnettle leaves
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 1 large diced shallot
  • 2 minced garlic cloves
  • 1 cup long-grain rice
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 2 cups (about 500 ml) chicken stock
Method
  1. Rinse about 2 cups of red deadnettle leaves and pat dry.
  2. Melt 2 tbsp butter in a lidded saucepan, soften 1 large diced shallot for 4–6 minutes, add 2 minced garlic cloves for a minute or two, then stir in 1 cup long-grain rice to coat it in the butter.
  3. Add the leaves and cook until wilted, 3–5 minutes, with 1 tsp salt.
  4. Pour in 2 cups (about 500 ml) chicken stock, bring to the boil, cover and simmer for 15 minutes, then fluff with a fork.

Deadnettle and chickweed fritters

Makes 4

Written for Lamium purpureum.

Ingredients
  • 1 tbsp coconut oil (plus another 1 tbsp for frying)
  • about 60 g finely chopped red deadnettle flowering tops
  • 2 minced garlic cloves
  • about 45 g finely chopped chickweed
  • 1 beaten egg
Method
  1. Melt 1 tbsp coconut oil in a frying pan over medium-low heat, add about 60 g finely chopped red deadnettle flowering tops and 2 minced garlic cloves and sauté for about 10 minutes, until the garlic just browns.
  2. Add about 45 g finely chopped chickweed and cook until tender, about 2 minutes.
  3. Tip into a bowl, mix in 1 beaten egg, add another 1 tbsp oil to the pan, and fry the mixture as 4 flattened fritters 5–7 cm across, 1–2 minutes a side, until brown and crisp.

Deadnettle with mint and smoked garlic

Red deadnettle rice bake

Serves 4

Written for Lamium purpureum; stinging nettle, dandelion or spinach work too.

Ingredients
  • 1 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 small chopped onion
  • 1 minced garlic clove
  • 1 cup (about 250 ml) washed, dried red deadnettle leaves
  • 1 cup cooked and cooled rice
  • 1 egg
  • 1 cup (250 ml) milk
  • ¼ cup grated cheddar
  • 1 tbsp soy sauce
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 1 tsp pepper
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180 °C and grease a 20 cm square baking dish.
  2. Warm 1 tbsp olive oil in a heavy frying pan over medium heat and sauté 1 small chopped onion, 1 minced garlic clove and 1 cup (about 250 ml) washed, dried red deadnettle leaves for 2 minutes.
  3. Tip into a bowl and mix well with 1 cup cooked and cooled rice, 1 egg, 1 cup (250 ml) milk, ¼ cup grated cheddar, 1 tbsp soy sauce, and 1 tsp each of salt and pepper.
  4. Pour into the dish and bake for 30 minutes.
  5. Serve straight away.

Red deadnettle pesto

Written for Lamium purpureum.

Ingredients
  • 3 packed cups red deadnettle flowering tops
  • 5 garlic cloves
  • ⅓ cup nuts (pecans, walnuts or pine nuts)
  • 1 tsp Italian seasoning
  • 2½ tbsp lemon juice
  • 2–4 pinches of sugar
  • ¾ cup grated parmesan
  • ½–1 cup (125–250 ml) olive oil
Method
  1. Pick the leafy flowering tops, rinse and dry them.
  2. In a food processor, blend 3 packed cups of the tops with 5 garlic cloves, ⅓ cup nuts (pecans, walnuts or pine nuts), 1 tsp Italian seasoning, 2½ tbsp lemon juice, 2–4 pinches of sugar and ¾ cup grated parmesan.
  3. Then drizzle in ½–1 cup (125–250 ml) olive oil until it is as thick as you like, then taste and adjust the seasoning.
  4. To freeze it, leave out the parmesan and stir it in after thawing.

Winter health boosting smoothie
