Red raspberry Rubus idaeus 2 recipes

Wild raspberry jam

Fills 2 jam jars

Written for wild raspberries.

Ingredients
  • About 570 ml (1 UK pint) wild raspberries, pressed down
  • about 285 ml (½ pint) sugar — half the volume of the berries
Method
  1. Put a small saucer in the freezer.
  2. Put the berries and sugar in a heavy-based pan, mash them gently with a potato masher and leave somewhere warm for half an hour so the sugar starts to dissolve in the juice.
  3. Stir well, then heat on low to medium, stirring until the last of the sugar has dissolved.
  4. Bring to a gentle boil; once bubbles cover the surface, skim off the froth and boil for 12 minutes (longer for a bigger batch).
  5. Take off the heat and drop a blob on the cold saucer: as it cools it should set to jam.
  6. If not, boil 2 minutes more and test again.
  7. Pour into sterilised jars and seal with sterilised lids.

Keeps six months unopened in a cupboard; it is ready once cool. The recipe uses about half the sugar of many jams. The author says the cold mashing step keeps more of the flavour.

Raspberry fool

Serves 6

Written for raspberries; the page names no species.

Ingredients
  • 800 g raspberries
  • 55 g icing sugar plus extra for dusting
  • 2 teaspoons rosewater
  • 2 drops vanilla essence
  • the finely grated zest of ¼ lemon
  • 450 ml cream (35% fat)
Method
  1. Put 300 g of the raspberries into 6 glasses.
  2. Blend 350 g more with the icing sugar to a thick purée, then stir in the rosewater, vanilla and lemon zest.
  3. Set aside 170 g of the purée and drizzle a generous tablespoon of the rest over the berries in each glass.
  4. Whip the cream to soft peaks and fold the reserved 170 g of purée through it.
  5. Share this between the glasses, spoon over the last of the purée, top with the remaining raspberries and dust with icing sugar.

The source serves it with home-made sponge fingers (6 eggs, 180 g caster sugar, 180 g plain flour, piped and baked at 220 °C for 7–9 minutes).

Rimu Dacrydium cupressinum 1 recipe

Rimu spruce beer

Written for rimu, from the beer James Cook's crew brewed at Dusky Sound, Fiordland, in March 1773, scaled down from their 10 gallons of molasses to 240 gallons of brew (1 part molasses to 24 parts brew).

Method
  1. Boil small branches of rimu and mānuka in water for two to four hours, until the bark strips off the branches easily, to make a strong brew.
  2. Take the branches out.
  3. Stir in 100 ml molasses for every 2.4 litres of brew (sugar can be used instead; the record gives no amount for it) and bring it back to the boil.
  4. Pour it into a clean fermenting vessel with an equal volume of cold water.
  5. When the whole is lukewarm, add yeast and leave it for a few days.

Rose geranium syrup

Ingredients
  • 250 ml water
  • 200 g sugar
  • 10–12 rose geranium leaves
Method
  1. Put 250 ml water, 200 g sugar and 10–12 rose geranium leaves in a small saucepan, bruising the leaves against the side of the pan with a spoon.
  2. Bring to the boil over moderate heat, cover, take off the heat and leave to stand for at least 30 minutes.
  3. Lift out the leaves and squeeze them into the syrup.

Keeps in the fridge for up to a month, or frozen for up to a year. The source uses it in a chocolate dessert.

View source recipe

Apple and rose geranium jelly

Makes about eight 250 ml jars

Ingredients
  • About 125 ml fresh rose geranium leaves and tender stems, firmly packed
  • 750 ml apple juice
  • one packet of powdered fruit pectin
  • 1.2 kg sugar
Method
  1. Firmly pack about 125 ml of fresh rose geranium leaves and tender stems.
  2. Bring them to the boil with part of 750 ml apple juice, take off the heat and steep for at least 15–20 minutes.
  3. Strain, add the rest of the juice and top up to 750 ml if needed.
  4. Put the juice in a heavy, large saucepan over high heat, add one packet of powdered fruit pectin and bring to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down.
  5. Add 1.2 kg sugar, keep stirring and bring back to a full rolling boil; boil hard for 1 minute, stirring all the time.
  6. Take off the heat, skim off the foam quickly and pour at once into sterilised jars — a whole leaf can be pressed into each jar.
  7. Seal and process for 5 minutes in a hot water bath, following the jar maker's instructions.
  8. Use it to fill or glaze cakes, as a sauce for fresh fruit, or with poultry.

The source's ingredient list also has 30 ml lemon juice, but its method does not say when it goes in.

View source recipe

Pineapple and rose geranium ice

Ingredients
  • 1 litre pineapple juice
  • 10 rose geranium leaves
  • 400 g sugar
  • 125 ml lime juice
  • scented geranium leaves and flowers, to garnish
Method
  1. Warm 1 litre pineapple juice slightly, add 10 rose geranium leaves and bruise them gently against the side of the container with a spoon.
  2. Cover and steep for 30 minutes, then take out the leaves.
  3. Stir in 400 g sugar and 125 ml lime juice until dissolved (warm it a little to speed this up).
  4. Cool, then freeze in an ice-cream maker, or pour into a shallow tray in the freezer and stir with a fork every 30–45 minutes until frozen.
  5. Garnish with scented geranium leaves and flowers.

View source recipe

Rose geranium cream

Ingredients
  • 300 ml fresh cream
  • 4 tablespoons caster sugar
  • 4–6 rose geranium leaves
  • 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed)
  • 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese)
Method
  1. Heat 300 ml fresh cream, 4 tablespoons caster sugar and 4–6 rose geranium leaves in a pot, stirring often, until just short of boiling; do not let it boil.
  2. Take off the heat and cool.
  3. Mash 6–8 boysenberries (fresh, or frozen and thawed) to a purée.
  4. Beat 250 g sour cream (or cream cheese) until smooth, then beat in the purée.
  5. Strain the leaves out of the cream and fold the cream gently into the berry mixture with a spoon.
  6. Cover and chill for several hours or overnight.
  7. Serve on fresh berries or fruit salad instead of cream or yoghurt.

View source recipe

Rose geranium rhubarb crumble

Ingredients
Fruit
  • 6–8 rose geranium leaves
  • the juice and grated rind of two oranges
  • about 190 ml more orange juice
  • 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks
  • about 150 g brown sugar
  • 2 tablespoons cornflour
Topping
  • about 150 g brown sugar
  • about 90 g whole rolled oats
  • about 90 g fine rolled oats
  • about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds)
  • 2 tablespoons soft butter
Method
  1. Roughly chop 6–8 rose geranium leaves and warm them gently with the juice of two oranges plus about 190 ml more orange juice; bring almost to the boil, take off the heat and leave to infuse as it cools.
  2. Cut 10–12 trimmed rhubarb stalks into 1 cm pieces — enough to fill, not overfill, the baking dish.
  3. In a large bowl mix about 150 g brown sugar, 2 tablespoons cornflour and the grated rind of the two oranges, tip in the rhubarb and mix well.
  4. Grease the dish and spread the rhubarb mixture back into it.
  5. Strain the juice over it.
  6. For the topping, mix about 150 g brown sugar, about 90 g whole rolled oats, about 90 g fine rolled oats and about 125 ml mixed seeds and chopped nuts (such as pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds, walnuts, almonds), then rub in 2 tablespoons soft butter.
  7. Press the topping firmly over the rhubarb and around the edges.
  8. Bake at 180 °C for 45 minutes.

Rose geranium sugar

Method
  1. Fill a dry glass jar with alternate layers of rose geranium leaves and caster sugar.
  2. Cover tightly and leave somewhere warm for a week or more, shaking it now and then.
  3. Sieve out the leaves before use, and sprinkle the sugar on custards, biscuits or sponge cakes.

View source recipe

Rose geranium lemonade

Ingredients
  • 250 ml water
  • 200 g sugar
  • 10 clean rose geranium leaves
  • 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice
  • chilled water and ice, to serve
  • a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals, to garnish
Method
  1. Boil 250 ml water with 200 g sugar in a small pot.
  2. Take off the heat, add 10 clean rose geranium leaves and leave until cold, overnight if you can.
  3. Squeeze the leaves out well (repeat with fresh leaves for a stronger flavour).
  4. Add 250 ml fresh lemon or lime juice, bottle and refrigerate; it keeps for up to two weeks.
  5. To serve, stir 1 tablespoon of the concentrate into each cup of chilled water and pour over ice, garnished with a small scented geranium leaf or rose petals.

View source recipe

Rose geranium shortbread

Makes 8 wedges

Ingredients
  • About 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter
  • about 60 g icing sugar
  • about 190 g plain flour
  • ¼ teaspoon salt
  • 1 teaspoon rose water
  • 8 large rose geranium leaves, washed and dried
  • 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar)
  • fresh rose geranium leaves, to serve
Method
  1. Cream about 170 g room-temperature unsalted butter with about 60 g icing sugar until light and fluffy.
  2. Mix about 190 g plain flour with ¼ teaspoon salt, add it to the butter, then mix in 1 teaspoon rose water.
  3. Gather into a ball, wrap and refrigerate for 4–6 hours.
  4. Let it soften a little.
  5. Butter and flour the base of a 20 cm round tin.
  6. On baking paper, pat the dough out to the size of the tin.
  7. Press 8 large, washed and dried rose geranium leaves into the dough in a circle about 2.5 cm in from the edge, lay the dough in the tin leaf side down and pat it out to the edges.
  8. Score it lightly into 8 wedges, sprinkle with 2 tablespoons sugar (or scented sugar) and chill for 45 minutes.
  9. Bake at 160 °C for about 20 minutes, until it just starts to colour.
  10. Cool in the tin, turn out, peel the baked leaves off the base, cut along the marks and serve with fresh rose geranium leaves.

View source recipe

Scented geranium and lemon icing

Written for scented geranium leaves, "preferably with a lemon scent"; no species named.

Ingredients
  • 2–3 scented geranium leaves
  • about 250 g sifted icing sugar
  • a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese
  • 2 teaspoons softened butter
  • 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind
  • lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel, to decorate (optional)
Method
  1. Tear 2–3 scented geranium leaves into small pieces and mix them with about 250 g sifted icing sugar in a small bowl.
  2. Leave somewhere warm overnight so the sugar takes up the scent, then pick out and discard the leaf pieces.
  3. Beat a generous 60 ml softened cream cheese, 2 teaspoons softened butter and 1 teaspoon grated lemon rind, gradually adding the scented icing sugar, until smooth.
  4. Spread over a cooled carrot cake and decorate, if you like, with lemon balm leaves or candied lemon peel.

Rowan tree Sorbus aucuparia 7 recipes

Rowan bud syrup

Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts.

Ingredients
  • Young rowan flower buds and very young leaf buds
  • cold water
  • 100 g sugar per 100 ml of water, or up to twice that
  • 10% vodka (optional)
Method
  1. Put young rowan flower buds and very young leaf buds in a pan and cover them with cold water, measuring the water.
  2. Add 100 g sugar per 100 ml of water, or up to twice that for a thicker syrup that keeps better.
  3. Heat, stirring to dissolve the sugar, and hold it at about 70 °C for a few minutes; the author simmers for no more than 5 minutes, as the almond flavour fades fast with heat.
  4. Leave to cool and strain into sterilised bottles, keeping the syrupy buds for the liqueur.
  5. Add 10% vodka to help it keep, or store it in the fridge, or freeze it in plastic bottles.

View source recipe

Rowan bud liqueur

Written for rowan buds; they contain a cyanogenic glycoside (see Warnings), so treat this as a flavouring in small amounts.

Ingredients
  • The syrup-coated buds left from the rowan bud syrup
  • cheap vodka
  • rowan bud syrup, to taste
Method
  1. Put the syrup-coated buds left from the rowan bud syrup in a jar, cover with cheap vodka and leave for about 4 weeks, shaking now and then.
  2. Strain, then sweeten to taste with the rowan bud syrup — the author aims for about 20–25% alcohol.

Adding more fresh buds to the vodka strengthens the almond flavour, but also extracts more of the cyanogenic glycoside; the author says to drink correspondingly less.

Rowan and crab apple jelly

Ingredients
  • 1.5 kg rowan berries
  • 1.5 kg crab apples (or Bramley apple cores)
  • white sugar, 450 g for every 600 ml of strained juice
  • juice of 1 lemon
Method
  1. Chop the crab apples without peeling or coring and put them in a large heavy pan with the rowan berries.
  2. Just cover with water, bring to the boil, then simmer for about 20 minutes until the fruit is very soft and broken down.
  3. Tip the pulp and liquid into a muslin or clean cotton cloth over a large bowl, tie it up and let it drip for at least 4 hours or overnight; do not squeeze it or the jelly will be cloudy.
  4. Measure the juice into a pan, add 450 g sugar for every 600 ml, add the lemon juice and bring to the boil.
  5. Boil hard for about 10 minutes, then test: spoon a little onto a fridge-cold plate, leave a minute and push it with a finger — if the surface wrinkles it is set; if not, boil a few minutes more and test again.
  6. Take off the heat, pour into clean sterilised jars and seal.
  7. Serve with cheese, game or lamb.

Rowan and orange curd

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 2 cups (500 ml) fresh or frozen rowan berries (freeze fresh ones overnight first)
  • 1/3 cup (80 ml) water
  • 125 g butter
  • 6 egg yolks
  • juice of 1 large orange (1/2 cup, 125 ml)
  • 2/3 cup (160 ml) sugar
Method
  1. Bring the berries and water to the boil in a small pan, then simmer for 10 minutes, pressing the berries now and then to break the skins.
  2. Take off the heat and push the berries through a sieve, keeping the juice and pulp and discarding the skins and seeds; you need 2/3 cup (160 ml), topped up with the cooking liquid if short.
  3. Mix it with the orange juice.
  4. Melt the butter in a heavy pan over medium heat, add the juice, sugar and egg yolks, and cook, whisking often, until thick, 10–15 minutes.
  5. Cool completely; blend it if you want it extra smooth.

Method
  1. Juice: 140 g rowan berries, frozen then thawed; 500 ml water.

  5. Butter a 15 cm square tin.

  7. Dissolve the gelatine in 120 ml just-boiled water, add the vanilla, stir it well into the rowan syrup, and pour half into the tin.
  8. Scatter over the pistachios, stir the rose water into the rest and pour it on top.
  9. Cool, then refrigerate overnight.
  10. Turn out, cut into cubes and roll each in arrowroot or cornflour.

Pan-fried snapper with sautéed sea parsley and warrigal greens

Serves 2

Written for sea parsley (Apium prostratum var. prostratum) sold by a Western Australian native-plant nursery; the recipe is by RiverMint Dining.

Ingredients
  • 350 g skin-on snapper fillets, scaled (keep the bones)
  • 100 g warrigal greens
  • 200 ml vegetable purée, such as turnip, potato or pea
  • 150 g cold butter, cubed
  • 2 sticks celery
  • half an onion, roughly chopped
  • 3 lemons
  • 20 sprigs dried native lemongrass
  • 3 sprigs sea parsley
  • salt and pepper
  • olive oil
Method
  1. Season and dry the fillets and fry them skin side down in hot olive oil for 2 minutes, pressing down so they don't shrink; turn and cook 2 minutes more.
  2. Add a squeeze of lemon and 15 ml (1 Tbsp) butter to the pan, baste, then keep the fish warm in a low oven.
  3. For the sauce, put the juice of a lemon, 10 lemongrass sprigs, the snapper bones, onion and celery in a pan, cover with water, bring to the boil and simmer 15 minutes, skimming.
  4. Strain out the bones, return to the pan and reduce by half, adding more lemongrass to taste; season and strain again.
  5. Over medium heat, whisk in the cold butter a few cubes at a time until the sauce thickens.
  6. Bash the warrigal greens with a rolling pin, boil them for 2 minutes to remove oxalic acid, then drain and squeeze dry.
  7. Blanch the sea parsley on its stems for 15 seconds so it keeps its crunch, refresh in iced water, then pick and dry the leaves and season them.
  8. Sauté the sea parsley and warrigal greens in hot butter.
  9. Spread the purée on the plates, top with the greens and the snapper, crisp skin up, drizzle with the lemongrass sauce and garnish with the sea parsley.
  10. Warrigal greens are New Zealand spinach, which is At Risk in the wild in New Zealand; use cultivated ones.

Shaggy inkcap Coprinus comatus 6 recipes

Shaggy inkcap soup

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 900 g shaggy inkcaps
  • 1 tbsp extra virgin olive oil
  • 1 tbsp unsalted butter
  • 1 large onion, diced
  • 2 celery sticks, diced
  • ½ tsp fine sea salt, plus more to taste
  • 5 garlic cloves, minced
  • 3 sprigs fresh thyme
  • 1 litre low-salt chicken or vegetable stock
  • 250 ml full-fat coconut cream
  • freshly ground black pepper
Method
  1. Wipe the mushrooms clean with a damp cloth or paper towel rather than rinsing them.
  2. Cut each in half, then roughly chop into 2.5 cm chunks.
  3. Heat the oil and butter in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat until the butter melts and foams.
  4. Add the onion, celery and ½ tsp salt and sweat for 7–8 minutes, until the onion is soft and translucent.
  5. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
  6. Add the mushrooms and thyme and cook, stirring now and then, for about 10 minutes, until the mushrooms have released all their liquid.
  7. Pour in the stock, bring to a low boil, then cover and simmer on low for 30 minutes.
  8. Take out the thyme sprigs and purée the soup smooth with a stick blender, or carefully in a blender.
  9. Stir in the coconut cream and cook for about 5 minutes, until slightly thickened and hot through.
  10. Season with salt and pepper.

  • 1 tbsp sliced fresh mint leaves
  • ¼ tsp crushed red pepper flakes
  • freshly ground black pepper
  • lemon wedges to serve (optional)
Method
  1. Cut the mushrooms into large pieces; halve smaller ones.
  2. Heat half the oil in a cast-iron or wide frying pan over medium heat, add the mushrooms and cook them slowly, turning now and then.
  3. If they soak up the oil, add more.
  4. Take your time, until they are golden brown on both sides, seasoning with a pinch of salt halfway.
  5. Push them to the side of the pan, add the garlic and drag the mushrooms through it to coat them in the oil.
  6. Stir in the chilli flakes and mint, check the seasoning and serve with lemon wedges as a side dish.

View source recipe

Stuffed shaggy parasol caps

Serves 3–4

Written for parasol mushrooms (Macrolepiota procera).

Ingredients
  • 6–8 medium caps, still slightly cupped
  • 150 g cream cheese or ricotta
  • 50 g grated parmesan
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
  • 50 g fresh spinach, chopped
  • 3 tbsp panko breadcrumbs
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • salt and black pepper
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 190 °C.
  2. Brush the caps clean and twist off the stems to leave a cavity.
  3. Brush the outside of each cap with olive oil and set them gill side up on a baking tray lined with baking paper.
  4. Wilt the spinach in a drop of oil in a frying pan for 1–2 minutes and squeeze out the excess water.
  5. Mix the cream cheese, spinach, most of the parmesan and the garlic, season and spoon the mixture into the caps.
  6. Mix the panko with a teaspoon of oil and the rest of the parmesan and sprinkle it over.
  7. Bake for 15–20 minutes, until the mushrooms are tender and the topping golden and crisp.
  8. Leave them for 5 minutes before serving; the filling is very hot.

View source recipe

Scrambled eggs with shaggy parasols

Serves 2

Written for parasol mushrooms (Macrolepiota procera).

Ingredients
  • 4 large eggs
  • 150 g mushroom caps, stems removed
  • 30 g butter
  • 1 small onion or shallot
  • 2 tbsp milk or cream
  • 1 tbsp chopped fresh chives
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Cut the caps into small bite-sized squares and finely dice the onion.
  2. Whisk the eggs with the milk, a pinch of salt and pepper until pale and slightly frothy.
  3. Melt half the butter in a non-stick frying pan over medium heat and soften the onion for 2–3 minutes.
  4. Add the mushrooms and cook for about 5 minutes, until tender and lightly browned.
  5. Lower the heat to medium-low, add the rest of the butter, then pour in the eggs.
  6. Let them sit a few seconds until the edges start to set, then push them gently from the edges to the centre with a spatula to form large, soft curds, until mostly set but still glossy.
  7. Take the pan off the heat, fold in the chives and serve at once.

Sheep sorrel Rumex acetosella 2 recipes

Sorrel soup

Serves 4 as a side

Written for sheep sorrel (adapted from Anja Dunk's sorrel soup).

Ingredients
  • 80–100 g sheep sorrel leaves (about 4 handfuls)
  • 60 g spinach leaves (2 large handfuls)
  • 40 g butter
  • 30 g plain flour
  • about 1 litre hot vegetable stock
  • 2 tbsp neutral oil
  • salt and black pepper
Method
  1. Put 80–100 g sheep sorrel leaves (about 4 handfuls) and 60 g spinach leaves (2 large handfuls) in a bowl of water, swish them about, let the dirt settle, then lift them out and dry them.
  2. In a saucepan over a medium heat, melt 40 g butter, add 30 g plain flour and stir for 3 minutes, until light tan.
  3. Whisk in about 1 litre of hot vegetable stock in a slow stream, then barely simmer for 10 minutes, until thickened.
  4. Meanwhile heat 2 tbsp neutral oil in a frying pan and wilt the greens for 60 seconds (the sorrel turns yellowish).
  5. Stir the greens into the soup, blend, and season with salt and black pepper.

Shanghai rice cake stir-fry with shepherd's purse

Ingredients
Ingredients (serves 4)
  • 170 g chicken breast cut into very small
  • thin strips, marinated with 1 teaspoon cornflour
  • 1 teaspoon Shaoxing wine
  • ½ teaspoon sesame oil
  • 1/8 teaspoon white pepper
  • 1/4 teaspoon salt
  • 2 tablespoons oil
  • 150 g shepherd's purse (the source uses frozen, washed, squeezed dry and finely chopped)
  • 1/3 teaspoon salt, or to taste
  • 1/4 teaspoon white pepper
  • 1 teaspoon sesame oil
  • 340 g (12 oz) sliced rice cakes (nian gao), thawed and rinsed
  • 120 ml water or chicken stock
Method
  1. Steps: Mix the chicken with its marinade and set aside while you prepare everything else.
  2. Heat the oil in a wok over high heat and stir-fry the chicken until opaque.
  3. Add the shepherd's purse, salt, white pepper and sesame oil and stir-fry for 30 seconds.
  4. Lay the rice cakes on top of the meat and greens so they don't touch the wok directly, pour in the water or stock, cover and cook for 2–3 minutes — no longer, or the greens turn yellow and the rice cakes go soggy.
  5. Once the rice cakes have softened, mix everything together and serve straight away.

Shepherd's purse and pork wontons (ji cai hun tun)

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 150 g minced pork
  • 150 g shepherd's purse, weighed after cleaning, blanching and squeezing
  • 1 packet shop-bought wonton wrappers
  • 1 spring onion
  • a small piece of ginger
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • 1 teaspoon light soy sauce
  • 1 teaspoon sesame oil
  • 2 teaspoons oil
  • a pinch of sugar or a little chicken bouillon
  • white pepper
  • a small piece of dried seaweed to serve
Method
  1. Steps: Clean the shepherd's purse and blanch it for 45 seconds.
  2. Squeeze out the water, weigh out 150 g (freeze the rest for later) and chop it finely.
  3. Blend the spring onion and ginger with 125 ml (1/2 cup) water to make ginger–spring onion water, and work it slowly into the pork with all the seasonings; leave to marinate about 10 minutes, then mix in the shepherd's purse.
  4. Put about 1/2 teaspoon of filling in the middle of each wrapper, fold and seal with a little water in any shape you like.
  5. Bring half a pot of water to the boil, add the wontons and cook for 3 minutes, add 2 tablespoons of water to calm the boil, and when it boils again they are cooked.
  6. Serve in hot broth with a little seaweed, or with red chilli oil, vinegar and soy sauce.

Naengi-guk (Korean shepherd's purse and clam soup)

Ingredients
Ingredients (serves four)
  • 1 litre water
  • 8–10 dried anchovies
  • a 3 × 4 cm piece of dashima (dried kelp)
  • 80 g shepherd's purse (naengi)
  • 20 g barley shoots (optional)
  • 200 g littleneck clams (about 20)
  • 1 clove garlic, sliced
  • 3 tablespoons doenjang (soybean paste)
  • ½ bundle dallae (Korean wild chive)
Method
  1. Steps: Wipe any white powder off the kelp with a damp paper towel rather than rinsing it.
  2. Soak the shepherd's purse in water for 20–30 minutes so the dirt sinks, rinse under cold running water, and remove wilted yellow leaves and any dirt at the base of the roots.
  3. Scrub the clams 2–3 times under cold running water.
  4. Bring the water, anchovies and kelp to the boil, then simmer on low for about 15 minutes.
  5. Meanwhile blanch the shepherd's purse in boiling water for 10–20 seconds, rinse it under cold water, squeeze out the moisture and cut it into bite-sized pieces.
  6. Lift out the anchovies and kelp, and press the doenjang through a small sieve into the stock to dissolve it.
  7. Add the shepherd's purse, garlic, clams and barley shoots.
  8. When the soup boils and the clams open, sprinkle in the roughly chopped dallae and turn off the heat at once.
  9. Serve hot with rice.

Method

Southern magnolia Magnolia grandiflora 3 recipes

Pickled magnolia petals

Makes 1 jar

Written for magnolias in general; the page names no species, and the author's tree flowers in early spring before its leaves come, so it is a different magnolia.

Ingredients
  • Magnolia petals, enough to fill the jar once chopped
  • 1 cup (250 ml) rice wine vinegar or apple cider vinegar
  • ¼ cup (about 50 g) white sugar
  • a pinch of salt
Method
  1. Pull the petals off the centre of each flower, which is bitter, and throw the centre away.
  2. Leave the petals out for half an hour so any insects can crawl off, then rinse them in cold water.
  3. Chop or shred the petals and pack them into a clean jar.
  4. Warm the vinegar with the sugar and salt over low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, pour it over the petals and press them down until covered.
  5. Let the jar cool to room temperature, then keep it in the fridge — this is a quick pickle, not a ferment.
  6. Taste after a few days.
  7. Use like pickled ginger, with sushi, in stir-fries or in sandwiches.

Magnolia syrup

Written for magnolias in general; the page names no species, and the author's tree flowers in early spring before its leaves come, so it is a different magnolia.

Ingredients
  • 2 cups (500 ml) water
  • 2 cups magnolia petals, more for a stronger taste
  • 1 cup (about 200 g) sugar
Method
  1. Pull the petals off the bitter centre of each flower, leave them out for half an hour for insects to leave, and rinse in cold water.
  2. Dissolve the sugar in the water over low heat, stirring often, then bring it to the boil, add the petals and simmer on low for about 20 minutes.
  3. Lift out the petals and keep simmering the syrup until it is as thick as you want.
  4. Mix with cold water for a drink, or pour over pancakes or ice cream.

Magnolia vinegar

Written for magnolias in general; the page names no species, and the author's tree flowers in early spring before its leaves come, so it is a different magnolia.

Method
  1. Magnolia petals and a vinegar of your choice.
  2. Pull the petals off the bitter centre of each flower, leave them out for half an hour for insects to leave, and rinse in cold water.
  3. Chop the petals, pack them into a jar and cover with unheated vinegar.
  4. Leave at room temperature for a couple of weeks, then strain out the petals and keep the vinegar in the fridge between uses.
  5. Use in salad dressings and marinades.
  6. Infuse petals in vinegar, never in oil: fresh plant material in oil can grow the bacteria that cause botulism.

Pine-fired mussels with orache

Serves 4

Written for spear-leaved orache, this plant.

Ingredients
  • 2 kg mussels, cleaned and de-bearded (foraged ones need thorough cleaning and checking)
  • a basket of very dry pine needles
  • malted barley, enough to cover the tray
  • a splash of whisky (the source uses Bowmore 12 Years Old)
  • 1 garlic clove
  • 2 handfuls of orache leaves
  • a knob of butter
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) olive oil
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Outside, scatter a layer of malted barley over a large metal tray, about 40–50 cm across.
  2. Lay the mussels hinge side up, side by side, in a big circle, and pile pine needles about 20 cm high over them.
  3. Light the needles in several places, upwind of the tray, and blow on them to get them going; the fire is dramatic, so choose the spot with care.
  4. When the needles have burnt down, after 5–10 minutes, pick the mussels out of their shells, carefully, as the shells can be hot.
  5. Heat the butter, olive oil and garlic in a pan over a medium heat for 1 minute, add the orache, cover and cook for 2–3 minutes.
  6. Add the mussels, season with salt and pepper and heat through.
  7. Mussels must be properly cooked: if in any doubt, bring them to a simmer and cook for 2 minutes.
  8. Serve in clean oyster shells.

The source lists the whisky but its method never says where it goes, and it uses the malted barley without listing it.

Stinging nettle Urtica dioica 10 recipes

Nettle pesto

Makes 1 jar

Ingredients
  • 50 g walnuts
  • 50 g nettle leaves (weighed after picking)
  • 20 g pine nuts
  • 2 garlic cloves, minced
  • 30 g basil (stalks and all)
  • the juice of 1 lemon
  • salt and black pepper
  • 125–175 ml extra virgin olive oil
Method
  1. Roast 50 g walnuts at 180 °C (fan) for 7–8 minutes, until lightly browned, and let them cool.
  2. Wearing gloves, pick the leaves off the nettles, discard the thick stalks and wash the leaves well.
  3. Blanch 50 g of leaves (weighed after picking) in boiling salted water for 20–30 seconds, until just wilted, lift them into iced water, then squeeze out as much water as you can — they no longer sting.
  4. Blend the walnuts and nettles with 20 g pine nuts, 2 minced garlic cloves, 30 g basil (stalks and all), the juice of 1 lemon, salt and black pepper, drizzling in 125–175 ml extra virgin olive oil until almost smooth.

Keeps up to a week in an airtight jar in the fridge.

Nettle beer

Makes 6 × 750 ml bottles

Ingredients
  • 1 kg nettle tops
  • 4 litres water
  • 750 g sugar
  • the juice of 1 lemon
  • 25 g cream of tartar
  • a sachet of ale yeast
Method
  1. Sterilise everything first — pots, demijohn, bottles and siphon tube.
  2. Wash and drain 1 kg nettle tops.
  3. Bring 4 litres of water to the boil, add the nettles, boil hard for 15 minutes, then strain into a clean pot.
  4. Stir in 750 g sugar, the juice of 1 lemon and 25 g cream of tartar until dissolved, and leave to cool to room temperature.
  5. Sprinkle a sachet of ale yeast over the surface, cover with muslin or a tea towel and leave overnight.
  6. Next day pour it into a demijohn with a bung and airlock and leave to ferment for up to 6 days.
  7. Siphon into brown bottles, cap them and chill in the fridge for a week before drinking.

Dock, dandelion and nettle puddings

Makes about 35 small puddings or one large one

Written for broad-leaved dock and dandelion, with stinging nettle as a swap for them (pick only the top six or so leaves, before the nettle flowers) and dried nettle in the coating.

Ingredients
  • 400 g pearl barley
  • 4 eggs, for hard-boiling
  • 2 large leeks
  • a little oil
  • about half a supermarket bag of dock and dandelion leaves, washed
  • 3 raw eggs, plus 1–2 more if needed
  • seasoning
  • flour
  • 1 beaten egg
  • 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs
  • 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle (optional)
  • garlic mayonnaise, to serve
Method
  1. Boil 400 g pearl barley until tender, drain and cool.
  2. Hard-boil 4 eggs and chop finely.
  3. Finely chop 2 large leeks and soften them in a little oil.
  4. Blanch about half a supermarket bag of washed dock and dandelion leaves in boiling water for 20 seconds, then plunge into iced water (skip this and the puddings are more bitter and less green); squeeze out every drop of water and chop finely.
  5. Mix the chopped eggs, leeks, barley and greens with 3 raw eggs, and season very well.
  6. Wrap the mixture tightly in a tray covered with cling film, set in a larger tray of hot water, or seal it in a pudding bowl with baking paper, foil and string and stand it in a pan of water reaching at least halfway up.
  7. Steam for 45–60 minutes, in a 160 °C oven or on the hob, until it holds together; if it won't roll into balls, mix in 1–2 more raw eggs and steam longer.
  8. Turn out and serve as one pudding, or roll into small balls while warm and chill them (they freeze individually at this stage).
  9. Roll the chilled balls in flour, then in 1 beaten egg, then in 4 tbsp fine dry breadcrumbs (mixed, if you like, with 4 tbsp dried, ground nettle), and deep-fry for 1–2 minutes until browned; or simply flour and fry them.

Nettle cordial

Ingredients
  • Water and white sugar in equal parts (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar)
  • at least a cupful (about 250 ml) of nettle tops, pressed down, or more
  • citric acid or lemon juice, or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar (optional)
Method
  1. Make a syrup of equal parts water and white sugar (for example 50 ml water to 50 g sugar), heating gently and stirring until the sugar dissolves.
  2. Add a load of nettle tops — the top 3 or 4 pairs of leaves and their stem, picked with gloves — at least a cupful (about 250 ml) pressed down, or more.
  3. Keep it on the heat until steaming hot, but don't let it boil.
  4. Leave to cool, then strain out the nettles (the author dries them in a dehydrator as nettle sweets).
  5. Stir in small amounts of citric acid or lemon juice until it tastes slightly sharp — or a dash of white wine or cider vinegar — or leave it as a syrup.

It keeps for several weeks in the fridge. The recipe works with dried nettles too, with a slightly different flavour.

Chestnut flour

Ingredients
  • Fresh sweet chestnuts
  • a steamer
  • a coarse sieve
  • 500 g resealable freezer bags
Method
  1. Leave freshly gathered nuts somewhere dry for a few days to sweeten.
  2. On a chopping board, cut off the base and brown skin of each nut with a sharp knife, throwing out any that show signs of rot.
  3. Steam them for about 20 minutes.
  4. While they are hot, push them a few at a time through a coarse sieve with the end of a rolling pin to remove the brown inner skin; if they are very hard to push through, they need more steaming.
  5. The sieving dries them to a breadcrumb-like texture.
  6. Pack into 500 g resealable bags and freeze, and thaw before baking or cooking.
  7. Frozen processed chestnuts are best used within six months, and a 500 g bag is enough for a couple of meals for two.

Written for chestnuts in Britain; the page does not name the species.

  • 1 litre vegetable stock
  • 400 g cooked, peeled chestnuts

Method
  1. Warm 1 tbsp of the oil with the butter over medium-low heat and soften the onion for about 10 minutes until translucent.

  3. Add the stock and all but a handful of the chestnuts, season, raise the heat and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring now and then.

  6. Slice the reserved chestnuts.
  7. Fry the extra sage leaves in the remaining oil over medium heat for a few seconds until crisp and drain on paper towels.
  8. Serve topped with the sliced chestnuts and crisp sage, a trickle of olive oil and plenty of black pepper.

The author notes fresh chestnuts work if blanched, peeled and simmered until tender first.

Walnut Juglans regia 3 recipes

Pickled green walnuts

Written for walnuts by New Zealand growers; the page does not name the species.

Ingredients
  • 1 kg fresh green walnuts
  • 250 g salt
  • 2 litres boiling water, in two lots
  • 1 litre malt vinegar
  • 400 g brown sugar
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 1 tsp pickling spice
  • 1 tsp black peppercorns
  • ½ tsp whole cloves
Method
  1. Pick the nuts early, around Christmas, while they are green and before the shell forms: push a sturdy needle through each and throw out any that will not pierce easily.
  2. Wear gloves, as the juice stains skin and is very hard to remove.
  3. Prick the walnuts all over with a fork and put them in a large bowl.
  4. Dissolve half the salt in 1 litre of boiling water, pour it over to cover and leave in a cool place for a week.
  5. Drain, cover with a second brine made the same way and leave another week.
  6. Drain and spread the nuts in one layer on a tray, and set them outside in a sunny spot for 3–4 days, bringing them in at night, until black and dry.
  7. Bring the vinegar, sugar, teaspoon of salt and spices to the boil and simmer about 5 minutes to dissolve the sugar, then cool and strain out the spices.
  8. Bring the liquid back to the boil, pack the walnuts into clean jars and pour it over so every nut is covered.
  9. Cover and keep somewhere dark for at least a month before eating; the growers find them better after 4 months.
  10. Use vinegar-proof lids, or put a layer of cling film between lid and liquid, as vinegar corrodes metal lids and taints the walnuts.

Steamed watercress

Serves 4

Written for wild watercress (Nasturtium officinale) by an American chef.

Ingredients
  • 450 g (1 lb) fresh watercress
  • salt
  • soft salted butter or extra virgin olive oil
  • lemon wedges or vinegar, to serve
Method
  1. Wash the watercress, picking out insects and debris, and dry it well, ideally in a salad spinner.
  2. Put a thin film of water in a large pot, fill the pot with the watercress and cover it.
  3. Set it over medium-high heat for a few minutes until the pot is very hot, then lift the lid and stir.
  4. Cover again for a minute or two, stir, and repeat until the watercress has wilted.
  5. Keep cooking and tasting, adding a splash of water if it dries out, until it is tender: young shoots are quick, older leaves can take 15 minutes or more.
  6. Turn off the heat and pour off what little water is left.
  7. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil and salt, taste, and serve with lemon or a dash of vinegar, or butter at the table.

The author also steams it in a steamer basket over 5–8 cm of boiling water, covered on low heat, until tender, but prefers the pot method for watercress.

Watercress and parmesan tart

Fills a 30 cm tart tin

Ingredients
Pastry
  • 125 g very cold butter
  • 250 g sieved plain flour
  • 50 g finely grated parmesan
  • 1 tsp icing sugar
  • salt
  • plenty of black pepper
  • just enough water
Filling
  • 500 g watercress leaves, with some white flowers kept for garnish
  • 20 g butter
  • the juice of 1 orange
  • 3 large eggs plus 2 extra yolks
  • 300 ml double cream
  • 200 g grated parmesan
  • salt and pepper
  • 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 180 °C.
  2. For the pastry, grate 125 g very cold butter into 250 g sieved plain flour, 50 g finely grated parmesan, 1 tsp icing sugar, salt and plenty of black pepper.
  3. Rub together lightly, keeping it cool, then add just enough water to form a rough ball (less water, less shrinking).
  4. Chill for 30 minutes, roll out and line the tin, patching where needed.
  5. Prick the base, chill for 20 minutes, then blind-bake with baking paper and beans for 15 minutes; remove them and bake on until lightly toasted.
  6. For the filling, strip 500 g watercress leaves from the fibrous stalks (some stalk is fine — just a coarser tart), keeping some white flowers for garnish.
  7. Melt 20 g butter in a large heavy pan over a medium heat, add the watercress and the juice of 1 orange, and sweat gently for 10 minutes, stirring often.
  8. Blitz it with its juices, then beat it hard with 3 large eggs and 2 extra yolks, 300 ml double cream, all but a handful of 200 g grated parmesan, and plenty of salt and pepper — the more air, the more it rises.
  9. Pour into the case, sprinkle with the reserved parmesan and 25 g pine nuts or chopped hazelnuts, and bake for 20–25 minutes, until bronzed and only slightly wobbly in the middle.
  10. Cool a little and scatter the watercress flowers on top.

White clover jelly

Ingredients
  • About 1 litre (4 cups) of fresh white clover blossoms, stems removed
  • 1 litre water
  • 60 ml bottled lemon juice (or 1 tsp citric acid)
  • one 50 g box of regular powdered pectin
  • 1.25 kg (5 cups) sugar
Method
  1. Pour the water, just boiled, over the blossoms, push them under and steep for 15–20 minutes.
  2. Strain, pressing the blossoms gently, and top the tea up with water to 1 litre if it is short.
  3. Stir in the lemon juice and bring it to the boil, then whisk in the pectin until it has dissolved and boil hard for a full minute.
  4. Only then add all the sugar at once — added earlier, the jelly will not set — stir until dissolved, return to a full rolling boil for exactly 1 minute, take it off the heat and skim.
  5. Ladle into prepared jars, leaving 5 mm headspace, and process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes.
  6. Cool undisturbed for 24 hours before checking the seals; refrigerate any that did not seal, and refrigerate after opening.
  7. Do not leave out the lemon juice: it helps the set and makes the jelly acidic enough to can.

White clover flour

Method
  1. Pick white clover blossoms; leaves and stems can stay in, but they taste stronger, so separate them out for a milder flour.
  2. Pick roughly 8 times the volume you want: it shrinks a lot — about 1 litre of blossoms with stems gave 500 ml of blossoms and about 125 ml of flour.
  3. Lay the blossoms out to dry on a screen somewhere well ventilated and out of direct sun (sun dries them in a few hours, but can cost them nutrients).
  4. Grind them in batches in a small blade coffee grinder, or all at once in a food processor on high for about 5 minutes.
  5. Use it for up to a quarter of the flour in a recipe: it will not hold baked goods together on its own.

The recipe gives a flour that tastes mildly sweet and green, like spring peas, with a spongy texture that suits biscuits and soft baking.

Method
  1. Smell each plant first: fennel smells of anise or liquorice, hemlock smells musty.

From Turkey, where wild radish is called eşek turpu or turp ot.

Ingredients
  • 1 bunch of wild radish
  • 45 ml (3 tbsp) olive oil
  • 2–3 garlic cloves
  • lemon juice
  • salt
Method
  1. Wash the leaves well, and pull off the older leaves and the thick lower part of the stems.
  2. Bring a pan of water to the boil, and meanwhile chop the leaves and young stems roughly.
  3. Drop them into the boiling water for only a few minutes, then lift them out and let them cool.
  4. Dress them with the garlic, chopped, the olive oil, lemon juice and salt.

Moroccan mint tea

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • Four teaspoons of gunpowder green tea
  • 1.2 litres of water
  • four teaspoons of sugar
  • four sprigs of fresh spearmint
Method
  1. Boil the water.
  2. Put the tea leaves in the teapot, pour over a cup of the boiling water, swirl, then strain and discard that water.
  3. Add the spearmint and sugar to the rinsed leaves, fill the pot with the rest of the boiling water and steep for 5 minutes.
  4. Pour into glasses from a height to raise a frothy head.

View source recipe

Spearmint sauce

Serves 2, with roast lamb

Ingredients
  • About 25 fresh spearmint leaves
  • 1½ teaspoons demerara sugar
  • about 10–20 ml malt vinegar, to taste
Method
  1. Pick the leaves off and discard the stalks.
  2. Wash the leaves and chop them roughly, adding the sugar as you chop so it blends in.
  3. Put the mint and sugar in a small serving bowl, stir in enough vinegar to cover the mint, and chill until serving.
  4. Best made about 2 hours ahead so the vinegar softens the leaves.

View source recipe

Spearmint syrup

Ingredients
  • About 28 g (1 ounce) fresh spearmint
  • about 1 cup chopped
  • stalks included if you like
  • 250 ml white sugar
  • 250 ml water
Method
  1. Wash and roughly chop the spearmint.
  2. Bring the sugar and water to the boil, lower the heat and cook 4–5 minutes until slightly reduced, then take off the heat.
  3. Stir in the chopped mint, cover and infuse 30–60 minutes.
  4. Strain into a glass jar.
  5. For sweetening cold drinks.

Keeps up to 1 month in the fridge; freeze for longer.

  1. Pour the boiling water over the leaves and steep for about 20 minutes.

Charred snap peas with mint and lemon

Ingredients
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 450 g snap peas
  • 2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced
  • 2 tbsp minced fresh mint
  • 2 tsp lemon zest
  • 1 tbsp lemon juice
  • salt
Method
  1. Heat the oil in a wok or large frying pan over medium-high heat.
  2. Add the peas and garlic and fry over high heat, stirring often, for about 5 minutes, until the peas are tender-crisp and starting to char or blister.
  3. Take off the heat and stir in the mint, lemon zest and juice and a pinch of salt.
  4. Taste, add more lemon juice if you like, and serve warm.

Pea soup with mint pesto

Ingredients
Soup
  • 1 tbsp olive oil
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 250 ml diced brown onion
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
  • 1 litre vegetable stock
  • 1.5 litres fresh or frozen peas
  • 2 spring onions, diced
  • 2 tbsp minced fresh mint
  • 60 ml sour cream
  • salt and pepper
Pesto
  • 125 ml parsley leaves
  • 60 ml mint leaves
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
  • 60 ml pine nuts
  • zest and juice of 1 lemon
  • 55 g Parmesan, grated
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
Method
  1. Heat the oil and butter in a large pot over medium-high heat and cook the onion 5–10 minutes until soft and clear.
  2. Add the soup garlic for a minute, then the stock, and bring to the boil.
  3. Add the peas, bring back to the boil and simmer 1–2 minutes.
  4. Off the heat, stir in the spring onions, mint, sour cream and a pinch of salt and pepper, then blend until smooth and season to taste.
  5. For the pesto, blend the parsley, mint, garlic, pine nuts and lemon zest and juice until smooth, blend in the Parmesan, then trickle in the oil.
  6. Serve warm or chilled, each bowl topped with a big spoonful of pesto.

Steak wraps with pickled vegetables and minted yoghurt

Ingredients
Marinade
  • 4 tbsp low-salt tamari
  • 4 tbsp olive oil
  • 2 tbsp brown rice vinegar
  • 2 tsp minced garlic
  • 1 tsp dried thyme

Pickles
  • 500 ml thinly sliced cucumber

Sauce

Za'atar with Central Otago wild thyme

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 2 tablespoons sesame seeds
  • 1½ tablespoons dried thyme or 2½ tablespoons fresh thyme
  • 2½ teaspoons sumac

Method
  1. Toast the sesame seeds in a dry frying pan over medium heat, tossing, until fragrant and starting to colour.

Wild thyme oatcakes

Makes about 24

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 240 g oats
  • 50 g pumpkin seeds
  • 100 ml boiling water
  • 4 tablespoons butter (or lard, ghee or coconut oil)
  • 20 g picked thyme leaves
  • 1 teaspoon sea salt plus extra to sprinkle
  • goat's cheese and honey to serve
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 165 °C.
  2. Blend half the oats with all the pumpkin seeds to the texture of wholemeal flour.
  3. Pour the boiling water over the butter and stir to melt.
  4. Mix all the dry ingredients in a bowl, then stir in the melted butter to make a soft dough.
  5. Roll it as thin as you can (about 2 mm) straight onto a baking-paper-lined tray, tidy the edges, mark squares and cut them diagonally into triangles.
  6. Sprinkle with sea salt and bake for 10–15 minutes until golden.
  7. Serve with goat's cheese and honey.

The source notes other herbs can be used.

View source recipe

Venison backstrap with Central Otago wild thyme

Method
  1. Pluck the tiny wild thyme leaves and crush them gently in a mortar and pestle, then add roughly ground black pepper and extra virgin olive oil (the source gives no amounts).
  2. Trim the silver skin off a venison backstrap and cut it into manageable lengths.
  3. Rub in the seasoning, wrap tightly in cling film and leave at room temperature for an hour or so before cooking.
  4. Heat the oven to 200 °C.
  5. Heat a heavy ovenproof pan until smoking, sear the backstrap a couple of minutes on each side until browned, then roast for about eight minutes, turning it over four minutes in.
  6. Rest for a good ten minutes, carve into thin slices (about 5 mm), spoon over the juices and scatter with wild thyme leaves and a few sprigs.
  7. Venison tenderloin can be cooked the same way.

Thyme, elderflower and lemon ice lollies

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 500 g golden caster sugar
  • 4 elderflower heads
  • 2 lemons
  • a small bunch of thyme
Method
  1. Put the sugar and 1 litre of water in a pan and bring to a simmer, making sure the sugar dissolves.
  2. Wash the elderflower heads gently under cold water and peel the rind of one lemon into strips.
  3. Take the syrup off the heat and add the elderflower, lemon strips, the juice of the peeled lemon and most of the thyme (keep 5 sprigs).
  4. Cool, cover and steep overnight.
  5. Strain through muslin or a clean tea towel; taste, and dilute with water and more lemon juice if too sweet (it should be a little sweeter than you like, as freezing dulls sweetness).
  6. Put a slice of the second lemon and a small thyme sprig in each of 10 ice-lolly moulds, pour in the liquid, add sticks and freeze overnight.

Purple sprouting broccoli and goat's cheese tart

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 500 g shortcrust pastry
  • plain flour for dusting
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
  • 2 garlic cloves (finely chopped)
  • 4 large eggs
  • 300 ml double cream
  • 100 ml whole milk
  • 1 teaspoon Dijon mustard
  • 4 spring onions (sliced)
  • 100 g soft goat's cheese (crumbled)
  • leaves from 2 thyme sprigs
  • 200 g purple sprouting broccoli (tough outer stem peeled, blanched until tender)
Method
  1. Roll the pastry on a floured surface to about the thickness of a coin, line a deep 24 cm tart tin, prick the base, trim and chill for 30 minutes.
  2. Heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan).
  3. Gently fry the garlic in the oil for 5 minutes until lightly golden.
  4. Line the pastry with baking paper and baking beans, bake 15 minutes, remove the paper and beans and bake 7–10 minutes more until very pale golden; turn the oven down to 160 °C (140 °C fan).
  5. Whisk the eggs, cream, milk and mustard, stir in the garlic and spring onions, pour into the case, scatter over the goat's cheese, thyme leaves and broccoli and press gently level.
  6. Bake 40 minutes until golden and just set, and cool completely before serving.

Braised shoulder of lamb with thyme and rosemary

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 2 tablespoons vegetable oil
  • 2.5 kg lamb shoulder
  • 4 celery sticks
  • 2 carrots and 2 onions (all quartered)
  • 6 garlic cloves
  • 1 bottle red wine
  • 1 litre lamb stock
  • ¼ bunch rosemary
  • ¼ bunch thyme
Method
  1. Season the lamb, brown it in the oil in a large frying pan, skin-side down first, for 4–5 minutes until browned on both sides, and move it to a large roasting tin.
  2. Heat the oven to 170 °C (150 °C fan).
  3. Brown the vegetables and garlic in the same pan for 3–4 minutes and add them to the tin.
  4. Bring the wine, stock, rosemary and thyme to a simmer in the pan and pour over the lamb.
  5. Cover with baking paper and foil and roast for 6 hours.
  6. Uncover, lift the lamb onto a platter and rest it loosely covered; strain the liquid, skim off the fat and simmer 5 minutes to reduce a little.
  7. Serve with the lamb.

Thyme crackers

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 3 teaspoons baking powder
  • 1 teaspoon sea salt
  • 350 g plain flour
  • 90 g cold unsalted butter (diced)
  • 5 sprigs fresh thyme (finely chopped)
  • 140 ml cold water
Method
  1. Mix everything in a mixer until it just forms a dough; do not overmix.
  2. Divide into 6 balls, wrap and chill for 1 hour.
  3. Bring the dough back to room temperature, then roll it through a pasta machine from the widest setting down to setting 2.
  4. Cut into long, thin triangles, lay them on a non-stick baking sheet and bake at 180 °C for 12 minutes.
  5. Cool and keep in an airtight container.

Thyme-roasted potatoes

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 1.2 kg floury potatoes (peeled and cut into chunks)
  • 300 ml vegetable oil
  • 2 tablespoons olive oil
  • 2 tablespoons fresh thyme
  • extra to garnish
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Parboil the potatoes in salted water for 8 minutes, drain, return to the pan and let them steam dry.
  2. Heat the oven to 250 °C and heat the vegetable oil in a large roasting tray until sizzling.
  3. Carefully toss the potatoes in the hot oil with the olive oil, thyme, salt and pepper until slightly roughed up.
  4. Turn the oven down to 180 °C and roast for 45 minutes to 1 hour, turning halfway, until crisp and golden.
  5. Garnish with more fresh thyme.

Willow weed and aubergine spring rolls

Ingredients
  • 200 g willow weed leaves, washed and picked over
  • 1 aubergine (about 300 g)
  • 1 small onion
  • olive oil
  • 1 tsp sun-dried tomato paste
  • 2 tsp tamari or soy sauce
  • a pinch of caster sugar
  • 1 fresh red chilli, seeded and finely chopped
  • 1 tbsp ground coriander seed
  • 4 cloves, ground
  • a little grated nutmeg
  • 12 sheets filo pastry
  • 50–75 g melted butter
  • salt and pepper
Dipping sauce
  • 3 tbsp tamari or soy sauce
  • 2 tbsp cider vinegar
  • 2 tbsp maple syrup, mixed
Method
  1. Heat the oven to 200 °C.
  2. Boil the leaves for 1 minute, cool them in cold water, dry them well in a tea towel and chop finely.
  3. Dice the aubergine and onion finely, toss them in olive oil and roast in a single layer for 25–30 minutes, stirring now and then, until lightly browned.
  4. In a large bowl mix the tomato paste, soy sauce and sugar, add the leaves and roasted vegetables, then the chilli and spices, and season.
  5. Keep the filo under a damp tea towel.
  6. Brush a sheet with butter, fold it in half lengthways, put a tablespoon of filling at one end and roll it up or fold it into triangles, seam underneath.
  7. Set the rolls on a lined baking sheet, brush the tops with butter, sprinkle with sesame seeds if you like, and bake for about 15 minutes until golden.
  8. Serve with the dipping sauce.

Wine-cap stropharia Stropharia rugosoannulata 6 recipes

Sautéed wine caps with garlic and parsley

Serves 2

Ingredients
  • 300 g wine caps
  • 2 tbsp (30 g) butter
  • 1 tbsp olive oil
  • 2 garlic cloves
  • 2 sprigs parsley
  • salt
  • black pepper
  • Wipe the mushrooms clean
  • rinsing quickly and patting dry only if dirty
  • slice caps and stems 5 mm thick

Slice the stems of big mushrooms a little thinner, as they can be fibrous.

Method
  1. Mince the garlic and chop the parsley.
  2. Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat and lay the mushrooms in one layer.
  3. Leave them for 4–5 minutes until deep golden underneath, then stir and cook 5 minutes more until their liquid has gone.
  4. Lower the heat, add the butter and garlic, and stir for 1–2 minutes until fragrant.
  5. Off the heat, season well and toss with the parsley.

View source recipe

Wine cap risotto

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 250 g arborio or carnaroli rice
  • 350 g wine caps
  • 1 litre vegetable or chicken stock
  • 2 shallots
  • 2 garlic cloves
  • 120 ml dry white wine
  • 50 g butter
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 60 g grated parmesan
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Dice the mushrooms, chop the shallots finely and mince the garlic; keep the stock at a gentle simmer.
  2. Fry the mushrooms in 1 tbsp of the oil over medium heat for 7–8 minutes until golden, then lift them out.
  3. Add the rest of the oil and 20 g of the butter and cook the shallots 3–4 minutes until translucent, then the garlic for 1 minute.
  4. Stir in the rice and toast it 2–3 minutes.
  5. Add the wine and stir until it has gone.
  6. Add the hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring often and letting each be absorbed, for 15–18 minutes, until the rice is just tender.
  7. Fold the mushrooms back in.
  8. Off the heat, beat in the remaining 30 g of butter and the parmesan, and season.
  9. For more flavour, steep a small handful of dried mushrooms in the stock first.

Wine cap tagliatelle with cream and thyme

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 300 g tagliatelle or pappardelle
  • 300 g wine caps
  • 150 ml cream
  • 1 small onion
  • 3 garlic cloves
  • 2 sprigs thyme
  • 30 g butter
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 50 g grated parmesan
  • salt and pepper
  • chopped parsley to serve
Method
  1. Cook the pasta in plenty of well-salted boiling water until al dente, keeping 250 ml of the cooking water.
  2. Meanwhile slice the mushrooms, dice the onion and mince the garlic.
  3. Heat the oil and butter in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and cook the onion about 4 minutes until soft.
  4. Add the mushrooms and thyme and cook 6–8 minutes until browned and tender, then the garlic for 1 minute.
  5. Lower the heat, pour in the cream and simmer 2 minutes.
  6. Add the drained pasta and toss, adding splashes of the pasta water until the sauce is smooth and glossy.
  7. Off the heat, remove the thyme stalks, fold in the parmesan, season, and serve with more parmesan and parsley.

Cream of wine cap soup

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 400 g wine caps
  • 700 ml vegetable or chicken stock
  • 150 ml cream
  • 150 g potatoes, peeled and diced
  • 1 large onion
  • 2 garlic cloves
  • 40 g butter
  • 1 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 tsp chopped thyme
  • salt and pepper
Method
  1. Roughly chop the mushrooms, dice the onion and mince the garlic.
  2. Heat the oil and butter in a heavy pot over medium heat and cook the onion about 5 minutes until translucent.
  3. Add the mushrooms and garlic and cook 8–10 minutes, stirring now and then, until shrunk and lightly browned.
  4. Stir in the thyme and potatoes, pour in the stock and bring to a gentle boil.
  5. Cover and simmer on low 15–20 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
  6. Blend about half the soup, leaving plenty of mushroom pieces.
  7. Stir in the cream and warm through on low without letting it boil.
  8. Season and serve with crusty bread.

Grilled wine cap caps

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 4–6 large wine cap caps, stems removed (keep them for stock or a sauté)
  • 4 tbsp olive oil
  • 2 tbsp balsamic vinegar
  • 1 tbsp soy sauce
  • 1 tsp garlic powder
  • ½ tsp dried oregano or thyme
  • ½ tsp black pepper
  • chopped parsley
Method
  1. Wipe the caps clean.
  2. Whisk the oil, vinegar, soy sauce, garlic powder, oregano and pepper, coat the caps all over and leave them 15–20 minutes.
  3. Heat a barbecue or grill pan to medium-high and oil the grill.
  4. Grill the caps gill side up for 4–5 minutes until marked and starting to soften, then turn them and grill 3–4 minutes more, brushing with the leftover marinade.
  5. Serve scattered with parsley, as a side or in a toasted bun with lettuce, tomato and garlic aioli as a vegetarian burger.

Wisteria Wisteria sinensis 1 recipe

Wisteria fizzy drink

Makes 5 litres

Method
  1. Use the flowers only; the rest of the plant is poisonous (see the warnings).
  2. 2–2.5 litres (8–10 cups) wisteria flowers, stripped from the stalks; 750 ml (3 cups) golden sugar; 4 lemons (2 sliced and the juice of the other 2); 5 litres water.
  3. Stir the sugar, water and lemon in a large jar until the sugar dissolves, add the flowers and push them under, leaving room in the jar because the mixture rises and falls as it ferments.
  4. Cover with muslin held by a rubber band, and date it.
  5. Stir hard every day for 3–4 days, until the flowers rise and bubbles appear when you stir.
  6. Strain through muslin into flip-top bottles, leave at room temperature for 1–2 days, checking the fizz, then keep it in the fridge and serve cold.

The source does not say which wisteria; Chinese wisteria is the one recorded wild in New Zealand.

Wood blewit Clitocybe nuda 3 recipes

Blewit omelette

Serves 2

Written for blewits (pied bleu), wild or shop-bought.

Ingredients
  • 100 g blewits
  • 2 eggs
  • 1 spring onion
  • 1 garlic clove
  • butter
  • olive oil
  • Parmesan
  • black pepper
Method
  1. Cut the caps into quarters, or eighths if large, and the stems into pieces of the same size.
  2. Slice the spring onion into thin rings, keeping the white and green apart.
  3. Fry the blewits in olive oil and butter for 5 minutes until well cooked, over moderate heat: too hot and they turn bitter.
  4. Add the white of the spring onion and the sliced or crushed garlic and fry a little longer, with more butter if needed.
  5. Turn the heat up, whisk the eggs well with the green of the spring onion and pour them into the pan.
  6. After a few seconds turn the heat right down and leave about 10 minutes, watching, until the egg is nearly set but still soft and runny on top.
  7. Serve on warm plates with grated Parmesan and black pepper.

Dry-sautéed blewits with shallot and tarragon

Serves 2

Written for blewits.

Ingredients
  • 115 g blewits
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) finely diced shallot
  • a pinch of chopped fresh tarragon
  • salt
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) neutral oil, or unsalted butter
Method
  1. Brush the blewits clean, or swish them in water and dry them on paper towels.
  2. Quarter large ones and halve or leave small ones whole.
  3. Heat a cast-iron pan until hot, add the blewits, season with salt and cook until they have wilted, browned lightly and given up their water.
  4. Add the oil, and a little more if the pan gets dry.
  5. Add the shallot, then the tarragon, and cook a minute or two; check the salt.
  6. Cook the blewits for at least 10 minutes in all.
  7. You can also toss the mushrooms with a small knob of unsalted butter.

View source recipe

Pheasant with blewits and cream

Written for any wild or shop mushrooms; the author made it with blewits.

Method
  1. Chicken or other poultry can replace the pheasant.
  2. 250 ml (1 cup) pheasant, chicken or beef stock; 450 g fresh blewits; 45 g (3 tbsp) butter; 125 ml (½ cup) minced shallot; salt; 5 ml (1 tsp) dried thyme; 60 ml (¼ cup) brandy; 125 ml (½ cup) cream; 450 g pheasant breasts; 250 ml (1 cup) chopped spinach or other greens.
  3. Boil the stock down to about 60 ml and set it aside.
  4. Cut the pheasant into strips or chunks and salt it well.
  5. Cut the blewits into large pieces.
  6. Heat a large frying pan over high heat for 2 minutes, add the blewits and dry-sauté them, shaking the pan often, until they give up their water and it has almost gone.
  7. Add the butter and shallot and cook, stirring, until the shallot is translucent and the blewits start to brown.
  8. Sprinkle over the thyme and a little salt, pour in the brandy and scrape up the browned bits; cook on medium-high until the brandy has almost gone.
  9. Add the reduced stock, the cream and the pheasant, bring to a gentle simmer, then cover and cook on low for about 5 minutes, until the pheasant is just cooked through.
  10. Stir in the greens and serve with crusty bread, egg noodles or mashed potato.

Wood ear Auricularia cornea 2 recipes

Stir-fried wood ear

Serves 2–4

Written for dried black fungus (wood ear); the page does not name the species.

Ingredients
  • 60 ml (¼ cup) dried wood ear
  • 1 tsp potato starch whisked smooth with 60 ml (¼ cup) cold water
  • 5 eggs
  • 1 tsp sesame oil
  • ½ tsp chicken stock powder or MSG
  • ½ tsp rice wine vinegar
  • 4 tbsp vegetable oil
  • 1 small green capsicum, cut in 3 cm pieces
  • 2 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
  • 3 thin slices ginger
  • 1 tbsp oyster sauce
  • 1 tsp Shaoxing wine
  • 1 tsp soy sauce
  • a good pinch of sugar
Method
  1. Soak the wood ear in hot water for 20 minutes, then drain, squeeze out the excess water, trim off the hard base and tear any large pieces smaller.
  2. Beat the eggs with the sesame oil, stock powder, vinegar and a generous drizzle of the starch slurry.
  3. Heat a wok over medium-high heat with 1 tbsp of the oil and stir-fry the capsicum, wood ear, garlic and ginger until the capsicum softens, then tip onto a plate.
  4. Add the rest of the oil and cook the eggs until barely set.
  5. Return the vegetables with the oyster sauce, Shaoxing wine, soy sauce and sugar, thicken with the remaining slurry, toss and serve straight away.

Hot and sour soup with wood ears

Serves 4

Written for wood ear; the recipe does not name the species.

Ingredients
soup
  • about 950 ml (4 cups) light chicken stock
  • ½ tsp grated ginger
  • a 6 mm slice of galangal (optional)
  • 2 tbsp rice wine vinegar
  • 2 tsp red hot sauce such as sambal or chilli-garlic sauce, or to taste
  • 2 tbsp light-coloured mushroom ketchup, or soy or fish sauce
  • about 55 g small fresh yellowfoot chanterelles, or another fresh mushroom such as buna-shimeji or shiitake
  • 5 g dried wood ear or 125 ml (½ cup) fresh
  • a few drops of toasted sesame oil
For finishing
  • about 140 g firm tofu, diced 1 cm (optional)
  • 2 tbsp cornflour mixed to a slurry with a splash of water
  • 1 large egg, beaten
  • a small handful of sliced spring onions

  • sliced culantro or coriander (optional)
Method
  1. If using galangal, bruise it with the back of a knife.
  2. Cover dried wood ear with hot water for 15 minutes, then lift it out, discard the soaking water and cut it into 6 mm strips.
  3. Bring all the soup ingredients, mushrooms included, to a simmer and let it bubble gently for 10 minutes.
  4. Stir in the cornflour slurry and the tofu and let it thicken for a minute or two.
  5. Stir the soup briskly clockwise a few times, then drizzle in the egg slowly in the same direction while it is still swirling.
  6. When the egg has set in ribbons, add the spring onions and coriander, divide among four cups and drizzle with chilli oil if you like.

  • 5 wall lettuce leaves

  • a few celery and small kale leaves, optional
Method
  1. Blend the leaves and flowers with 500–750 ml (2–3 cups) water, then add 1 punnet of strawberries, 1 red apple, 2 kiwifruit and 2 bananas and blend again.

Wild strawberry and redcurrant jam

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 500 g wild strawberries
  • 500 g jam (gelling) sugar
  • 250 ml fresh redcurrant juice (made by cooking about 500 g redcurrants with just enough water to stop them catching for one or two minutes, then sieving)
Method
  1. If possible do not wash the strawberries.
  2. Mix them with half the sugar and leave covered in the fridge overnight.
  3. Heat the rest of the sugar with the redcurrant juice until the sugar dissolves, add the strawberry mixture and cook for about 15 minutes.
  4. Pour straight into sterilised jars and close them tightly.

The source suggests bulking out with homegrown strawberries if you cannot gather 500 g of wild ones.

Alpine strawberry jam

Makes about 500 ml (2 cups)

Written for alpine strawberries, the cultivated form of this species.

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • about 360 g alpine strawberries
  • 400 g sugar
  • 30 ml lemon juice
  • no added pectin
Method
  1. Put everything in a deep saucepan or jam pot and mash with the back of a spoon so some berries break up and release their juice.
  2. Bring to the boil over medium-high heat and boil hard, stirring often, for about 8 to 10 minutes until the jam reaches gel stage.
  3. Ladle into prepared jars leaving about 6 mm (1/4 inch) headspace.
  4. To keep on the shelf, process in a water-bath canner for 10 minutes; otherwise refrigerate and use within a few weeks.

Strawberry vinegar

From the Herb Federation of New Zealand's wild strawberry sheet.

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 500 g berries
  • 750 ml (3 cups) sugar
  • about 940 ml (3¾ cups) wine or cider vinegar
Method
  1. Put the berries in a saucepan, just cover with water and simmer, partly covered, for 30 minutes.
  2. Strain off the juice, ideally overnight, without squeezing the fruit or the vinegar will be cloudy.
  3. Add the vinegar and sugar to the juice and stir over the heat until the sugar dissolves, then bring to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes.
  4. Pour into sterilised bottles.
  5. Use it like a balsamic, for example in dressings.

Wild strawberry cranachan

Ingredients
  • Ingredients for 2 large bowls or 4 small glasses: 240 g (1 cup) Greek or thick yoghurt or whipped cream
  • 200 g (1 cup) wild strawberries
  • 100 g oats
  • a generous knob of butter
  • 2 tablespoons whisky or rum (leave it out for children)
  • 2 tablespoons brown sugar or honey
Method
  1. Melt the butter in a large frying pan and toast the oats until they have soaked up the fat and turned golden brown; let them cool a little.
  2. Fold the sugar or honey and the whisky into the yoghurt or cream.
  3. Spread a layer of oats in the bowls or glasses, cover with the cream mixture, then a generous layer of strawberries, and repeat the layers until full.
  4. Finish with a few strawberries and a sprig of fresh mint.

Roasted wild strawberry jam with balsamic and pepper

Written for wild strawberries or garden strawberries.

Ingredients
Ingredients
  • 400 g wild strawberries
  • 2–3 tablespoons honey
  • 2 tablespoons balsamic vinegar
  • 2 teaspoons freshly cracked black pepper
  • no pectin
Method
  1. Wash the strawberries (garden strawberries are hulled and quartered), mix everything in a shallow baking dish and leave while the oven heats to 120 °C.
  2. Roast for 2–3 hours, stirring a few times, until the berries have shrivelled and reduced to a syrup.
  3. Cool to room temperature, purée if you like it smooth, and keep in an airtight jar in the fridge for up to a few weeks.

Wild strawberry cupcakes

Makes 12

Ingredients
Cupcakes
  • 115 g softened butter
  • 115 g golden caster sugar
  • 2 large eggs
  • ½ teaspoon vanilla extract
  • 115 g self-raising flour with a pinch of salt
Buttercream
  • 150 g softened butter
  • 300 g icing sugar
  • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
  • 3 tablespoons milk
Method
  1. A handful of freshly picked wild strawberries.
  2. Heat the oven to 180 °C (160 °C fan) and line a 12-hole muffin tin.
  3. Beat the butter and sugar until pale, add the eggs gradually with the vanilla, then fold in the flour and salt.
  4. Divide between the cases and bake for about 15 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean.

Yarrow Achillea millefolium 2 recipes

Penne aglio olio with yarrow

Serves 4

Ingredients
  • 8 oz (about 225 g) dried penne
  • 4 tablespoons finely chopped fresh garlic
  • kosher salt
  • 3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
  • 3 tablespoons grapeseed or canola oil
  • 1 teaspoon crushed red pepper flakes, or more to taste
  • a large handful of yarrow leaves, picked from the stem and chopped to give 2 teaspoons
  • ¼ cup (about 60 ml) dry white wine
  • 4 anchovy fillets in oil, rinsed and chopped (optional)
  • Parmesan to serve
Method
  1. Pile the chopped yarrow and the chilli flakes together and mince them finely.
  2. Bring a pot of water to the boil, salt it until it tastes like the sea, and cook the penne until al dente.
  3. Meanwhile, warm the garlic with both oils and the anchovy in a 10-inch (about 25 cm) sauté pan over low heat until fragrant and lightly browned; do not let the garlic burn.
  4. Take the pan off the heat, swirl it for a minute to cool, then add the wine.
  5. Drain the pasta, add it to the pan and toss to coat; cook for a minute to drive off the raw wine flavour.
  6. Add the yarrow and chilli mixture and toss just to heat through.
  7. Divide among 4 bowls, top with Parmesan and a little more olive oil if you like, and serve at once with a big green salad.

Yew Taxus baccata 4 recipes

Yew aril and apple jam

Written for yew.

Ingredients
  • 400 g yew aril flesh, seeds taken out
  • 1 sweet-sour apple
  • 1 vanilla pod
  • 200 g 2:1 jam-setting sugar
Method
  1. Rinse the fruit and pull the flesh off every seed by hand before anything is cooked.
  2. Peel, core and chop the apple.
  3. Cook the aril flesh with the apple and the vanilla pod for about 20 minutes.
  4. Take out the vanilla pod and purée.
  5. Stir in the jam-setting sugar, bring to the boil and boil hard for about 4 minutes, then pour hot into sterilised jars.

View source recipe

Yew aril jam

Written for yew.

Ingredients
  • Separate every aril from its seed by hand
  • using the blunt side of a fork
  • do not try to boil the seeds out
Method
  1. Put the seeded flesh in a pan with just enough water to cover, bring to the boil and simmer until it reaches a jam-like consistency, which comes quickly because the flesh is very gloopy.
  2. Mashed crab apple can be added to help it set, though it dulls the pink colour.
  3. If it is too sweet, add lemon juice to taste and simmer again to jam consistency.
  4. Spoon into a sterilised jar, lay a circle of greaseproof paper on top and screw on the lid.
  5. Eat on sourdough with something sour such as goat’s cheese, or freeze in ice cubes for drinks.

View source recipe

Yew aril fruit leather

Written for wild fruit, yew included.

Method
  1. Take the seed out of every yew aril before cooking.
  2. Cook the seeded flesh, alone or with other fruit such as chopped crab apples, in a large pan on low heat with just enough water to stop it sticking, until it is thoroughly mushy.
  3. Pass it through a fine sieve and add sugar or honey to taste.
  4. Spread the purée no more than 3 mm thick on lined baking trays and dry it overnight in a very low oven, no hotter than 50 °C, with the fan on or the door slightly open.
  5. Roll the leathers in cling film or cut them up into a sealed tub; they keep a month or two in the fridge.

Yew berry tart

Makes two 10 cm tarts

Written for yew.

Ingredients
  • Before you start: arum (Arum maculatum) is poisonous raw and edible only as flour from well-roasted root
  • cherry plum kernels contain cyanogenic glycosides (see cherry plum's page)
  • the author himself calls yew berries and cherry plum kernels toxicologically ambiguous foods and the tart 'somewhat extreme and absurd'
Pastry
  • 150 g arum flour
  • 50 g sweet chestnut flour
  • 50 g wild oat flour
  • 50 g mixed wild grass seed flour
  • 100 g walnut oil or animal fat, or a mix
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) yew aril juice concentrated three times, made from seeded flesh
  • 15 ml (1 tbsp) verjuice or staghorn sumac extract
  • a little cold water if needed
Method
  1. Sift the flours into a bowl, rub in the fat or oil with your fingertips until it looks like crumbs, make a well, pour in the verjuice or sumac and the yew syrup, and mix to a smooth dough without overworking it, adding a little cold water if needed.
  2. Wrap and chill for a couple of hours.
  3. Crème pâtissière: 570 ml cherry plum kernel milk; 1.8 litres water; a large handful of dried, sun-bleached carrageen seaweed; 100 g wild pear juice concentrated five times; 60 g arum flour.
  4. Boil the seaweed in the water for 30 minutes, cool slightly, strain through muslin, and simmer the liquid gently until about 280 ml is left; set aside to cool.
  5. For the kernel milk, grind two large handfuls of washed, dried cherry plum stones, stir into about 1.1 litres of hot water for a minute, leave 15 minutes, strain, boil the liquid down by half, mix in the pear concentrate and cool.
  6. Whisk the cooled kernel milk into the seaweed extract and chill.
  7. Topping: 300 g fully ripe yew arils; 5 sweet wild apples; 250 ml (1 cup) wild apple juice; 1 heaped teaspoon of jam and 15 ml (1 tablespoon) water for the glaze.
  8. To finish: roll each half of the pastry about 2 mm thick on a work surface dusted with arum flour and line two greased 10 cm loose-bottomed flan tins about 2.5 cm deep, leaving a 0.5 cm overlap that you crimp between finger and thumb.
  9. Rest the cases an hour in the fridge or freezer, prick the bases with a fork and bake 15 minutes at 180 °C until barely coloured.
  10. Juice three apples; peel, core and thinly slice the other two and stew the slices in the juice for a couple of minutes, then cool.
  11. Re-whisk the chilled crème and spread it in the cases, leaving room for the fruit.
  12. Take the seed out of each yew aril with tweezers without damaging the seed, and set the arils on the crème in shrinking circles from the edge, leaving a 4 cm circle of crème in the middle.
  13. Fan the apple slices over that.
  14. Heat the jam with the water until it thickens and brush or drip it over the tops.
